# Differential geometry {#sec-differential-geometry}

Differential geometry is calculus on curved spaces. A manifold is a space covered by charts, open pieces that look like open sets of $\mathbb{R}^n$; on it one defines tangent vectors and vector fields, one-forms, tensors and differential forms; a metric then measures lengths, angles and volumes; a connection differentiates vectors along curves, and its failure to commute is the curvature; and the flows of vector fields describe motions of the manifold, the Killing vectors being those that preserve the metric. The chapter follows this order in five parts: charts and manifolds, vector fields and tensors, metrics, connections and curvature, flows and Killing vectors. The sphere, the torus, the plane in polar coordinates and the group $SU(2)$ are the running examples throughout.

## Charts and manifolds {#sec-charts-manifolds}

A manifold is a space that looks locally like $\mathbb{R}^n$: around every point one can lay down coordinates, but
no single coordinate system need cover the whole space. This chapter builds that idea in three sections. Charts and
atlases introduces the local coordinate systems, the charts, the collections of them that cover a space, the
atlases, and the transition maps that convert one set of coordinates into another on the overlaps, with the circle
and the sphere as running examples and the stereographic projection as the central construction. Manifolds turns
a space with a smooth atlas into a smooth manifold and defines, chart by chart, the smooth functions, maps and
curves on it, and the product of two manifolds, with the torus and the group $SU(2)$, which is the three-sphere, as
the new examples. Embeddings and Gram matrices realises manifolds as surfaces in Euclidean space through
parametrisations, studies the velocities of the coordinate curves, singles out the parametrisations that are
embeddings, and collects the inner products of the coordinate velocities in the Gram matrix, the first encounter
with a metric. Every statement is followed by three examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of
increasing difficulty with hidden solutions; the computations are carried out with SageManifolds, and the
algebraic identities behind the stereographic atlas, the $SU(2)$ determinant and the two Gram matrices are stated
as propositions. The reader who knows this material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; the conventions for
indices are those of @sec-conventions.

### Charts and atlases {#sec-charts}

A sphere cannot be covered by a single coordinate system without singular points, and on a circle any angle
coordinate necessarily jumps somewhere. The way out is to use several coordinate systems, each valid on a piece,
and to record how they are related on the overlaps. This section defines charts, coordinate curves, atlases,
transition maps and smooth atlases, with the circle and the sphere as running examples, and ends with the
proposition that makes the stereographic atlas of the sphere rigorous.

#### Charts

The first question is what a coordinate system is when the space is not $\mathbb{R}^n$ itself. The answer is a
labelling of the points of a piece of the space by $n$ numbers, one label per point and every label in an open
region used; the picture to keep is a map of a region of the Earth, flat paper labelling points of a curved surface.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-chart}
#### Chart

A **chart** on a set $M$ is a bijection $x : U \to V$ from a subset $U \subseteq M$, the chart's **domain**,
onto an open subset $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. It assigns to every point $p \in U$ its $n$ **coordinates**
$x^i(p)$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, and the inverse $x^{-1} : V \to U$ parametrises the domain by coordinates.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest curved space is the circle, and its natural coordinate is the angle. The first example shows that the
angle is a chart only after one point is removed, because a full turn would label that point twice; this one
missing point is the whole reason atlases are needed.

::: {#exm-circle-chart}
#### The angle chart on the circle

On the unit circle $S^1 = \{(X, Y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : X^2 + Y^2 = 1\}$ the angle $\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)$ is a chart
with inverse
$$
\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi),
$$ {#eq-circle-embedding}
whose domain is the circle minus the point $(1, 0)$. The coordinate $\varphi$ is periodic: $\varphi$ and
$\varphi + 2\pi$ would label the same point, which is why the chart stops short of a full turn. This periodicity
is what quantises charge in Part III.
:::

One dimension up, the sphere has the familiar latitude and longitude. The second example records them as a chart
and locates exactly where they fail: a half-meridian is missing for the same reason as the point of the circle,
and the two poles are missing for a new reason, that longitude has no value there.

::: {#exm-sphere-chart}
#### Spherical coordinates on the sphere

On the unit sphere $S^2 = \{(X, Y, Z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1\}$ the spherical coordinates
$(\theta, \varphi) \in (0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi)$ form a chart with inverse
$$
(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),
$$ {#eq-sphere-embedding}
shown in @fig-s2-chart. Its domain misses the two poles $Z = \pm 1$, where $\theta = 0, \pi$ and $\varphi$ is
undefined, and the half-meridian $\varphi = 0$. At the poles the map @eq-sphere-embedding is still defined but
ceases to be a chart: all values of $\varphi$ give the same point.
:::

![The spherical chart on $S^2$: parallels $\theta = \text{const}$ (black), meridians $\varphi = \text{const}$
(grey), the two poles where the chart degenerates (red), and the point $(\theta, \varphi) = (\pi/3, \pi/4)$ with
the two coordinate curves that lead to it from the pole and from the meridian $\varphi = 0$ (green). Generated by
`figures/s2_chart.sage`.](figures/s2_chart.png){#fig-s2-chart width=55%}

{{< interactive s2_chart 460 >}}

A different chart on the same sphere misses a single point instead of a half-meridian and two poles. The third
example is the stereographic projection, a construction from a straight line through a pole, whose domain is the
whole sphere minus that pole and whose image is the whole plane; it is the chart on which the rest of the section
is built.

::: {#exm-sphere-stereographic}
#### Stereographic coordinates on the sphere

The **stereographic projection** from the north pole $N = (0, 0, 1)$ sends a point $p$ of the sphere to the point
$(u, v)$ where the line through $N$ and $p$ meets the plane $Z = 0$ (@fig-stereographic): $(u, v) = (X, Y)/(1 - Z)$.
Solving for the point with given $(u, v)$ gives the inverse chart
$$
(u, v) \mapsto \left( \frac{2u}{1 + u^2 + v^2},\ \frac{2v}{1 + u^2 + v^2},\ \frac{u^2 + v^2 - 1}{1 + u^2 + v^2} \right),
\qquad (u, v) \in \mathbb{R}^2 ,
$$ {#eq-stereographic}
whose domain is the sphere minus $N$: as $u^2 + v^2 \to \infty$ the point approaches $N$. That the right-hand
side lies on the sphere is @prp-stereographic.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![Stereographic projection from the north pole $N$, in a plane through the axis: each point $p$ of the sphere is
sent to the point $u$ where the line $Np$ meets the equatorial plane. Points near $N$ go far away, $N$ itself has
no image, and the south pole $S$ goes to the origin. Generated by
`figures/stereographic.sage`.](figures/stereographic.svg){#fig-stereographic width=45%}

The definition asks for a bijection onto an open set, and the first exercise checks both halves of that condition
on the circle by hand. Reading off the angle of a few given points is the computational part; the argument that
no point is labelled twice and every point of the domain is labelled is the conceptual one.

::: {#exr-chart-circle-inverse}
#### Reading the angle chart

Find the coordinate $\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)$ of the points $(0, 1)$, $(-1, 0)$, $(0, -1)$ and $(\tfrac12, -
\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$ of the circle, and show that the angle chart of @exm-circle-chart is a bijection from
$S^1 \setminus \{(1, 0)\}$ onto the open interval $(0, 2\pi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\varphi = \pi/2$, $\pi$, $3\pi/2$ and $5\pi/3$ respectively, since $\cos(5\pi/3) = \tfrac12$ and $\sin(5\pi/3)
= -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Every unit vector is $(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ for exactly one $\varphi \in [0, 2\pi)$,
because $\cos\varphi$ fixes $\varphi$ up to sign and $\sin\varphi$ fixes the sign; the value $\varphi = 0$ gives
the excluded point $(1, 0)$, so $\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ is a bijection from $(0, 2\pi)$ onto
$S^1 \setminus \{(1, 0)\}$, and its inverse is the chart.
:::

Charts need not be angles. The second exercise uses the two Cartesian coordinates $X, Y$ themselves as a chart on
the upper hemisphere, where the third coordinate is recovered by a square root, and compares the result with the
stereographic chart from the south pole, which also covers the hemisphere, with Sage doing the algebra.

::: {#exr-chart-hemisphere}
#### The hemispherical chart

Show that $(X, Y)$ is a chart on the upper hemisphere $Z > 0$ of $S^2$ with image the open unit disc, write down
its inverse, and compute the south stereographic coordinates $(u', v') = (X, Y)/(1 + Z)$ of its points. Check with
Sage that the hemisphere is sent into the open unit disc $u'^2 + v'^2 < 1$ and compute the Jacobian determinant of
$(X, Y) \mapsto (u', v')$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $Z > 0$ the point is recovered from $(X, Y)$ as $(X, Y, \sqrt{1 - X^2 - Y^2})$, so the map is injective, and
the image is the open disc $X^2 + Y^2 < 1$ (the equator $Z = 0$ would give the boundary circle, which is excluded).
Substituting, $u'^2 + v'^2 = (1 - Z)/(1 + Z) < 1$, with equality only at $Z = 0$; the Jacobian determinant is
$1/(Z(1 + Z)^2)$, finite and positive on the hemisphere:

{{< sage exr-chart-hemisphere >}}
:::

Polar coordinates on the plane are a chart too, and the third exercise asks where. The point of the exercise is
that the origin can never be included, whatever intervals are chosen for $r$ and $\varphi$, and that the same
obstruction reappears for spherical coordinates on space along a whole axis.

::: {#exr-chart-polar}
#### Polar and spherical coordinates as charts

Polar coordinates $(r, \varphi) \in (0, \infty) \times (0, 2\pi)$ have inverse $(r\cos\varphi, r\sin\varphi)$.
Find the domain of this chart on the plane, explain why no choice of intervals makes the origin part of the domain
of a polar chart, and determine on which subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$ the spherical coordinates $(\rho, \theta,
\varphi) \in (0, \infty) \times (0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi)$, with inverse $\rho$ times @eq-sphere-embedding, form a
chart.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The image of $(0, \infty) \times (0, 2\pi)$ is the plane minus the closed half-line $\{Y = 0, X \geq 0\}$, which
is the domain. At the origin every value of $\varphi$ gives the same point $(0, 0)$, so a map including $r = 0$ is
not injective, and no interval for $\varphi$ can repair this; the origin is for polar coordinates what the poles
are for spherical ones. In space, $\rho$ times @eq-sphere-embedding is injective on the stated box with image
$\mathbb{R}^3$ minus the closed half-plane $\{Y = 0, X \geq 0\}$, which contains the whole $Z$-axis (where
$\theta = 0, \pi$) and the half-plane $\varphi = 0$; that complement is the domain of the chart.
:::
::::

#### Coordinate curves

A chart does more than label points: it draws a grid on its domain. The next definition names the lines of that
grid, obtained by letting one coordinate vary while the others are frozen; on a map of the Earth they are the
parallels and meridians, and their velocities will become the basic tangent vectors in @sec-tangent-vectors.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-coordinate-curve}
#### Coordinate curve

The $i$-th **coordinate curve** through a point of a chart domain is the curve along which only the coordinate
$x^i$ varies, the others being held fixed: $t \mapsto x^{-1}(x^1, \dots, x^i + t, \dots, x^n)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The spherical chart gives the grid everyone has seen on a globe. The first example identifies its two families
with the black and grey curves of the figure above, and fixes which coordinate is varying along each.

::: {#exm-coordinate-curves-sphere}
#### Parallels and meridians

In the spherical chart the $\theta$-curves are the meridians ($\varphi$ fixed) and the $\varphi$-curves are the
parallels ($\theta$ fixed), the black and grey lines of @fig-s2-chart.
:::

The same plane carries two different grids depending on the chart. The second example contrasts the rays and
circles of polar coordinates with the straight lines of Cartesian ones, a reminder that coordinate curves belong
to the chart and not to the space.

::: {#exm-coordinate-curves-polar}
#### Rays and circles

In polar coordinates on the plane the $r$-curves are rays from the origin and the $\varphi$-curves are circles
around it, the grid of @fig-jacobian-polar; in Cartesian coordinates both families are straight lines.
:::

For the stereographic chart the grid is less obvious, because it is the image of the Cartesian grid of the plane
under a map that bends lines into circles. The third example describes one family and explains the geometric
reason, which the exercises below verify algebraically.

::: {#exm-coordinate-curves-stereographic}
#### Stereographic coordinate curves

The $u$-curves of the stereographic chart are the images on the sphere of the horizontal lines $v = \text{const}$
of the plane: circles through the north pole, since every straight line of the plane projects to a circle through
$N$ (@fig-stereographic).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The torus has a chart with two angles, and its coordinate curves are the two kinds of circles one sees on a
doughnut. The first exercise asks the reader to identify both families from the formula alone and to find their
radii, which will reappear as the entries of the torus's Gram matrix.

::: {#exr-coordinate-curves-torus}
#### The coordinate curves of the torus

In the chart $(a, b)$ of the torus with inverse $(a, b) \mapsto ((R + r\cos a)\cos b,\ (R + r\cos a)\sin b,\
r\sin a)$, describe the $a$-curves and the $b$-curves as circles in space, giving the centre, the plane and the
radius of each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
An $a$-curve ($b$ fixed) is $a \mapsto (R\cos b, R\sin b, 0) + r(\cos a\cos b, \cos a\sin b, \sin a)$: a circle of
radius $r$ centred at $(R\cos b, R\sin b, 0)$ in the vertical plane through the axis at angle $b$, a circle around
the tube. A $b$-curve ($a$ fixed) is a horizontal circle of radius $R + r\cos a$ at height $r\sin a$, centred on
the axis, a circle around the axis; its radius ranges from $R - r$ on the inside to $R + r$ on the outside. These
are the red and blue circles of @fig-product-square.
:::

The claim that stereographic coordinate curves are circles through the pole can be checked exactly. The second
exercise does so for one family by exhibiting the plane that contains each curve, and then computes the radius of
the circle, which depends on the frozen coordinate; Sage handles the rational functions.

::: {#exr-coordinate-curves-stereographic-v}
#### Stereographic coordinate curves are circles

Show that the $v$-curve $u = c$ of the north stereographic chart lies on the plane $X = c(1 - Z)$, which passes
through $N$, so that it is a circle through the north pole; find the radius of that circle and identify the curve
for $c = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From @eq-stereographic with $u = c$, $X = 2c/(1 + c^2 + v^2)$ and $1 - Z = 2/(1 + c^2 + v^2)$, so $X = c(1 - Z)$
for every $v$; the plane $X + cZ = c$ contains $N = (0, 0, 1)$. Its distance from the centre of the sphere is
$|c|/\sqrt{1 + c^2}$, so it cuts the sphere in a circle of radius $\sqrt{1 - c^2/(1 + c^2)} = 1/\sqrt{1 + c^2}$.
For $c = 0$ the plane is $X = 0$ and the curve is a great circle, the meridian through the poles in the
$YZ$-plane; as $|c|$ grows the circles shrink towards the pole. The $u$-curves $v = c$ lie on $Y = c(1 - Z)$ in the
same way:

{{< sage exr-coordinate-curves-stereographic-v >}}
:::

The velocity of a coordinate curve is a vector, and comparing the velocities of the two families at a point tells
how the grid is shaped there. The third exercise computes them for polar coordinates, finds that the grid is
orthogonal, and reads off from the lengths why the chart must fail at the origin.

::: {#exr-coordinate-curves-polar-velocity}
#### Velocities of the polar coordinate curves

Compute the velocity vectors of the $r$-curve and the $\varphi$-curve of polar coordinates through the point with
coordinates $(r, \varphi)$, show that they are orthogonal, find their lengths, and interpret the length of the
$\varphi$-velocity as $r \to 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $r$-curve is $t \mapsto (r + t)(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ with velocity $(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$, of
length $1$; the $\varphi$-curve is $t \mapsto r(\cos(\varphi + t), \sin(\varphi + t))$ with velocity $r(-\sin\varphi,
\cos\varphi)$, of length $r$. Their dot product is $r(-\cos\varphi\sin\varphi + \sin\varphi\cos\varphi) = 0$. As
$r \to 0$ the $\varphi$-curves are circles shrinking to the origin and their velocity vanishes: the chart
degenerates there, exactly as the spherical chart does at the poles where the parallels shrink to a point. The two
lengths squared, $1$ and $r^2$, are the diagonal entries of the Gram matrix of polar coordinates (@def-gram).
:::
::::

#### Atlases

Since one chart rarely covers a whole space, several are needed, and the next definition asks only that together
their domains leave nothing out. The picture is a book of maps, each page covering a region of the Earth and the
pages together covering all of it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-atlas}
#### Atlas

An **atlas** on $M$ is a collection of charts, all with the same $n$, whose domains cover $M$: every point lies in
the domain of at least one chart.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the circle two angle charts suffice, as long as they miss different points. The first example takes the chart
of @exm-circle-chart together with a shifted copy and notes that SageManifolds, the Sage module used throughout
the chapter, records exactly this pair as the atlas of the circle.

::: {#exm-atlas-circle}
#### Two angle charts cover the circle

The chart $\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)$ misses $(1, 0)$, and the chart $\varphi' \in (-\pi, \pi)$ misses $(-1, 0)$;
together they cover $S^1$ (@fig-atlas-circle), and SageManifolds records them as the atlas of the circle in
`figures/atlas_circle.sage`.
:::

For the sphere there are two natural atlases of very different sizes. The second example gives the two-chart atlas
of stereographic projections from the two poles and the six-chart atlas of hemispheres, and explains with a
topological argument why one chart can never be enough.

::: {#exm-atlas-sphere}
#### Two stereographic charts cover the sphere

Projection from the north pole covers $S^2 \setminus \{N\}$ and projection from the south pole, $(u', v') =
(X, Y)/(1 + Z)$, covers $S^2 \setminus \{S\}$. Six hemispherical charts, $(X, Y)$ on the hemisphere $Z > 0$ and so
on, form another atlas. No single chart covers the sphere, which is compact, since an open subset of
$\mathbb{R}^2$ is not (@sec-compact-connected).
:::

At the other extreme, a space that is already an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ needs no gluing at all. The third
example records the one-chart atlas of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and contrasts it with the torus, where the two angle charts
of each circle factor combine into four charts.

::: {#exm-atlas-rn}
#### One chart suffices for $\mathbb{R}^n$

The identity is a chart on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and on any open subset of it, forming an atlas with one chart; the
torus $S^1 \times S^1$ needs at least four product charts built from the two angle charts of each factor.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![An atlas of the circle. Left: the two angle charts, $\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)$ (blue, missing $(1, 0)$) and
$\varphi' \in (-\pi, \pi)$ (red, drawn inside, missing $(-1, 0)$). Right: the transition map between them,
$\varphi' = \varphi$ on the upper half of the overlap and $\varphi' = \varphi - 2\pi$ on the lower half.
Generated by `figures/atlas_circle.sage`.](figures/atlas_circle.svg){#fig-atlas-circle width=85%}

The overlap of two charts is where the real information of an atlas sits, and the first exercise describes it for
the circle. It also asks for the topological reason that a single angle chart cannot do the job, the same
compactness argument as for the sphere.

::: {#exr-circle-atlas}
#### The overlap of the angle charts

Describe the overlap of the charts $\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)$ and $\varphi' \in (-\pi, \pi)$ on the circle, write
the transition map on each piece, and explain why a single angle chart cannot cover the whole circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The overlap is the circle minus the two points $(\pm 1, 0)$, two open arcs: the upper arc, where $\varphi \in
(0, \pi)$ and $\varphi' = \varphi$, and the lower arc, where $\varphi \in (\pi, 2\pi)$ and $\varphi' = \varphi -
2\pi$ (@fig-atlas-circle). A chart is a bijection onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$, which is not compact, while
the circle is compact and a continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism
(@sec-compact-connected); so no chart has the whole circle as domain.
:::

The same atlas can be built in SageManifolds, which is how every later computation on a manifold will start. The
second exercise introduces the three ingredients, a manifold, open subsets declared to cover it, and a chart on
each, and checks that the two inverse charts land on the circle and miss different points.

::: {#exr-atlas-circle-sagemanifolds}
#### The circle in SageManifolds

Build the circle in SageManifolds as a one-dimensional manifold with two open subsets $U = S^1 \setminus \{(1,
0)\}$ and $V = S^1 \setminus \{(-1, 0)\}$ declared to cover it, a chart $\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)$ on $U$ and a
chart $\varphi' \in (-\pi, \pi)$ on $V$, and the inclusion into $\mathbb{R}^2$ given in each chart by
@eq-circle-embedding. Check that both inverse charts land on $X^2 + Y^2 = 1$, that the points they miss differ,
and find the coordinates of the point $(0, -1)$ in both charts.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`Manifold(1, "S^1")` with `open_subset`, `declare_union` and `chart` sets up the atlas, and `diff_map` into
$\mathbb{R}^2$ holds the two expressions of the inclusion; `S1.atlas()` lists the two charts. The limits
$\varphi \to 0$ and $\varphi' \to \pm\pi$ give the missed points $(1, 0)$ and $(-1, 0)$, so every point lies in
$U$ or in $V$. The point $(0, -1)$ has $\varphi = 3\pi/2$ and $\varphi' = -\pi/2$:

{{< sage exr-atlas-circle-sagemanifolds >}}
:::

For the torus the count of charts is a small combinatorial puzzle. The third exercise asks the reader to find the
two circles the standard chart misses, to check that the four shifted charts cover the torus, and to show that
three of them never do, which generalises the two-chart count of the circle.

::: {#exr-atlas-torus-four}
#### Four charts for the torus

The chart $(a, b) \in (0, 2\pi)^2$ of the torus of @exr-coordinate-curves-torus misses two circles. Identify
them, show that the four charts obtained by taking $a \in (0, 2\pi)$ or $a' \in (-\pi, \pi)$ together with $b \in
(0, 2\pi)$ or $b' \in (-\pi, \pi)$ cover the torus, and show that no three of them do.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The chart misses the points with $a \equiv 0$ (the outer equator, a circle around the axis) and those with $b
\equiv 0$ (the tube circle in the half-plane $Y = 0$, $X > 0$). The chart $(a', b)$ misses $a \equiv \pi$ or
$b \equiv 0$, $(a, b')$ misses $a \equiv 0$ or $b \equiv \pi$, and $(a', b')$ misses $a \equiv \pi$ or $b \equiv
\pi$. A point missed by the first two must have $b \equiv 0$ (since $a \equiv 0$ and $a \equiv \pi$ cannot both
hold), and a point missed by the last two must have $b \equiv \pi$; no point does both, so the four charts cover.
Omitting $(a', b')$ leaves the point $a \equiv b \equiv 0$ uncovered, and by symmetry omitting any chart leaves
uncovered the point whose angles are the two values that chart alone handles; so four is the minimum for this
kind of chart, as two is for the circle.
:::
::::

#### Transition maps

Where two pages of the book of maps overlap, the same point has two sets of coordinates, and the next definition
names the rule that converts one into the other. Everything that is later required of an atlas is a requirement
on these conversion rules, which are ordinary maps between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-transition-map}
#### Transition map

Where two charts $x$ and $x'$ of an atlas overlap, the **transition map** $x' \circ x^{-1}$ converts the
coordinates of one into those of the other; it is a bijection between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$, the images
of the overlap in the two charts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest transition map is a shift. The first example reads it off the right panel of @fig-atlas-circle for
the two angle charts of the circle, where the shift is zero on one arc of the overlap and $2\pi$ on the other.

::: {#exm-transition-circle}
#### Between the angle charts

On the overlap of the two angle charts of the circle, $\varphi' = \varphi$ for $\varphi < \pi$ and $\varphi' =
\varphi - 2\pi$ for $\varphi > \pi$ (@fig-atlas-circle): a shift by a constant on each of the two arcs.
:::

For the two stereographic charts the transition map is a classical transformation of the plane. The second
example identifies it as the inversion in the unit circle, an involution, and points to the proposition and the
exercise where this is verified.

::: {#exm-transition-stereographic}
#### Between the stereographic charts

On the sphere minus both poles the transition map between the north and south stereographic charts is the
inversion in the unit circle, $(u', v') = (u, v)/(u^2 + v^2)$ (@prp-stereographic, @exr-stereographic-transition);
it is its own inverse.
:::

Charts of different kinds can be compared too. The third example gives the transition map from spherical to
stereographic coordinates, a trigonometric formula this time, and notes where the equator goes; it is the formula
used whenever a function given in spherical coordinates is needed in stereographic ones.

::: {#exm-transition-spherical}
#### From spherical to stereographic

On the overlap of the spherical chart and the north stereographic chart, $u = \sin\theta\cos\varphi/(1 -
\cos\theta)$ and $v = \sin\theta\sin\varphi/(1 - \cos\theta)$ (@exr-sphere-chart-transition); the equator
$\theta = \pi/2$ goes to the unit circle $u^2 + v^2 = 1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Two hemispherical charts overlap on a quarter of the sphere, and their transition map involves a square root. The
first exercise asks for the overlap as seen from each chart, for the transition map and for its Jacobian
determinant, all by hand, as a warm-up for the SageManifolds computations that follow.

::: {#exr-transition-hemispheres}
#### Between two hemispherical charts

Consider the hemispherical charts $(X, Y)$ on $Z > 0$ and $(Y, Z)$ on $X > 0$. Describe the overlap in each
chart, compute the transition map from the first to the second and its Jacobian determinant, and check that the
determinant does not vanish on the overlap.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The overlap is the quarter sphere $X > 0$, $Z > 0$. In the first chart it is the half disc $\{X > 0,\ X^2 + Y^2
< 1\}$, in the second the half disc $\{Z > 0,\ Y^2 + Z^2 < 1\}$. The transition map is $(X, Y) \mapsto (Y,
\sqrt{1 - X^2 - Y^2})$, with Jacobian matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -X/Z & -Y/Z \end{pmatrix}$ and
determinant $X/Z$, which is positive on the overlap and tends to $0$ or $\infty$ only on its boundary, where one of
the charts ends.
:::

Transition maps are what SageManifolds' `transition_map` computes, and the second exercise applies it to the
spherical and stereographic charts. The Jacobian determinant and the image of the equator are the two checks, and
both confirm the formulas quoted in @exm-transition-spherical.

::: {#exr-sphere-chart-transition}
#### From spherical to stereographic coordinates

Compute the transition map from the spherical chart to the north stereographic chart and its Jacobian
determinant, and find the image of the equator.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $(u, v) = (X, Y)/(1 - Z)$ and @eq-sphere-embedding, $u = \sin\theta\cos\varphi/(1 - \cos\theta)$, $v =
\sin\theta\sin\varphi/(1 - \cos\theta)$; the determinant is $-\sin\theta/(1 - \cos\theta)^2$, non-zero on the
chart domain; $u^2 + v^2 = \sin^2\theta/(1 - \cos\theta)^2$ equals $1$ at $\theta = \pi/2$:

{{< sage exr-sphere-chart-transition >}}
:::

The third exercise builds the full stereographic atlas of the sphere in SageManifolds and establishes everything
the examples claimed about it: the transition map is the inversion, its Jacobian never vanishes, and the inverse
chart lands on the sphere. The same algebraic identities return as a proposition at the end of the section.

::: {#exr-stereographic-transition}
#### The stereographic atlas

Build the sphere with its two stereographic charts in SageManifolds, compute the transition map and its Jacobian
determinant, and check that the north chart's inverse lands on the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The south projection sends $p = (X, Y, Z)$ to $(u', v') = (X, Y)/(1 + Z)$. Substituting @eq-stereographic,
$1 + Z = 2(u^2 + v^2)/(1 + u^2 + v^2)$, so $u' = u/(u^2 + v^2)$, $v' = v/(u^2 + v^2)$: the inversion in the unit
circle, a smooth bijection of the punctured plane (its own inverse) with Jacobian determinant $-1/(u^2 + v^2)^2
\neq 0$. In SageManifolds:

{{< sage exr-stereographic-transition >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The inversion undoing itself is the Lean theorem below.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.inversion_inversion >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

#### Smooth atlases

An atlas lets one speak of continuity, but calculus on the space needs more: a function that is differentiable in
one chart should be differentiable in every overlapping chart. The next definition imposes exactly the condition
that makes this automatic, smoothness of the transition maps, and names the atlases that agree about it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-smooth-atlas}
#### Smooth atlas

An atlas is **smooth** if every transition map is a diffeomorphism (@def-diffeomorphism) between open subsets
of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Two smooth atlases are **compatible** if their union is again smooth; a compatible atlas defines
the same notion of smoothness on $M$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A shift by a constant is as smooth as a map can be. The first example disposes of the circle in one line, reading
off the derivative of the transition map on each piece of the overlap.

::: {#exm-smooth-atlas-circle}
#### The circle

The transition map of @exm-transition-circle is a shift on each piece of the overlap, with derivative $1$: the angle
atlas of the circle is smooth.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** The derivative of the transition map is checked in `figures/atlas_circle.sage`.
:::

For the sphere two facts are needed, that the stereographic atlas is smooth and that the spherical chart may be
added to it. The second example reads both off the Jacobian determinants computed in the exercises above, which
are non-zero wherever the charts overlap.

::: {#exm-smooth-atlas-sphere}
#### The sphere

The inversion of @exm-transition-stereographic is smooth on the punctured plane with Jacobian determinant
$-1/(u^2 + v^2)^2 \neq 0$ and is its own inverse, so the stereographic atlas is smooth; the spherical chart is
compatible with it, since @exm-transition-spherical has Jacobian determinant $-\sin\theta/(1 - \cos\theta)^2 \neq
0$ on its domain (@exr-sphere-chart-transition).
:::

Smoothness is a genuine restriction, and the third example shows an atlas that fails it on the simplest possible
space. Two one-chart atlases on the real line are each smooth, but their union is not, and the lesson is that
the same set can carry different smooth structures.

::: {#exm-smooth-atlas-not}
#### An atlas that is not smooth

On the real line, the identity chart and the chart $y = x^3$ each form an atlas, but their union is not smooth: the
transition map $x = y^{1/3}$ is not differentiable at $0$ (@exm-diffeo-cube). The two charts define different
smooth structures on the same set, and a function smooth in one need not be smooth in the other.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Cartesian and polar coordinates on the plane are the first pair of charts every reader has converted between,
and the first exercise checks that they are compatible in the sense just defined. SageManifolds computes the
transition map and its Jacobian; the only subtlety is writing the inverse so that the angle lands in $(0, 2\pi)$.

::: {#exr-smooth-atlas-polar}
#### Cartesian and polar coordinates are compatible

On the plane minus the half-line $\{y = 0, x \geq 0\}$, define the Cartesian chart $(x, y)$ and the polar chart
$(r, \varphi)$ in SageManifolds, give the transition map $(r, \varphi) \mapsto (r\cos\varphi, r\sin\varphi)$ and
its inverse, and compute the Jacobian determinant to show that the two charts form a smooth atlas.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Jacobian matrix of the transition map is $\begin{pmatrix} \cos\varphi & -r\sin\varphi \\ \sin\varphi &
r\cos\varphi \end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $r > 0$ (@prp-polar-jacobian), and the inverse $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$,
$\varphi = \operatorname{atan2}(-y, -x) + \pi$ is smooth away from the removed half-line and takes values in
$(0, 2\pi)$; both maps are smooth with smooth inverse, so the atlas is smooth:

{{< sage exr-smooth-atlas-polar >}}
:::

The non-smooth atlas of @exm-smooth-atlas-not deserves a closer look, because it shows that "smooth function" is
a property of the atlas and not of the set. The second exercise asks which functions are smooth for the cubic
chart and then shows that the two smooth structures, though incompatible, are nevertheless diffeomorphic.

::: {#exr-smooth-atlas-cube}
#### Two smooth structures on the line

Let $\mathbb{R}_x$ be the real line with the identity chart $x$ and $\mathbb{R}_y$ the real line with the single
chart $y = x^3$. Show that the function $p \mapsto x(p)$ is smooth on $\mathbb{R}_x$ but not on $\mathbb{R}_y$,
while $p \mapsto x(p)^3$ is smooth on both; then show that the identity map $\mathbb{R}_x \to \mathbb{R}_y$ is not
a diffeomorphism, but the map $\Phi : \mathbb{R}_x \to \mathbb{R}_y$ sending $p$ to the point $q$ with $y(q) =
x(p)$ is.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A function is smooth if its expression in the chart is smooth. On $\mathbb{R}_y$ the function $x$ reads $y^{1/3}$,
not differentiable at $y = 0$, so it is not smooth there, while $x^3$ reads $y$, which is smooth; on
$\mathbb{R}_x$ both $x$ and $x^3$ are smooth. The identity map has chart expression $y \circ \mathrm{id} \circ
x^{-1}(s) = s^3$, smooth, but its inverse has expression $s^{1/3}$, which is not: a smooth bijection that is not a
diffeomorphism. The map $\Phi$ has expression $y \circ \Phi \circ x^{-1}(s) = s$, the identity of $\mathbb{R}$, so
$\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism: $\mathbb{R}_x$ and $\mathbb{R}_y$ are the same manifold presented with different
coordinates, as $q = p^{1/3}$ shows.
:::

Compatibility of the hemispherical charts with the stereographic atlas is the last check needed for the sphere,
after which every chart of the section belongs to one smooth structure. The third exercise computes the
transition map, which contains a square root, and shows that its Jacobian determinant is nevertheless finite and
non-zero on the whole overlap.

::: {#exr-smooth-atlas-hemisphere-stereographic}
#### The hemispherical chart is compatible with the stereographic atlas

Compute in SageManifolds the transition map from the hemispherical chart $(X, Y)$ on $Z > 0$ to the north
stereographic chart, $(u, v) = (X, Y)/(1 - \sqrt{1 - X^2 - Y^2})$, and its inverse; show that the Jacobian
determinant equals $-1/(Z(1 - Z)^2)$ with $Z = \sqrt{1 - X^2 - Y^2}$, and conclude.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The overlap is the upper hemisphere minus $N$, where $0 < Z < 1$; there the determinant $-1/(Z(1 - Z)^2)$ is
finite and non-zero, and the inverse $(X, Y) = (2u, 2v)/(1 + u^2 + v^2)$ is a rational map, so the transition map
is a diffeomorphism and the hemispherical chart is compatible with the stereographic atlas. The hemisphere
corresponds to the exterior $u^2 + v^2 > 1$ of the unit circle, where the point $(X, Y) = (3/5, 0)$ becomes
$(u, v) = (3, 0)$:

{{< sage exr-smooth-atlas-hemisphere-stereographic >}}
:::
::::

#### The stereographic atlas

The examples of this section rested on three algebraic facts about the stereographic charts that were quoted
rather than proved: the inverse chart lands on the sphere, the transition map is the inversion, and the inversion
undoes itself. The following proposition collects them, and each is a polynomial identity in $u$ and $v$ once the
denominators $1 + u^2 + v^2$ and $u^2 + v^2$ are cleared.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-stereographic}
#### The stereographic chart

The point @eq-stereographic lies on the unit sphere for every $(u, v)$; its south stereographic coordinates
$(X, Y)/(1 + Z)$ are the inversion $(u, v)/(u^2 + v^2)$; and the inversion applied twice is the identity away from
the origin.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.stereoInv_on_sphere`, `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.south_of_north` and
`KaluzaKlein.Geometry.inversion_inversion`, each proved by `field_simp` and `ring` after clearing the denominators.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.south_of_north >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The proposition becomes concrete on a few points. The first example follows the unit circle of the plane, which
the inversion fixes pointwise, and finds that it corresponds to the equator, the one curve on which both
stereographic charts assign the same coordinates.

::: {#exm-stereographic-equator}
#### The equator has the same coordinates in both charts

For $(u, v) = (1, 0)$ the point @eq-stereographic is $(1, 0, 0)$, on the equator, and its south coordinates are
$(1, 0)/1 = (1, 0)$: the inversion fixes the unit circle. In general $u^2 + v^2 = 1$ gives $Z = 0$, so the equator
is the unit circle in both charts, and the two charts agree there and nowhere else, since $(u, v) = (u, v)/(u^2 +
v^2)$ forces $u^2 + v^2 = 1$.
:::

The poles are where one chart ends, and the second example checks that the proposition knows this. The origin of
the north chart is the south pole, which the inversion cannot handle, and this is consistent, since the south
pole has no south stereographic coordinates.

::: {#exm-stereographic-poles}
#### The poles and the origin

For $(u, v) = (0, 0)$ the point @eq-stereographic is $(0, 0, -1) = S$, and the inversion is undefined there,
exactly as it should be: $S$ lies outside the domain of the south chart, and the transition map is only defined
on the overlap $S^2 \setminus \{N, S\}$, the punctured plane in either chart. Symmetrically the north pole has
south coordinates $(0, 0)$ and no north coordinates; "far away" in one chart is "near the origin" in the other.
:::

Writing $w = u + iv$ turns the plane into the complex plane and the inversion into a one-line formula. The third
example records it and points ahead to the Riemann sphere, where the south chart is conjugated so that the
transition map becomes the holomorphic map $w \mapsto 1/w$.

::: {#exm-stereographic-riemann-sphere}
#### Complex notation and the Riemann sphere

With $w = u + iv$ the inversion is $w' = 1/\bar w$, since $1/\bar w = w/|w|^2 = (u + iv)/(u^2 + v^2)$. Composing
the south chart with the reflection $v' \mapsto -v'$ turns the transition map into $w \mapsto 1/w$, a holomorphic
map (@exr-stereographic-complex); the sphere with this pair of complex charts is the Riemann sphere of
@exm-riemann-sphere, on which rational functions become smooth maps.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks for the geometry of the inversion in words: which points it fixes, which it swaps, and
what this means on the sphere. The answers are short consequences of the formula $(u, v)/(u^2 + v^2)$ and of the
third component of @eq-stereographic.

::: {#exr-stereographic-fixed-circle}
#### What the inversion does to the plane

Show that the inversion $(u, v) \mapsto (u, v)/(u^2 + v^2)$ fixes every point of the unit circle, exchanges the
inside and the outside of that circle, and preserves every ray from the origin; translate each statement into one
about the two hemispheres of the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $u^2 + v^2 = 1$ the formula returns $(u, v)$ itself. A point at distance $\rho$ from the origin is sent to the
point at distance $1/\rho$ on the same ray, since $(u, v)/\rho^2$ is a positive multiple of $(u, v)$ of length
$1/\rho$; so $\rho < 1$ goes to $1/\rho > 1$ and conversely, and rays are preserved. On the sphere, $Z = (\rho^2 -
1)/(\rho^2 + 1)$ is negative for $\rho < 1$: the inside of the unit circle in the north chart is the southern
hemisphere, which the south chart sees as the outside of its unit circle, and the rays are the meridians, which
both charts draw as rays from the origin.
:::

The complex notation of @exm-stereographic-riemann-sphere can be checked symbolically. The second exercise
separates real and imaginary parts, computes the two Jacobian determinants, one negative and one positive, and
verifies the Cauchy-Riemann equations for $1/w$, which is why the reflected transition map is holomorphic.

::: {#exr-stereographic-complex}
#### The transition map as a complex function

With $w = u + iv$, check that $1/\bar w$ has real and imaginary parts $u/(u^2 + v^2)$ and $v/(u^2 + v^2)$; compute
the Jacobian determinant of the inversion and of the map $w \mapsto 1/w$ (the inversion followed by $v \mapsto -
v$); and verify that $1/w$ satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations while $1/\bar w$ does not preserve orientation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1/\bar w = w/(w\bar w) = (u + iv)/(u^2 + v^2)$. The inversion has Jacobian determinant $-1/(u^2 + v^2)^2 < 0$, so
it reverses orientation; composing with the reflection gives $w \mapsto 1/w = (u - iv)/(u^2 + v^2)$, with real part
$P = u/(u^2 + v^2)$ and imaginary part $Q = -v/(u^2 + v^2)$ satisfying $P_u = Q_v$ and $P_v = -Q_u$, and with
Jacobian determinant $1/(u^2 + v^2)^2 = |f'(w)|^2$ for $f(w) = 1/w$, positive:

{{< sage exr-stereographic-complex >}}
:::

Nothing in the construction depends on the radius being one, and the third exercise redoes it for a sphere of
radius $a$. The projection formulas acquire factors of $a$, and the transition map becomes the inversion in the
circle of radius $a$, which reduces to the proposition when $a = 1$.

::: {#exr-stereographic-radius}
#### Stereographic projection of a sphere of radius $a$

For the sphere $X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = a^2$ and the projection from $N = (0, 0, a)$ onto the plane $Z = 0$, find the
coordinates $(u, v)$ of a point $(X, Y, Z)$, the inverse map, and the transition map to the projection from the
south pole $(0, 0, -a)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The line from $N$ through $p$ meets $Z = 0$ at $(u, v) = a(X, Y)/(a - Z)$. Writing $\rho^2 = u^2 + v^2$, the
inverse is $(X, Y, Z) = (2a^2u, 2a^2v, a(\rho^2 - a^2))/(\rho^2 + a^2)$, which satisfies $X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = a^2$
since $4a^4\rho^2 + a^2(\rho^2 - a^2)^2 = a^2(\rho^2 + a^2)^2$. The south projection is $(u', v') = a(X, Y)/(a +
Z)$, and $a + Z = 2a\rho^2/(\rho^2 + a^2)$ gives $(u', v') = a^2(u, v)/\rho^2$: the inversion in the circle of
radius $a$, which fixes that circle (the image of the equator) and is again its own inverse. Setting $a = 1$
recovers @prp-stereographic.
:::
::::

### Manifolds {#sec-manifolds}

With charts and atlases in hand, a manifold is simply a space with a smooth atlas, and everything smooth on it is
defined chart by chart. This section defines smooth manifolds, smooth functions and maps on them, curves, and
product manifolds, the construction behind cylinders, tori and every space of the form "one space times another".
The running examples are the circle, the sphere, the torus and the group $SU(2)$, which is the three-sphere.

#### Smooth manifolds

The definition that the whole chapter has been preparing can now be stated in one sentence: a manifold is a space
with a smooth atlas. The picture is the sphere with its stereographic charts; the one technical condition added,
that the space be Hausdorff, rules out pathologies in which two distinct points cannot be separated by open sets.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-manifold}
#### Smooth manifold

A **smooth manifold of dimension $n$** is a Hausdorff topological space $M$ (@def-hausdorff) with a smooth atlas
(@def-smooth-atlas) of charts onto open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$, whose charts are homeomorphisms onto their
images. Any notion defined in one chart and invariant under smooth changes of coordinates is a property of the
manifold itself; that is the point of the definition.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The Lean library works inside one chart at a time (`Fin n → ℝ`), and a statement about a manifold is a statement
about one of its charts together with a hypothesis excluding the points where the chart degenerates.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Every space of the previous section now qualifies. The first example lists them with their dimensions and the
atlases that were shown to be smooth, so that the reader can see the definition is not empty.

::: {#exm-manifolds-list}
#### Manifolds met so far

The circle (dimension $1$, two angle charts), the sphere (dimension $2$, two stereographic charts or several
spherical ones), the plane and $\mathbb{R}^n$ (one chart, the identity), and any open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
:::

The torus is the first genuinely new surface, and the second example gives it a chart with two angles whose
domain misses two circles, completed to an atlas by shifted copies exactly as for the circle. Its product
structure will be made explicit at the end of the section.

::: {#exm-torus-chart}
#### The torus

The torus is the surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$ swept by a circle of radius $r$ whose centre moves on a circle of
radius $R > r$ in the $XY$-plane. With the angle $a$ around the tube and the angle $b$ around the axis,
$$
(a, b) \mapsto \left( (R + r\cos a)\cos b,\ (R + r\cos a)\sin b,\ r\sin a \right), \qquad a, b \in (0, 2\pi),
$$ {#eq-torus-embedding}
is the inverse of a chart whose domain misses two circles; shifted angle charts complete the atlas as for $S^1$
(@fig-product-square). The torus is a manifold of dimension $2$, and it reappears in Part VI as the internal space
of toroidal reductions.
:::

The third example is a manifold that is also a group, the first of many in this book. A unitary $2 \times 2$ matrix
of determinant one is determined by two complex numbers on the unit sphere of $\mathbb{C}^2$, so $SU(2)$ is the
three-sphere; the Euler angles provide a chart with the same kind of degeneration as spherical coordinates.

::: {#exm-su2-chart}
#### The group $SU(2)$ as the three-sphere

The group $SU(2)$ of $2 \times 2$ unitary matrices of determinant one (groups are defined in @sec-groups) is the
set of matrices
$$
g = \begin{pmatrix} a & -\bar b \\ b & \bar a \end{pmatrix}, \qquad a, b \in \mathbb{C}, \quad |a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1,
$$ {#eq-su2-matrix}
since $\det g = |a|^2 + |b|^2$ (@prp-su2-det), and $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$ says that $(\operatorname{Re} a,
\operatorname{Im} a, \operatorname{Re} b, \operatorname{Im} b)$ lies on the unit sphere $S^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$:
$SU(2)$ is a manifold of dimension $3$. The **Euler angles** $(\theta, \varphi, \psi) \in (0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi)
\times (0, 4\pi)$ are a chart, with inverse
$$
g(\theta, \varphi, \psi) = e^{\varphi T_3}\, e^{\theta T_1}\, e^{\psi T_3},
$$ {#eq-euler-angles}
where $T_a$ are the matrices of @sec-conventions-lie and $e^A = \sum_k A^k/k!$ is the matrix exponential; the
exponentials are computed in @sec-exponential. The chart degenerates at $\theta = 0, \pi$, where only
$\varphi \pm \psi$ matters, as the spherical chart does at the poles. The range $\psi \in (0, 4\pi)$, twice that of
$\varphi$, reflects that $SU(2)$ covers the rotation group $SO(3)$ twice (@sec-lie-groups).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The claim that $SU(2)$ consists exactly of the matrices @eq-su2-matrix is a small exercise in linear algebra, and
the first exercise asks for it in both directions. The determinant identity is quoted from the proposition that
follows; the rest is multiplying out $g^\dagger g$ and comparing two formulas for the inverse.

::: {#exr-su2-sphere}
#### $SU(2)$ is the three-sphere

Show that a matrix of the form @eq-su2-matrix is unitary with determinant one exactly when $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$,
and that every $SU(2)$ matrix has this form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g^\dagger g = (|a|^2 + |b|^2)\, 1$ by direct multiplication, and $\det g = |a|^2 + |b|^2$ (@prp-su2-det), so $g
\in SU(2)$ iff $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$. Conversely, for a unitary $g = \begin{pmatrix} a & c \\ b & d \end{pmatrix}$ of
determinant one, $g^{-1} = g^\dagger$ and $g^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} d & -c \\ -b & a \end{pmatrix}$ give $d = \bar
a$, $c = -\bar b$.
:::

Many manifolds arise as open pieces of known ones, and the second exercise establishes the general principle and
applies it to the group of invertible matrices. The argument is that charts restrict to open subsets, and the
application is that a continuous function's non-zero set is open.

::: {#exr-manifold-open-subset}
#### Open subsets are manifolds

Show that an open subset $W$ of a manifold $M$ of dimension $n$ is itself a manifold of dimension $n$. Deduce that
the general linear group $GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ of invertible $n \times n$ matrices is a manifold of dimension $n^2$,
and that the non-zero complex numbers form a manifold of dimension $2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Restrict every chart $x : U \to V$ of $M$ to $U \cap W$: since $x$ is a homeomorphism onto $V$, the image $x(U
\cap W)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the restrictions are bijections onto open sets, their transition maps are
restrictions of the original ones, hence smooth, and the Hausdorff property is inherited; so $W$ has a smooth
atlas of dimension $n$. The determinant is a polynomial in the entries, hence continuous (@def-continuous-map),
so $GL(n, \mathbb{R}) = \det^{-1}(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\})$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ and is a manifold of
dimension $n^2$ with the identity chart. Likewise $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\} = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$ is
open in the plane, a manifold of dimension $2$; it is the polar-coordinate domain of @exr-chart-polar with the
half-line put back.
:::

The three-sphere of @exm-su2-chart deserves its own atlas, and the third exercise builds one that does not use
Euler angles at all: stereographic projection works in every dimension. SageManifolds verifies that the inverse
chart lands on $S^3$ and that the transition map is the inversion in the unit sphere of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

::: {#exr-manifold-s3-charts}
#### A stereographic atlas for $S^3$

Build $S^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ in SageManifolds with the north stereographic chart $(u, v, w) \mapsto (2u, 2v,
2w, \rho^2 - 1)/(1 + \rho^2)$, $\rho^2 = u^2 + v^2 + w^2$, and the south chart $(X_1, X_2, X_3)/(1 + X_4)$. Check
that the inverse chart lands on $S^3$, compute the transition map and its Jacobian determinant, and conclude that
$S^3$, hence $SU(2)$, is a smooth manifold of dimension $3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The sum of squares of the four components is $(4\rho^2 + (\rho^2 - 1)^2)/(1 + \rho^2)^2 = 1$. The south
coordinates of the point are $(u, v, w)/\rho^2$, the inversion in the unit sphere of $\mathbb{R}^3$, with Jacobian
determinant $-1/\rho^6$, non-zero on the overlap $\rho \neq 0$; the two charts cover $S^3$ and form a smooth
atlas. Under the identification $(X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4) = (\operatorname{Re} a, \operatorname{Im} a,
\operatorname{Re} b, \operatorname{Im} b)$ this is an atlas of $SU(2)$ with two charts, in place of the
Euler-angle chart that degenerates at $\theta = 0, \pi$:

{{< sage exr-manifold-s3-charts >}}
:::
::::

#### The determinant of $SU(2)$

The description of $SU(2)$ as a three-sphere rests on one identity, that the determinant of the matrix
@eq-su2-matrix is the squared length of $(a, b) \in \mathbb{C}^2$. The proposition records it; the proof expands
the $2 \times 2$ determinant and rewrites $|a|^2$ and $|b|^2$ as $\bar a a$ and $\bar b b$, after which the identity
is a polynomial one.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-su2-det}
#### The determinant of the $SU(2)$ matrix form

For $g$ as in @eq-su2-matrix, $\det g = |a|^2 + |b|^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2Matrix_det`, proved by expanding the determinant, rewriting $|a|^2 = \bar a a$ and
$|b|^2 = \bar b b$, and `ring`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2Matrix_det >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two simplest points of $S^3$ give the two simplest matrices. The first example evaluates the form at $(a, b)
= (1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ and recognises the identity and a rotation by a right angle, both with determinant one as
the proposition predicts.

::: {#exm-su2-det-identity}
#### The identity and a quarter turn

For $a = 1$, $b = 0$ the matrix @eq-su2-matrix is the identity, with $\det = 1 + 0$. For $a = 0$, $b = 1$ it is
$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, the rotation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by a right angle read as a complex
matrix, again with $\det = 0 + 1 = 1$; its square is $-1$, so it plays the role of $i$ inside $SU(2)$. Both points
lie on $S^3$ and both are in $SU(2)$.
:::

The one-parameter families $e^{tT_a}$ that build the Euler angles are also of the form @eq-su2-matrix. The second
example computes two of them and checks that $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$ is the determinant identity in disguise; the
third exponential and the full product are left to an exercise.

::: {#exm-su2-det-exponentials}
#### The exponentials $e^{tT_3}$ and $e^{tT_1}$

With $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ (@sec-conventions-lie), $e^{tT_3} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{-it/2}, e^{it/2})$
is the form @eq-su2-matrix with $a = e^{-it/2}$, $b = 0$, and $e^{tT_1} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(t/2) & -
i\sin(t/2) \\ -i\sin(t/2) & \cos(t/2) \end{pmatrix}$ is the form with $a = \cos(t/2)$, $b = -i\sin(t/2)$; in
both cases $\det = |a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$, by $\cos^2(t/2) + \sin^2(t/2) = 1$ in the second. The product
@eq-euler-angles of three such matrices is verified in @exr-su2-det-euler.
:::

The identity holds for every $a, b$, not only on the unit sphere, and the third example uses this. Matrices of the
form @eq-su2-matrix with $(a, b) \neq 0$ have positive determinant and can be rescaled onto $SU(2)$; they are the
non-zero quaternions, and $SU(2)$ is their unit sphere.

::: {#exm-su2-det-scaling}
#### Rescaling onto the sphere

For $a = 2$, $b = 1$ the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $5 = |a|^2 + |
b|^2$ and is not in $SU(2)$, but dividing by $\sqrt5$ gives a matrix of the same form with determinant $1$. Every
non-zero $(a, b) \in \mathbb{C}^2$ can be rescaled in this way, so the matrices @eq-su2-matrix with $(a, b) \neq
0$ form a four-dimensional real manifold ($\mathbb{R}^4 \setminus \{0\}$, open) that contains $SU(2)$ as its unit
sphere; they are closed under products (@exr-su2-det-product), and they are the non-zero quaternions.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The inverse of an $SU(2)$ matrix should again be an $SU(2)$ matrix, and the first exercise finds it explicitly.
The computation is the one of @exr-su2-sphere read backwards, and it identifies which point of the three-sphere
the inverse corresponds to.

::: {#exr-su2-det-inverse}
#### The inverse in $SU(2)$

For $g$ of the form @eq-su2-matrix with $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$, show that $g^{-1} = g^\dagger$ and write $g^{-1}$ in
the form @eq-su2-matrix; which point of $S^3$ is it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g^\dagger = \begin{pmatrix} \bar a & \bar b \\ -b & a \end{pmatrix}$ and $g^\dagger g = (|a|^2 + |b|^2)\, 1 =
1$, so $g^{-1} = g^\dagger$; it is the form @eq-su2-matrix with $(a, b)$ replaced by $(\bar a, -b)$, the point
$(\operatorname{Re} a, -\operatorname{Im} a, -\operatorname{Re} b, -\operatorname{Im} b)$ of $S^3$, the
reflection of $(a, b)$ in the first coordinate axis. Its determinant is again $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$ by
@prp-su2-det.
:::

The Euler-angle formula @eq-euler-angles was asserted to produce the matrix @eq-su2-matrix with specific $a$ and
$b$. The second exercise computes the three matrix exponentials in Sage, multiplies them, and checks the two
entries, the determinant and unitarity; it also shows what happens at $\theta = 0$, where the chart degenerates.

::: {#exr-su2-det-euler}
#### The Euler-angle matrix

With $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$, compute the matrix exponentials $e^{\varphi T_3}$, $e^{\theta T_1}$ and
$e^{\psi T_3}$ in Sage, form the product @eq-euler-angles, and show that it has the form @eq-su2-matrix with $a =
\cos(\theta/2)\, e^{-i(\varphi + \psi)/2}$ and $b = -i\sin(\theta/2)\, e^{i(\varphi - \psi)/2}$; verify $\det g
= 1$ and $g^\dagger g = 1$, and evaluate $g$ at $\theta = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{\varphi T_3} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\varphi/2}, e^{i\varphi/2})$ and $e^{\theta T_1} = \cos(\theta/2)\,
1 - i\sin(\theta/2)\,\sigma_1$, since $\sigma_1^2 = 1$ makes the exponential series split into a cosine and a sine.
The product is $\begin{pmatrix} \cos(\theta/2) e^{-i(\varphi + \psi)/2} & -i\sin(\theta/2) e^{-i(\varphi -
\psi)/2} \\ -i\sin(\theta/2) e^{i(\varphi - \psi)/2} & \cos(\theta/2) e^{i(\varphi + \psi)/2} \end{pmatrix}$,
whose entries are $a$, $-\bar b$, $b$, $\bar a$ with the stated $a, b$; $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = \cos^2(\theta/2) +
\sin^2(\theta/2) = 1$. At $\theta = 0$ the matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i(\varphi + \psi)/2}, e^{i(\varphi +
\psi)/2})$, which depends on $\varphi + \psi$ only. Sage computes the exponentials exactly, with a `trig_reduce`
to collapse the half-angle expressions:

{{< sage exr-su2-det-euler >}}
:::

That $SU(2)$ is a group needs the product of two matrices of the form @eq-su2-matrix to have the same form and
determinant one. The third exercise proves this with Sage for symbolic $a, b, a', b'$ and recognises the result as
the multiplication rule of quaternions and the four-square identity of Euler.

::: {#exr-su2-det-product}
#### Products of $SU(2)$ matrices

Show with Sage that the product of two matrices of the form @eq-su2-matrix, with parameters $(a, b)$ and $(a',
b')$, is again of that form with parameters $(aa' - \bar b b',\ ba' + \bar a b')$, and that the determinant is
multiplicative: $|aa' - \bar b b'|^2 + |ba' + \bar a b'|^2 = (|a|^2 + |b|^2)(|a'|^2 + |b'|^2)$. Conclude that
$SU(2)$ is closed under products.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Writing $a = a_1 + ia_2$ and so on with real symbols and expanding, the product has top row $(aa' - \bar b b',\ -
(\bar a \bar b' + \bar b a'))$ and bottom row $(ba' + \bar a b',\ \bar a\bar a' - b\bar b')$, which is the form
with $a'' = aa' - \bar b b'$, $b'' = ba' + \bar a b'$. The determinant identity is @prp-su2-det applied to $g g'$
together with $\det(gg') = \det g \det g'$, and expanding both sides in the eight real variables confirms it; with
$|a|^2 + |b|^2 = |a'|^2 + |b'|^2 = 1$ the product again has $|a''|^2 + |b''|^2 = 1$. The rule $(a, b)(a', b')
= (aa' - \bar b b', ba' + \bar a b')$ is the multiplication of quaternions $a + bj$, and the identity is Euler's
four-square identity:

{{< sage exr-su2-det-product >}}
:::
::::

#### Functions, maps and curves

A function on a manifold has no formula until a chart is chosen, and the next definition says when such a function
deserves to be called smooth: its formula in every chart must be smooth. The smoothness of the transition maps is
what makes it enough to check one chart around each point.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-smooth-function}
#### Smooth function on a manifold

A **function** $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is **smooth** if its expression $f(x^1, \dots, x^n)$ in every chart is a
smooth function of the coordinates (@def-smooth-map). Since transition maps are smooth, it suffices to check one
chart around each point.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The height of a point of the sphere is the first example, a single function with two very different formulas. The
example gives both, notes that they agree where the charts overlap, and locates the maximum, which happens to be
the one point the stereographic formula does not reach.

::: {#exm-height-function}
#### The height on the sphere

$Z = \cos\theta$ in spherical coordinates and $Z = (u^2 + v^2 - 1)/(1 + u^2 + v^2)$ in stereographic coordinates:
both expressions are smooth, and they agree on the overlap (@exr-height-charts). Its maximum $Z = 1$ is the north
pole.
:::

A coordinate is not automatically a function on the manifold, and the second example makes the point for the
angle on the circle. The angle is only defined on a chart domain and jumps at the missing point, while its cosine
and sine extend smoothly; this is the origin of the periodicity conditions on fields on a circle.

::: {#exm-angle-not-function}
#### The angle is not a function

$\varphi$ itself is not a smooth function on the circle: it jumps by $2\pi$ at the point the chart misses. The
functions $\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$ are smooth on the whole circle. Fields on a circle must be periodic in
$\varphi$, which is the origin of the Kaluza-Klein tower in Part III.
:::

On a group of matrices the trace is the most natural function, and the third example writes it in Euler angles.
The formula is manifestly smooth on the chart, and the values $\pm 2$ pick out the two central elements $\pm 1$ of
$SU(2)$, which lie outside the chart domain.

::: {#exm-trace-function}
#### The trace on $SU(2)$

$g \mapsto \operatorname{tr} g = a + \bar a = 2\operatorname{Re} a$ is a smooth function on $SU(2)$; in Euler
angles it is $2\cos(\theta/2)\cos((\varphi + \psi)/2)$, a smooth expression. It takes the value $2$ only at the
identity and $-2$ only at $-1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The claims of @exm-angle-not-function can be checked in the second angle chart, and the first exercise does so.
The cosine and sine are seen to be smooth on the whole circle because their formulas in the two charts are the
same function, while the angle $\varphi$ acquires a jump in the chart that covers the point it misses.

::: {#exr-smooth-function-circle}
#### Smooth and non-smooth functions on the circle

Show that $\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$ are smooth functions on the whole circle by writing their expressions in
the chart $\varphi' \in (-\pi, \pi)$, and show that the function $p \mapsto \varphi(p)$, defined on $S^1 \setminus
\{(1, 0)\}$, has no continuous extension to the circle by writing its expression in the chart $\varphi'$ near
$\varphi' = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exm-transition-circle, $\varphi = \varphi'$ on the upper arc and $\varphi = \varphi' + 2\pi$ on the lower arc,
so $\cos\varphi = \cos\varphi'$ and $\sin\varphi = \sin\varphi'$ on the whole overlap: in both charts the two
functions are cosine and sine of the coordinate, smooth, and since the charts cover the circle they are smooth
everywhere. The function $\varphi$ reads $\varphi'$ for $\varphi' \in (0, \pi)$ and $\varphi' + 2\pi$ for
$\varphi' \in (-\pi, 0)$: its one-sided limits at $\varphi' = 0$, the point $(1, 0)$, are $0$ and $2\pi$, so no
value at $(1, 0)$ makes it continuous, let alone smooth.
:::

The agreement of the two formulas for the height is a computation with the transition map, and the second
exercise performs it in SageManifolds, whose scalar fields carry one expression per chart and convert between
them automatically. It also records why the angle $\varphi$ itself cannot be converted.

::: {#exr-height-charts}
#### The height in two charts

Define the height $Z$ on the sphere as a SageManifolds scalar field by its spherical expression $\cos\theta$,
obtain its stereographic expression through the transition map, and compare with $(u^2 + v^2 - 1)/(u^2 + v^2 +
1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $\cos\theta = Z$ and the inverse transition map $\theta = 2\arctan(1/\sqrt{u^2 + v^2})$, $\varphi =
\operatorname{atan2}(v, u)$, SageManifolds produces the stereographic expression and it simplifies to $(u^2 + v^2 -
1)/(u^2 + v^2 + 1)$; the angle $\varphi$ has no such single-valued expression, since $\operatorname{atan2}$ jumps by
$2\pi$ across the half-line $v = 0$, $u < 0$:

{{< sage exr-height-charts >}}
:::

The trace formula of @exm-trace-function and the location of its extreme values are the subject of the third
exercise. Sage derives the formula from the explicit $a$ and shows that on the chart domain the trace stays
strictly between $-2$ and $2$, the values at $\pm 1$ being reached only at $\theta = 0$.

::: {#exr-smooth-function-trace-su2}
#### The trace in Euler angles

From $a = \cos(\theta/2)\, e^{-i(\varphi + \psi)/2}$ derive $\operatorname{tr} g = 2\cos(\theta/2)\cos((\varphi +
\psi)/2)$, show that $|\operatorname{tr} g| < 2$ on the Euler chart $0 < \theta < \pi$, and find the matrices
with $\operatorname{tr} g = \pm 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{tr} g = a + \bar a = 2\operatorname{Re} a = 2\cos(\theta/2)\cos((\varphi + \psi)/2)$. On $0 <
\theta < \pi$, $0 < \cos(\theta/2) < 1$ and $|\cos((\varphi + \psi)/2)| \leq 1$, so $|\operatorname{tr} g| < 2$.
The value $2$ needs $\cos(\theta/2) = 1$, that is $\theta = 0$ (outside the chart), and $\cos((\varphi + \psi)/2)
= 1$, giving $g = \operatorname{diag}(e^{-i(\varphi + \psi)/2}, e^{i(\varphi + \psi)/2}) = 1$; the value $-2$
needs $\theta = 0$ and $(\varphi + \psi)/2 = \pi$, giving $g = -1$. A smooth function on a compact manifold attains
its extremes, here at the two points the Euler chart does not see:

{{< sage exr-smooth-function-trace-su2 >}}
:::
::::

Maps from one manifold to another are handled the same way as functions: choose a chart on each side and look at
the resulting map between open subsets of Euclidean spaces. The next definition says this and names the maps that
can be undone smoothly, the diffeomorphisms, which are the isomorphisms of the subject.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-smooth-map-manifolds}
#### Smooth map between manifolds

A map $F : M \to N$ between manifolds is **smooth** if its expression in charts, $y \circ F \circ x^{-1}$, is a
smooth map between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ for all charts $x$ of $M$ and $y$ of $N$. A
smooth bijection with smooth inverse is a **diffeomorphism** of manifolds.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the inclusion of a surface into the space around it, whose chart expression is the
parametrisation itself. The components of @eq-sphere-embedding are smooth, and the same holds for every manifold
of this chapter sitting in a Euclidean space.

::: {#exm-map-inclusion}
#### Inclusions

The inclusion $S^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is smooth: in the spherical chart it is @eq-sphere-embedding, whose
components are smooth. Likewise the inclusions $S^1 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ and $SU(2) \to \mathbb{C}^4$.
:::

The second example is smooth and surjective but far from bijective: the line wraps around the circle infinitely
often. In the angle chart it is the identity up to a constant, which shows that smoothness is a local matter and
says nothing about how many times a point is covered.

::: {#exm-map-covering}
#### The circle covered by the line

$\mathbb{R} \to S^1$, $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$, is smooth: in the angle chart it reads $\varphi = t$ (up to a
constant). It is surjective but not injective, winding the line around the circle infinitely often; it is the
quotient map of @exm-quotient-circle.
:::

The third example is a diffeomorphism, a rotation of the sphere, whose stereographic expression turns out to be a
rotation of the plane. It also introduces the orbit map of a group acting on a manifold, a smooth surjection that
is the starting point of the theory of coset spaces.

::: {#exm-map-rotation}
#### Rotations of the sphere

A rotation $R \in SO(3)$ restricts to a diffeomorphism of $S^2$; in stereographic coordinates the rotation about the
$Z$-axis by $\alpha$ is the rotation $(u, v) \mapsto (u\cos\alpha - v\sin\alpha, u\sin\alpha + v\cos\alpha)$ of the
plane, smooth with smooth inverse. The orbit map $SO(3) \to S^2$, $g \mapsto g \cdot N$, is a smooth surjection
(@sec-coset-spaces).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The antipodal map exchanges the poles, so no single stereographic chart can express it everywhere, and the first
exercise shows how the freedom to choose different charts on the two sides resolves this. In one pair of charts
the map is singular at the origin, in another it is a reflection.

::: {#exr-smooth-map-antipodal}
#### The antipodal map in charts

The antipodal map $p \mapsto -p$ of $S^2$ sends $(X, Y, Z)$ to $(-X, -Y, -Z)$. Write it with the north chart on
both sides and with the north chart on the source and the south chart on the target, and explain why the second
choice shows that the map is a diffeomorphism while the first does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The north coordinates of $-p$ are $(-X, -Y)/(1 + Z) = -(u', v') = -(u, v)/(u^2 + v^2)$, the inversion followed by
the reflection through the origin: this is smooth only on the punctured plane, because the source point $S$ (the
origin) is sent to $N$, which has no north coordinates. The south coordinates of $-p$ are $(-X, -Y)/(1 - Z) = -
(u, v)$, a linear map of the whole plane, smooth with smooth inverse. Since the north chart on the source and
the south chart on the target are defined wherever the map is to be checked ($p \neq N$ and $-p \neq S$ are the
same condition), the second expression covers all of $S^2 \setminus \{N\}$ at once, and the symmetric expression
covers $S^2 \setminus \{S\}$: the antipodal map is a diffeomorphism, its own inverse.
:::

The rotation of @exm-map-rotation can be defined in SageManifolds as a map from the sphere to itself, and the
second exercise checks that it is the restriction of the rotation of space by composing it with the embedding.
The Jacobian determinant and the inverse rotation complete the proof that it is a diffeomorphism.

::: {#exr-smooth-map-rotation-check}
#### A rotation of the sphere in SageManifolds

Define on $S^2 \setminus \{N\}$ the map $(u, v) \mapsto (u\cos\alpha - v\sin\alpha,\ u\sin\alpha + v\cos\alpha)$
as a SageManifolds `diff_map`, compose it with the inverse stereographic chart @eq-stereographic, and check that
the result equals the rotation $R_z(\alpha)$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ applied to @eq-stereographic. Compute the Jacobian
determinant and show that the rotation by $-\alpha$ is the inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $E$ the inverse chart, $E \circ \mathrm{rot}_\alpha$ and $R_z(\alpha) \circ E$ agree component by component
because $u^2 + v^2$ is invariant under the plane rotation and the first two components of $E$ transform as the
vector $(u, v)$; the Jacobian determinant is $\cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\alpha = 1$, and $\mathrm{rot}_{-\alpha} \circ
\mathrm{rot}_\alpha$ is the identity of the chart. The south pole, the origin of the chart, is fixed, as a
rotation about the $Z$-axis must:

{{< sage exr-smooth-map-rotation-check >}}
:::

Maps of the circle to itself illustrate the three possibilities, diffeomorphism, smooth non-injective map and
orientation-reversing diffeomorphism. The third exercise asks the reader to write each in the angle charts and to
decide, and generalises the winding map to any integer.

::: {#exr-smooth-map-circle-maps}
#### Maps of the circle

Decide which of the following maps $S^1 \to S^1$ are smooth and which are diffeomorphisms: the rotation
$(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi) \mapsto (\cos(\varphi + c), \sin(\varphi + c))$, the doubling map $(\cos\varphi,
\sin\varphi) \mapsto (\cos 2\varphi, \sin 2\varphi)$, and the reflection $(X, Y) \mapsto (X, -Y)$. What about
$\varphi \mapsto k\varphi$ for an integer $k$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In angle charts the rotation reads $\varphi \mapsto \varphi + c$ (modulo $2\pi$, that is up to the constant shift
of the transition map), smooth with smooth inverse $\varphi \mapsto \varphi - c$: a diffeomorphism. The doubling
map reads $\varphi \mapsto 2\varphi$, smooth with derivative $2 \neq 0$, so it is a local diffeomorphism, but
$\varphi$ and $\varphi + \pi$ have the same image: smooth, surjective, two-to-one, not a diffeomorphism. The
reflection reads $\varphi \mapsto 2\pi - \varphi$ in the chart $(0, 2\pi)$ and $\varphi' \mapsto -\varphi'$ in the
other, smooth and its own inverse: a diffeomorphism that reverses the direction of travel. For integer $k$ the map
$\varphi \mapsto k\varphi$ is smooth, $|k|$-to-one for $k \neq 0$ and a diffeomorphism exactly for $k = \pm 1$;
for $k = 0$ it is the constant map to $(1, 0)$.
:::
::::

Curves are maps from an interval into the manifold, and the next definition fixes what their coordinate expression
and their velocity are. The chain rule it quotes is the formula that will later turn velocities into tangent
vectors: the rate of change of any function along the curve is a linear combination of its partial derivatives
with the coordinate velocities as coefficients.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-curve}
#### Curve

A **curve** in $M$ is a smooth map $\gamma : (a, b) \to M$ from an open interval, with coordinate expression
$x^i(t)$ in a chart. The function $f \circ \gamma$ is the value of $f$ along the curve, and its derivative at $t$
is, by the chain rule,
$$
\frac{d}{dt} f(\gamma(t)) = \frac{dx^i}{dt}\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i} .
$$ {#eq-velocity}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first curve is a parallel of the sphere, along which the height is constant. The example checks @eq-velocity
in the trivial case where the only non-zero coordinate velocity multiplies a vanishing partial derivative.

::: {#exm-parallel-curve}
#### A parallel

$\gamma(t) = (\theta_0, \varphi_0 + t)$ runs along a parallel of the sphere; $\dot x = (0, 1)$, and the height
$Z = \cos\theta_0$ is constant along it, in agreement with @eq-velocity: $\partial_\varphi\cos\theta = 0$.
:::

A meridian is the other coordinate curve, and along it the height does change. The second example computes its
rate of change by the chain rule and finds the expected $-\sin t$, fastest at the equator and zero at the poles.

::: {#exm-meridian-curve}
#### A meridian

$\gamma(t) = (t, \varphi_0)$, $t \in (0, \pi)$, runs from pole to pole along a meridian; $\dot x = (1, 0)$ and the
height changes at the rate $dZ/dt = \partial_\theta\cos\theta = -\sin t$.
:::

Curves on the torus can close or not depending on an arithmetic condition, and the third example gives one of
each. The rational slope $2$ produces a closed curve that winds around the tube once and around the axis twice,
while an irrational slope produces a curve that never closes and fills the torus densely.

::: {#exm-torus-curve}
#### A closed curve on the torus

$\gamma(t) = (t, 2t)$ in the torus chart winds once around the tube and twice around the axis before closing at
$t = 2\pi$ (@exr-torus-curve, the green curve of @fig-product-square); the curve $(t, \alpha t)$ with $\alpha$
irrational never closes and comes arbitrarily close to every point of the torus.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Running along the same path at a different speed changes the velocity but not the path, and the first exercise
checks that @eq-velocity scales accordingly. It then derives the general rule for a reparametrised curve, which
is the chain rule once more.

::: {#exr-curve-reparametrisation}
#### Reparametrising a curve

For $\tilde\gamma(t) = (\theta_0, \varphi_0 + 2t)$ on the sphere, compute the velocity and the derivative of $f =
