\sin\theta\cos\varphi$ along $\tilde\gamma$ both directly and from @eq-velocity. Then show that for a curve
$\gamma$ and a smooth function $h$ of one variable, the reparametrised curve $\gamma \circ h$ has velocity
$h'(t)\, \dot x^i(h(t))$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dot x = (0, 2)$, twice the velocity of the parallel of @exm-parallel-curve. Directly, $f(\tilde\gamma(t)) =
\sin\theta_0 \cos(\varphi_0 + 2t)$ has derivative $-2\sin\theta_0 \sin(\varphi_0 + 2t)$; from @eq-velocity, $0
\cdot \partial_\theta f + 2\,\partial_\varphi f = 2\sin\theta_0 \cdot (-\sin\varphi)$ evaluated at $\varphi =
\varphi_0 + 2t$, the same. For $\gamma \circ h$ the coordinate expression is $x^i(h(t))$, whose derivative is
$h'(t)\, \dot x^i(h(t))$ by the one-variable chain rule; so $f \circ \gamma \circ h$ has derivative $h'(t)$ times
the derivative of $f \circ \gamma$ at $h(t)$, and velocities rescale by $h'$ while the path is unchanged.
:::

A great circle through the poles leaves the north chart at the pole, and the second exercise follows it in
stereographic coordinates until it does. SageManifolds' curve objects hold the chart expression, and the chain
rule @eq-velocity is checked against the direct derivative of the height.

::: {#exr-curve-meridian-stereographic}
#### A great circle in the stereographic chart

The great circle $t \mapsto (\cos t, 0, \sin t)$ passes through both poles. Write it as a SageManifolds curve in
the north stereographic chart for $t \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$, compute its velocity, check @eq-velocity for the height
$Z$ against $dZ/dt = \cos t$, and describe what happens to the velocity as $t \to \pi/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(u, v) = (\cos t/(1 - \sin t), 0)$, with velocity $du/dt = 1/(1 - \sin t)$ and $dv/dt = 0$; the chain rule gives
$(du/dt)\, \partial_u Z = \cos t$ after substitution, as it must. At $t = -\pi/2$ the curve passes the south pole
$u = 0$ with speed $1/2$; as $t \to \pi/2$ it approaches the north pole, $u \to \infty$ and $du/dt \to \infty$:
the curve itself is perfectly regular there (its velocity in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has unit length), but the chart ends,
and the south chart must take over:

{{< sage exr-curve-meridian-stereographic >}}
:::

The closed curve of @exm-torus-curve is the third exercise, carried out with SageManifolds' curve objects and the
embedding of the torus. Composing the curve with the embedding gives its image in space, and comparing the two
endpoints shows that it closes after one period.

::: {#exr-torus-curve}
#### A curve on the torus

With SageManifolds' curve objects, define $\gamma(t) = (t, 2t)$ on the torus with $R = 2$, $r = 1$, compose it with
the embedding @eq-torus-embedding, and check that it closes after one period.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The velocity in the chart is $(1, 2)$, so over $t \in (0, 2\pi)$ the angle $a$ makes one turn and $b$ makes two;
the image in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a trigonometric curve whose values at $t = 0$ and $t = 2\pi$ coincide at $(3, 0,
0)$, the outer equator point:

{{< sage exr-torus-curve >}}
:::
::::

#### Products

Two manifolds can be multiplied, and the result has charts made from pairs of charts of the factors. The next
definition records this construction, whose dimension is the sum of the dimensions; the torus as a product of two
circles is the picture to keep.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-product-manifold}
#### Product manifold

The **product** $M \times N$ of manifolds of dimensions $m$ and $n$ is the Cartesian product (@def-product) with
the atlas of **product charts** $(x, y) : U \times U' \to V \times V' \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m + n}$, one for each pair
of charts; it is a manifold of dimension $m + n$, and the projections onto the factors are smooth.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the torus seen as a product, where the chart $(a, b)$ of @exm-torus-chart is recognised as
the product of two angle charts. The coordinate square with its edges identified is the product's own picture of
itself, next to the embedded surface.

::: {#exm-product-torus}
#### The torus as $S^1 \times S^1$

The torus is the product of two circles: the chart $(a, b)$ of @eq-torus-embedding is the product of two angle
charts, and @fig-product-square shows the coordinate square with opposite edges identified next to the embedded
torus. The product atlas has four charts.
:::

The second example is the product construction that motivates much of this book: a spacetime times a compact
internal space. The product charts are the familiar spacetime coordinates together with angles, and fields on the
product are functions of both, periodic in the angles.

::: {#exm-product-kk}
#### Kaluza-Klein spaces

The five-dimensional space $M_4 \times S^1$ of Part III has product charts $(x^\mu, \varphi)$, and $M_4 \times
S^2$ of Part IV has $(x^\mu, \theta, \varphi)$; a field on the product is a function of both sets of coordinates,
periodic in the internal angles.
:::

The third example gives the Euclidean spaces as products of smaller ones and introduces the cylinder, the product
of a circle and a line. These are the simplest cases, with one chart on the non-compact factor, and they show
that a product of a compact and a non-compact manifold is non-compact.

::: {#exm-manifold-product-rn}
#### $\mathbb{R}^n$ and cylinders

$\mathbb{R}^{m + n} = \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n$ with the identity chart as product chart; the cylinder
$S^1 \times \mathbb{R}$ has charts $(\varphi, z)$, and $S^2 \times \mathbb{R}$ is the space of the "spacetime with a
sphere" examples of Part IV before the time direction is added.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The torus as a product. Left: the coordinate square $(a, b) \in (0, 2\pi)^2$ with opposite edges identified
(matching arrows), a tube circle $a = 1$ (red), an axis circle $b = 2$ (blue) and the closed curve $(t, 2t)$
(green). Generated by `figures/product_chart.sage`.](figures/product_chart.svg){#fig-product-square width=40%}

![The embedded torus with the three curves of @fig-product-square, drawn through the embedding with
SageManifolds. Generated by `figures/product_square.sage`.](figures/product_square.png){#fig-product-torus width=45%}

{{< interactive product_square 460 >}}

The number of product charts is the product of the numbers of charts of the factors, and the first exercise
counts them for a few products and adds up dimensions. Writing one product chart explicitly shows what the
coordinates of a point of $S^1 \times S^2$ look like.

::: {#exr-product-charts-count}
#### Counting product charts

How many charts does the product atlas of $S^1 \times S^2$ have, if the circle carries its two angle charts and
the sphere its two stereographic charts, and how many does the $n$-torus $T^n = S^1 \times \dots \times S^1$ have?
What is the dimension of $S^1 \times S^2 \times SU(2)$? Write one product chart of $S^1 \times S^2$ with its
domain.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each product chart is a pair of charts, so $S^1 \times S^2$ has $2 \cdot 2 = 4$ and $T^n$ has $2^n$ (the four
charts of @exr-atlas-torus-four for $n = 2$). Dimensions add: $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$. One product chart of $S^1 \times
S^2$ is $(\varphi, u, v)$ on the domain $(S^1 \setminus \{(1, 0)\}) \times (S^2 \setminus \{N\})$, with image
$(0, 2\pi) \times \mathbb{R}^2$, an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
:::

The torus has another home besides $\mathbb{R}^3$: inside the three-sphere, as the set of $SU(2)$ matrices whose
two entries have equal modulus. The second exercise maps the product chart $(a, b)$ into $S^3$ and finds, with
Sage, that the two coordinate velocities are orthogonal and of equal constant length, so this torus is flat.

::: {#exr-product-clifford-torus}
#### The Clifford torus in $SU(2)$

Show that $(a, b) \mapsto (\cos a, \sin a, \cos b, \sin b)/\sqrt2$ sends the product chart of $S^1 \times S^1$
into $S^3$, that the corresponding $SU(2)$ matrix has $|a| = |b| = 1/\sqrt2$ in @eq-su2-matrix, and compute the
inner products of the two coordinate velocities. Is the map injective on $(0, 2\pi)^2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The sum of squares is $(1 + 1)/2 = 1$, so the image lies on $S^3$; the complex entries $a = (\cos a + i\sin
a)/\sqrt2$ and $b = (\cos b + i\sin b)/\sqrt2$ have $|a|^2 = |b|^2 = 1/2$ and the matrix has determinant $1$. The
coordinate velocities $(-\sin a, \cos a, 0, 0)/\sqrt2$ and $(0, 0, -\sin b, \cos b)/\sqrt2$ are orthogonal and
each has length $1/\sqrt2$: the Gram matrix (@def-gram) is the constant $\tfrac12\, 1$, so distances on this torus
are those of the flat square, unlike the torus in $\mathbb{R}^3$ whose Gram matrix depends on $a$. The map is
injective because $(\cos a, \sin a)$ determines $a$ and $(\cos b, \sin b)$ determines $b$ in $(0, 2\pi)$:

{{< sage exr-product-clifford-torus >}}
:::

Smoothness on a product is checked factor by factor, and the third exercise establishes the two rules that make
this precise: the projections are smooth, and a map into a product is smooth exactly when its two components are.
It ends with two functions on the torus, one smooth and one not, for the same reason as the angle on the circle.

::: {#exr-product-functions}
#### Smooth maps into and out of a product

Show that the projections $M \times N \to M$ and $M \times N \to N$ are smooth, and that a map $F = (F_1, F_2) : P
\to M \times N$ is smooth if and only if $F_1 : P \to M$ and $F_2 : P \to N$ are. Decide whether $f(a, b) = \cos
a\cos b + \sin(a + b)$ and $g(a, b) = a + b$ define smooth functions on the torus.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In a product chart $(x, y)$ the first projection reads $(x, y) \mapsto x$, a linear map, smooth; likewise the
second. If $F$ is smooth so are the compositions $F_1 = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ F$ and $F_2 = \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ F$;
conversely the chart expression of $F$ is the pair of chart expressions of $F_1$ and $F_2$, and a map into
$\mathbb{R}^{m + n}$ is smooth iff its components are. The function $f$ is a trigonometric polynomial in $a$ and
$b$, $2\pi$-periodic in each, so it has the same smooth expression in all four product charts of
@exr-atlas-torus-four: smooth on the torus. The function $g$ is not even continuous on the torus: in the chart $(a',
b)$ it reads $a' + b$ on one half of the overlap and $a' + 2\pi + b$ on the other, jumping by $2\pi$ across the
circle $a \equiv 0$, as $\varphi$ does on the circle (@exr-smooth-function-circle).
:::
::::

### Embeddings and Gram matrices {#sec-embeddings}

Every example so far was described by a map from coordinates into some $\mathbb{R}^N$ whose image is the
manifold: the circle in the plane, the sphere and the torus in space, $SU(2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^4$. This is the most
concrete way to picture a manifold, and it comes with a way to measure: the lengths and angles of the coordinate
velocities, collected in the Gram matrix. The Gram matrix is the first encounter with a metric; in
@sec-induced-metrics it becomes the round metric of the sphere.

#### Parametrisations and their velocities

The inverse of a chart is a map from coordinates to points, and when the points live in a Euclidean space it is a
map between Euclidean spaces that calculus can handle directly. The next definition names such maps; the picture
is a sheet of coordinate paper being bent into a surface in space.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-parametrisation}
#### Parametrisation

A **parametrisation** of a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ is a smooth map $E : V \to \mathbb{R}^N$ from an open
set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ whose image is $S$ (or a piece of it); when $E$ is injective, $E^{-1}$ is a chart on
its image. The inverses of the charts of @sec-charts are parametrisations.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The circle is parametrised by its angle, and the first example notes that the same formula serves two purposes
depending on its domain. On an interval of length $2\pi$ it is the inverse of a chart; on the whole real line it is
a many-to-one parametrisation of the whole circle.

::: {#exm-parametrisation-circle}
#### The circle

@eq-circle-embedding, $\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ on $(0, 2\pi)$, parametrises the circle minus
a point; on all of $\mathbb{R}$ it parametrises the whole circle but is not injective.
:::

The sphere has been parametrised twice in this chapter, by angles and by the stereographic plane. The second
example puts the two side by side and records what each misses, a half-meridian and two poles against a single
point.

::: {#exm-parametrisation-sphere}
#### The sphere, twice

@eq-sphere-embedding parametrises the sphere by spherical coordinates and @eq-stereographic by stereographic
coordinates; both are injective on their domains and their images are the sphere minus a half-meridian and minus
a point respectively.
:::

The Euler angles parametrise a group, and the third example writes the four real components explicitly, which
realises $SU(2)$ as a surface in $\mathbb{R}^4$. The formulas for $a$ and $b$ are those of @exr-su2-det-euler.

::: {#exm-parametrisation-su2}
#### $SU(2)$ by Euler angles

The Euler angles @eq-euler-angles parametrise $SU(2) = S^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ by the four real numbers
$(\operatorname{Re} a, \operatorname{Im} a, \operatorname{Re} b, \operatorname{Im} b)$ with
$a = \cos(\theta/2)\, e^{-i(\varphi + \psi)/2}$ and $b = -i\sin(\theta/2)\, e^{i(\varphi - \psi)/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** This parametrisation is the map `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2Embed` of the Lean library.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The cylinder is the product of the circle with a line, and its parametrisation combines the angle with a height.
The first exercise asks for its image and for the set it misses, and repeats the observation about domains made
for the circle.

::: {#exr-parametrisation-cylinder}
#### The cylinder

Show that $(\varphi, z) \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi, z)$ on $(0, 2\pi) \times \mathbb{R}$ parametrises
the cylinder $X^2 + Y^2 = 1$ minus a line, that it is injective there, and that on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$
it parametrises the whole cylinder without being injective.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi = 1$ puts the image on the cylinder, and every point $(X, Y, z)$ of the cylinder
with $(X, Y) \neq (1, 0)$ is reached exactly once, by the $\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)$ of @exr-chart-circle-inverse and
the given $z$; the missing set is the vertical line $X = 1$, $Y = 0$. On $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ the line is
covered too, but $(\varphi, z)$ and $(\varphi + 2\pi, z)$ have the same image. The inverse of the restricted map is
the product chart $(\varphi, z)$ of the cylinder $S^1 \times \mathbb{R}$ (@exm-manifold-product-rn).
:::

Stretching the sphere along its axes gives an ellipsoid, and the spherical parametrisation stretches with it. The
second exercise checks this with Sage and observes that the injectivity question is answered by the sphere, since
the stretching is an invertible linear map; it also shows that the coordinate grid is no longer orthogonal.

::: {#exr-parametrisation-ellipsoid}
#### The ellipsoid

Show that $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (A\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ B\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ C\cos\theta)$
parametrises the ellipsoid $X^2/A^2 + Y^2/B^2 + Z^2/C^2 = 1$, that it is the spherical parametrisation followed
by the scaling $\operatorname{diag}(A, B, C)$, and deduce where it is injective; compute its two coordinate
velocities and decide when they are orthogonal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Dividing each component by its semi-axis returns @eq-sphere-embedding, whose squares sum to $1$; so $E =
\operatorname{diag}(A, B, C)\, S$ with $S$ the spherical parametrisation, and since the scaling is invertible for
$ABC \neq 0$, $E$ is injective exactly where $S$ is, on $(0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi)$. The velocities are
$\partial_\theta E = (A\cos\theta\cos\varphi, B\cos\theta\sin\varphi, -C\sin\theta)$ and $\partial_\varphi E =
(-A\sin\theta\sin\varphi, B\sin\theta\cos\varphi, 0)$, with inner product $(B^2 - A^2)\sin\theta\cos\theta
\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$: orthogonal everywhere only when $A = B$, the ellipsoid of revolution:

{{< sage exr-parametrisation-ellipsoid >}}
:::

The torus formula on all of $\mathbb{R}^2$ covers each point infinitely often, in a regular pattern. The third
exercise identifies the set of preimages of a point as a shifted lattice and uses it to say exactly which open sets
of the plane give injective parametrisations, the general version of "an interval of length at most $2\pi$".

::: {#exr-parametrisation-lattice}
#### Preimages under the torus parametrisation

Show that @eq-torus-embedding, extended to all $(a, b) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, is surjective onto the torus and that the
preimage of each point is a lattice $\{(a + 2\pi m, b + 2\pi n) : m, n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. Deduce for which open sets
$V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ the restriction to $V$ is injective, and show that no open set larger than an open
square of side $2\pi$ works.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The formula is $2\pi$-periodic in $a$ and in $b$, so every point of the torus, which is reached for some $(a, b) \in
[0, 2\pi)^2$, is reached by the whole lattice translate. Conversely, if $E(a, b) = E(a', b')$ then $r\sin a = r\sin
a'$ and $R + r\cos a = R + r\cos a'$ (the distance from the axis), so $a' \equiv a$, and then $(\cos b, \sin b) =
(\cos b', \sin b')$ gives $b' \equiv b$ modulo $2\pi$: the preimage is exactly the lattice translate. The
restriction to $V$ is injective iff $V$ contains no two points differing by a non-zero element of $2\pi\mathbb{Z}^2$;
an open square of side $2\pi$ qualifies, while any open set containing a closed square of side $2\pi$ contains two
points $(a, b)$ and $(a + 2\pi, b)$ with the same image.
:::
::::

Differentiating a parametrisation with respect to each coordinate gives a vector in the ambient space, the velocity
of the corresponding coordinate curve. The next definition arranges these vectors as the columns of the Jacobian
matrix, which from now on carries the local geometry of the parametrised surface.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-coordinate-velocity}
#### Coordinate velocity

The **coordinate velocities** of a parametrisation $E$ are the columns $\partial_i E = \partial E/\partial x^i$ of
its Jacobian matrix (@def-jacobian), the velocities of the coordinate curves (@def-coordinate-curve) seen as
vectors in $\mathbb{R}^N$:
$$
J^k{}_i = \frac{\partial E^k}{\partial x^i}, \qquad k = 1, \dots, N,\ i = 1, \dots, n .
$$ {#eq-jacobian}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the circle there is a single coordinate and a single column. The first example computes it and recognises
the unit tangent vector, which is why arc length along the circle equals the angle.

::: {#exm-jacobian-circle}
#### The circle

For @eq-circle-embedding the Jacobian is the single column $\partial_\varphi E = (-\sin\varphi, \cos\varphi)$: the
velocity of the point moving around the circle, tangent to it and of unit length.
:::

The sphere has two columns, tangent to the meridian and to the parallel through the point. The second example
writes them out and shows them in a figure at three latitudes, where one can see the parallel's velocity shrink
towards the pole and vanish there.

::: {#exm-jacobian-sphere}
#### The sphere

For @eq-sphere-embedding the two columns are
$$
\partial_\theta E = (\cos\theta\cos\varphi,\ \cos\theta\sin\varphi,\ -\sin\theta), \qquad
\partial_\varphi E = (-\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ 0),
$$ {#eq-sphere-jacobian}
tangent to the meridian and to the parallel through the point (@fig-coordinate-velocities). At the poles
$\partial_\varphi E = 0$: the parallel has shrunk to a point.
:::

![Coordinate velocities of the spherical parametrisation at three points of the meridian $\varphi = 7\pi/4$:
$\partial_\theta E$ (red) has unit length everywhere, $\partial_\varphi E$ (green) has length $\sin\theta$ and
shrinks towards the pole. Generated by
`figures/coordinate_velocities.sage`.](figures/coordinate_velocities.png){#fig-coordinate-velocities width=55%}

The torus's two columns are tangent to the tube circle and to the axis circle, and their lengths are the radii of
those circles found in @exr-coordinate-curves-torus. The third example records this; unlike the sphere, neither
length ever vanishes.

::: {#exm-jacobian-torus}
#### The torus

For @eq-torus-embedding, $\partial_a E = (-r\sin a\cos b,\ -r\sin a\sin b,\ r\cos a)$ has length $r$ and
$\partial_b E = (-(R + r\cos a)\sin b,\ (R + r\cos a)\cos b,\ 0)$ has length $R + r\cos a$, the radius of the axis
circle through the point (@exr-torus-gram).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Jacobian of the polar map is the first one every student computes, and the first exercise asks for it again
in the language of coordinate velocities. Its columns are the vectors found in @exr-coordinate-curves-polar-velocity
and its determinant is the $r$ of the change-of-variables formula.

::: {#exr-velocity-polar}
#### The Jacobian of polar coordinates

Write the Jacobian matrix of $(r, \varphi) \mapsto (r\cos\varphi, r\sin\varphi)$, identify its columns with the
velocities of the polar coordinate curves, find their lengths and the determinant, and relate the determinant to
the area of a small coordinate rectangle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$J = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\varphi & -r\sin\varphi \\ \sin\varphi & r\cos\varphi \end{pmatrix}$; the first column
$\partial_r E = (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ is the unit radial vector and the second $\partial_\varphi E =
r(-\sin\varphi, \cos\varphi)$ is tangent to the circle of radius $r$, with lengths $1$ and $r$ and $\det J = r$
(@prp-polar-jacobian). The two columns are orthogonal, so the coordinate rectangle of sides $dr$ and $d\varphi$ is
mapped to a rectangle of sides $dr$ and $r\, d\varphi$, of area $r\, dr\, d\varphi = |\det J|\, dr\, d\varphi$, the
area element of @thm-change-of-variables.
:::

The stereographic parametrisation has a Jacobian with no zero columns anywhere, and the second exercise computes
it with Sage. The two columns turn out to be tangent to the sphere, orthogonal and of equal length, a strong
property called conformality that is the subject of @exr-stereographic-gram.

::: {#exr-velocity-stereographic}
#### Coordinate velocities of the stereographic chart

Compute the coordinate velocities $\partial_u E$ and $\partial_v E$ of @eq-stereographic, check that both are
tangent to the sphere (orthogonal to the position vector $E$), that they are orthogonal to each other, and that
both have length $2/(1 + u^2 + v^2)$; where is this length largest?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating the rational functions and simplifying, $E \cdot \partial_u E = E \cdot \partial_v E = 0$ (as must
be, since $E \cdot E = 1$ is constant), $\partial_u E \cdot \partial_v E = 0$, and $|\partial_u E|^2 = |\partial_v
E|^2 = 4/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$. The length is largest at the origin, where it equals $2$: the south pole, nearest to
the projection plane, is where a unit step in the plane moves the point on the sphere fastest; towards the north
pole, $u^2 + v^2 \to \infty$, the length tends to $0$. The Jacobian has rank $2$ everywhere:

{{< sage exr-velocity-stereographic >}}
:::

Surfaces of revolution include the sphere, the torus and the cylinder, and the third exercise computes their
coordinate velocities once and for all. The result explains why the coordinate grids of all three were orthogonal
and gives the general formula for the lengths, to be specialised in each case.

::: {#exr-velocity-revolution}
#### Surfaces of revolution

For the surface of revolution $(s, \varphi) \mapsto (f(s)\cos\varphi,\ f(s)\sin\varphi,\ g(s))$ with $f > 0$,
compute the two coordinate velocities, show that they are orthogonal and find their lengths. Recover the sphere
($f = \sin s$, $g = \cos s$), the torus ($f = R + r\cos s$, $g = r\sin s$) and the cylinder ($f = 1$, $g = s$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_s E = (f'\cos\varphi, f'\sin\varphi, g')$ and $\partial_\varphi E = (-f\sin\varphi, f\cos\varphi, 0)$;
their inner product is $-ff'\cos\varphi\sin\varphi + ff'\sin\varphi\cos\varphi = 0$, and the lengths are
$\sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2}$ and $f$. For the sphere $f'^2 + g'^2 = \cos^2 s + \sin^2 s = 1$ and $f = \sin s$, the
lengths of @exm-jacobian-sphere; for the torus $f'^2 + g'^2 = r^2$ and $f = R + r\cos s$, those of
@exm-jacobian-torus; for the cylinder both lengths are $1$. The $\varphi$-velocity vanishes exactly where the
profile curve meets the axis, $f = 0$, which happens for the sphere at the poles and never for the torus or the
cylinder.
:::
::::

#### Embeddings

Not every parametrisation produces a decent surface: the map may fold, cross itself or have a cusp. The next
definition lists the three conditions that exclude these, injectivity, full rank of the Jacobian and continuity
of the inverse, and names the maps that satisfy them; their images are the surfaces on which the inverse map is a
chart.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-embedding}
#### Embedding

An **embedding** of an open set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ into $\mathbb{R}^N$ is a smooth injective map
$E : V \to \mathbb{R}^N$ whose Jacobian has **rank** $n$ (its $n$ columns are linearly independent,
@def-linear-independence) at every point, and which is a homeomorphism onto its image. The image $E(V)$ is then
an $n$-dimensional **embedded submanifold** of $\mathbb{R}^N$ and $E^{-1}$ is a chart on it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The spherical parametrisation is the first test case, and the first example shows that the rank condition is
exactly what fails at the poles. Away from them the two columns are orthogonal and non-zero, hence independent.

::: {#exm-embedding-sphere}
#### The spherical chart is an embedding away from the poles

The columns @eq-sphere-jacobian are linearly independent exactly where $\sin\theta \neq 0$, since
$|\partial_\varphi E| = \sin\theta$ and the two columns are orthogonal; so @eq-sphere-embedding restricted to
$(0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi)$ is an embedding, and the map extended to $\theta = 0$ is not.
:::

The torus and the stereographic plane are embeddings on their whole domains, and the second example says why,
pointing to the Gram-matrix exercises where the orthogonality and the lengths are computed. The stereographic case
is the first embedding of an entire plane.

::: {#exm-embedding-torus}
#### The torus and the stereographic map

For the torus @eq-torus-embedding the columns have lengths $r$ and $R + r\cos a$, never zero, and are orthogonal
(@exr-torus-gram): the parametrisation is an embedding everywhere. The stereographic inverse @eq-stereographic is an
embedding of the whole plane, the image being the sphere minus a point (@exr-stereographic-gram).
:::

Each of the three conditions can fail on its own, and the third example gives one curve for each failure. A cusp
appears where the rank drops, a circle traced repeatedly is where injectivity fails, and a figure eight is a curve
whose inverse is not continuous although the other two conditions hold.

::: {#exm-embedding-not}
#### Maps that are not embeddings

$t \mapsto (t^2, t^3)$ is injective but its Jacobian $(2t, 3t^2)$ vanishes at $t = 0$: the image has a cusp.
$t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has rank one everywhere but is not injective. The figure eight
$t \mapsto (\sin 2t, \sin t)$ on $(0, 2\pi)$ is injective with rank one, but is not a homeomorphism onto its image
near the crossing point.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A helix is a curve in space that satisfies all three conditions, and the first exercise verifies them one by one.
The continuity of the inverse is the one most often forgotten, and here it follows from the fact that the height
coordinate alone recovers the parameter.

::: {#exr-embedding-helix}
#### The helix

Show that $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t, t)$ is an embedding of $\mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{R}^3$: check injectivity,
compute the velocity and its length, and show that the inverse map from the image to $\mathbb{R}$ is continuous.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The third coordinate is $t$ itself, so the map is injective and its inverse is the restriction to the helix of the
projection $(X, Y, Z) \mapsto Z$, a continuous map; hence the map is a homeomorphism onto its image. The velocity
$(-\sin t, \cos t, 1)$ has length $\sqrt2$ at every point, so the single column of the Jacobian never vanishes and
the rank is $1$. All three conditions of @def-embedding hold; the circle $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ of
@exm-embedding-not is the same curve with the height forgotten, and forgetting it destroys injectivity.
:::

An embedding is a property of the map, not of its image, and the second exercise makes this vivid with a
parametrisation of a smooth parabola that is nevertheless not an embedding. Finding a second parametrisation of
the same parabola that is an embedding shows that the image can be perfectly smooth while a particular map fails.

::: {#exr-embedding-parabola-cube}
#### A bad parametrisation of a good curve

Show that $t \mapsto (t^3, t^6)$ is injective with image the whole parabola $Y = X^2$, but is not an embedding;
then give a parametrisation of the same parabola that is an embedding. Which condition of @def-embedding fails,
and at which point?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$t \mapsto t^3$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$, so the map is injective and, as $(t^3)^2 = t^6$, its image is the
whole parabola; the inverse $(X, Y) \mapsto X^{1/3}$ is continuous, so it is a homeomorphism onto the image. The
Jacobian $(3t^2, 6t^5)$ vanishes at $t = 0$, so the rank condition fails at the origin and the map is not an
embedding; the velocity comes to a halt at the vertex and starts again, as in @exm-smooth-atlas-not. The map $s
\mapsto (s, s^2)$ has the same image, is injective, has Jacobian $(1, 2s) \neq 0$ and continuous inverse $(X, Y)
\mapsto X$: an embedding. The parabola is an embedded submanifold; only the first map was unsuitable.
:::

The figure eight of @exm-embedding-not fails the subtlest condition, and the third exercise proves the three
claims made about it. Sage settles the rank and the injectivity by exact trigonometry, and the two one-sided limits
at the ends of the interval show where the inverse breaks down.

::: {#exr-embedding-figure-eight}
#### The figure eight

For $E(t) = (\sin 2t, \sin t)$ on $(0, 2\pi)$, show that the velocity never vanishes, that $E$ is injective, and
that $E$ is not a homeomorphism onto its image by computing the limits of $E(t)$ as $t \to 0^+$ and $t \to
2\pi^-$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The velocity $(2\cos 2t, \cos t)$ vanishes only if $\cos t = 0$, but then $\cos 2t = 2\cos^2 t - 1 = -1 \neq 0$.
If $E(s) = E(t)$ then $\sin s = \sin t$, so $s = t$ or $s = \pi - t$ modulo $2\pi$; on the second branch $\sin 2s = -
\sin 2t$, so $\sin 2t = 0$ and $t \in \{\pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\}$, where the partner $\pi - t$ is either $t$ itself or
$0 \equiv 2\pi$, outside the interval: $E$ is injective. Both ends of the interval tend to $(0, 0) = E(\pi)$, so
points of the image near the crossing have parameters near $0$, near $\pi$ and near $2\pi$, and the inverse is not
continuous at the crossing:

{{< sage exr-embedding-figure-eight >}}
:::
::::

#### The Gram matrix

The lengths of the coordinate velocities and the angles between them are what the eye reads off a coordinate grid
drawn on a surface, and the next definition packages them into a matrix of inner products. Its determinant
detects where the columns become dependent, and its square root is the area factor of integration on the surface.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gram}
#### Gram matrix

The **Gram matrix** of a parametrisation is the $n \times n$ matrix of inner products of its coordinate
velocities,
$$
G_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{\partial E^k}{\partial x^i} \frac{\partial E^k}{\partial x^j} = (J^{\mathsf{T}} J)_{ij} .
$$ {#eq-gram}
It is a symmetric bilinear form (@def-symmetric-form) at each point, $\det G > 0$ exactly where the columns are
linearly independent, so $\det G \neq 0$ is the rank condition of @def-embedding, and $\sqrt{\det G}$ is the
area factor of the parametrisation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the circle the Gram matrix is a single number, and the first example finds it equal to one. The consequence
is that the angle measures arc length, the simplest instance of a metric reading off lengths.

::: {#exm-circle-gram}
#### The circle

$G = (\partial_\varphi E \cdot \partial_\varphi E) = (1)$, $\det G = 1$ everywhere: the angle chart is regular at
every point of its domain, and arc length equals angle.
:::

The sphere's Gram matrix is the computation behind the familiar $\sin\theta$ of spherical integrals. The second
example carries it out entry by entry from the columns @eq-sphere-jacobian and finds a diagonal matrix whose
determinant vanishes at the poles.

::: {#exm-sphere-gram}
#### The sphere

From @eq-sphere-jacobian,
$$
\begin{aligned}
G_{\theta\theta} &= \cos^2\theta\cos^2\varphi + \cos^2\theta\sin^2\varphi + \sin^2\theta = 1, \\
G_{\theta\varphi} &= -\cos\theta\sin\theta\cos\varphi\sin\varphi + \cos\theta\sin\theta\sin\varphi\cos\varphi = 0, \\
G_{\varphi\varphi} &= \sin^2\theta\sin^2\varphi + \sin^2\theta\cos^2\varphi = \sin^2\theta ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-sphere-gram}
so $G = \operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$ and $\det G = \sin^2\theta$ (@prp-sphere-gram); the area factor
$\sin\theta$ is the one of spherical integrals.
:::

The Gram matrix of $SU(2)$ in Euler angles is the first one with an off-diagonal entry. The third example states
it and reads off the geometric meaning: two of the coordinate curves are not orthogonal, so the three-sphere is
not a product of circles in these coordinates.

::: {#exm-su2-gram}
#### $SU(2)$

The Gram matrix of the Euler-angle parametrisation is
$$
G = \frac14 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \cos\theta \\ 0 & \cos\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix},
$$ {#eq-su2-gram}
with $\det G = \sin^2\theta/64$: regular away from $\theta = 0, \pi$. The off-diagonal entry says that the
$\varphi$- and $\psi$-curves are not orthogonal, which is why $SU(2)$ is not a product of circles
(@prp-su2-gram).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
SageManifolds computes Gram matrices as pullbacks of the Euclidean metric, and the first exercise uses this on the
torus and compares with the direct formula $J^{\mathsf{T}} J$. The determinant is a product of two squares that
never vanish, which is the regularity claimed in @exm-embedding-torus.

::: {#exr-torus-gram}
#### The Gram matrix of the torus

Compute the Gram matrix of the torus parametrisation @eq-torus-embedding as the pullback of the Euclidean metric
with SageManifolds, compare with $J^{\mathsf{T}} J$, and find where the parametrisation is regular.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$G_{aa} = r^2$, $G_{ab} = 0$, $G_{bb} = (R + r\cos a)^2$, $\det G = r^2(R + r\cos a)^2 > 0$ everywhere because
$R > r$. In SageManifolds:

{{< sage exr-torus-gram >}}
:::

The equal lengths and orthogonality found in @exr-velocity-stereographic mean that the stereographic Gram matrix
is a multiple of the identity, and the second exercise computes it. A chart with this property preserves angles,
which is why the stereographic projection is the basis of so many maps of the Earth.

::: {#exr-stereographic-gram}
#### The Gram matrix of the stereographic parametrisation

Compute the Gram matrix of @eq-stereographic and show that it is a multiple of the identity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$G = \dfrac{4}{(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$: the stereographic chart is
**conformal**, it preserves angles and scales all lengths at a point by the same factor, which shrinks far from
the origin where the sphere's north pole is approached. The determinant never vanishes.

{{< sage exr-stereographic-gram >}}
:::

The determinant criterion of the definition can be applied to the sphere without any new computation, and the
third exercise asks for the one-line argument, which needs nothing beyond the determinant of @eq-sphere-gram.
This is the pattern for every regularity statement in the book: a determinant and the set where it vanishes.

::: {#exr-gram-regular}
#### Where is the spherical chart regular?

Show, from the Gram matrix, that the spherical chart is regular exactly where $\sin\theta \neq 0$, and describe
the points where it fails to be regular.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @def-gram the chart is regular where $\det G \neq 0$, and @eq-sphere-gram gives $\det G = \sin^2\theta$, which
vanishes exactly at $\theta = 0, \pi$: the chart fails to be regular exactly at the two poles, where the whole
line $\theta = 0$ (or $\theta = \pi$) of the parameter plane collapses to a single point.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.sphere_gram_det`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.sphere_gram_det >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

#### The Gram matrix of the sphere

The computation of @exm-sphere-gram is short enough to be checked line by line, and it is also the first metric of
the book, so it deserves to be stated as a proposition. Each of the four entries is a derivative computation
followed by the identity $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$, and the determinant follows.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sphere-gram}
#### The Gram matrix of the spherical chart

The Gram matrix of @eq-sphere-embedding is $\operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$ with $\det G = \sin^2\theta$, so
the chart is regular exactly away from the poles.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.sphere_gram` and `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.sphere_gram_det`; each entry is a derivative
computation closed by `ring` with $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.sphere_gram >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$ is best understood by evaluating it at a few latitudes. The
first example does so at the equator and at a parallel of radius one half, where the second entry says how much
shorter the parallel's velocity is than the meridian's.

::: {#exm-sphere-gram-values}
#### The Gram matrix at a few latitudes

At the equator $\theta = \pi/2$, $G = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1)$: the two coordinate velocities are orthogonal
unit vectors, and the chart is locally a faithful map there. At $\theta = \pi/6$, $G = \operatorname{diag}(1,
\tfrac14)$: the parallel is a circle of radius $\sin(\pi/6) = \tfrac12$, so a step $d\varphi$ along it moves the
point only half as far as the same step would at the equator. At the poles $G_{\varphi\varphi} \to 0$.
:::

The square root of the determinant is the area factor, and the second example uses it to recover the area of the
sphere. The integral is the elementary one of spherical coordinates, seen now as an instance of the
change-of-variables formula with $\sqrt{\det G}$ in place of the Jacobian determinant.

::: {#exm-sphere-gram-area}
#### The area of the sphere

$\sqrt{\det G} = \sin\theta$, so the area element of the sphere in spherical coordinates is $\sin\theta\,
d\theta\, d\varphi$ and the total area is $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi \sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\varphi = 2 \cdot 2\pi
= 4\pi$. The missing half-meridian and poles have zero area and do not affect the integral; this is the surface
version of @thm-change-of-variables, with $\sqrt{\det G}$ as the factor.
:::

Scaling the sphere scales the Gram matrix by the square of the radius, and the third example records the result
for a sphere of radius $a$. It is the round metric of radius $a$ that the chapter on induced metrics takes as its
starting point.

::: {#exm-sphere-gram-radius}
#### A sphere of radius $a$

The parametrisation $a\, E$ of the sphere of radius $a$ has Jacobian $a J$ and Gram matrix $a^2 G =
\operatorname{diag}(a^2, a^2\sin^2\theta)$, with $\det = a^4\sin^2\theta$ and area $\int a^2\sin\theta = 4\pi
a^2$. This is the round metric of radius $a$ (@sec-induced-metrics); every length on the sphere scales by $a$ and
every area by $a^2$, while angles between coordinate curves are unchanged.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Gram matrix gives the length of any curve through the formula $\int\sqrt{G_{ij}\dot x^i \dot x^j}\, dt$, and
the first exercise applies it to the two kinds of coordinate curves. The result is the circumference of a
parallel and the length of a meridian, both read off the diagonal entries.

::: {#exr-sphere-gram-lengths}
#### Lengths of parallels and meridians

Using $G = \operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$, compute the length of the parallel $\theta = \theta_0$ and of a
meridian from pole to pole, and check the first against the radius of the parallel as a circle in space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Along the parallel $\gamma(t) = (\theta_0, t)$, $t \in (0, 2\pi)$, the speed is $\sqrt{G_{\varphi\varphi}} =
\sin\theta_0$, so the length is $2\pi\sin\theta_0$; the parallel is the circle of radius $\sin\theta_0$ at height
$\cos\theta_0$, with the same circumference. Along the meridian $\gamma(t) = (t, \varphi_0)$, $t \in (0, \pi)$,
the speed is $\sqrt{G_{\theta\theta}} = 1$ and the length is $\pi$, half a great circle. The equator, $\theta_0 =
\pi/2$, is the longest parallel, with length $2\pi$.
:::

Areas of regions bounded by parallels follow from the area factor by one integration, and the second exercise
computes the area of a polar cap and of a zone. The result that a zone's area depends only on its height is a
theorem of Archimedes, here a two-line consequence of $\sqrt{\det G} = \sin\theta$.

::: {#exr-sphere-gram-cap}
#### Caps and zones

Compute from $\sqrt{\det G}$ the area of the polar cap $\theta < \theta_0$ and check the cases $\theta_0 = \pi/2$
and $\theta_0 = \pi$. Show that the area of the zone $\theta_1 < \theta < \theta_2$ depends only on the difference
of heights $\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Area of the cap: $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\theta_0} \sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\varphi = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0)$,
which is $2\pi$ for the hemisphere and $4\pi$ for the whole sphere. For the zone, $2\pi\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}
\sin\theta\, d\theta = 2\pi(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2) = 2\pi\,(Z_1 - Z_2)$: the area equals $2\pi$ times the
height of the zone, the same as the area of the band of the circumscribed cylinder between the same two heights.
:::

A Gram matrix is attached to a parametrisation, and changing coordinates changes it by a definite rule, $G' =
J^{\mathsf{T}} G J$ with $J$ the Jacobian of the change. The third exercise checks the rule between the
stereographic and spherical charts with Sage: the conformal Gram matrix of one becomes the diagonal one of the
other.

::: {#exr-sphere-gram-transform}
#### Changing coordinates in the Gram matrix

Let $J$ be the Jacobian of the transition map $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (u, v)$ of @exm-transition-spherical and
$G_{\text{ste}} = 4/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$ times the identity the Gram matrix of the stereographic chart. Show with
Sage that $J^{\mathsf{T}} G_{\text{ste}} J = \operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$ and that $\det G$ transforms
by the factor $(\det J)^2$; explain why the rule holds in general.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The spherical parametrisation is $E_{\text{ste}} \circ T$ with $T$ the transition map, so by the chain rule its
Jacobian is $J_{\text{ste}} J$ and its Gram matrix is $(J_{\text{ste}} J)^{\mathsf{T}} (J_{\text{ste}} J) =
J^{\mathsf{T}} G_{\text{ste}} J$; taking determinants gives $\det G_{\text{sph}} = (\det J)^2 \det
G_{\text{ste}}$. Substituting $u, v$ in terms of $\theta, \varphi$ turns the conformal factor into $(1 -
\cos\theta)^2$, and the matrix product simplifies to $\operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$; with $\det J =
-\sin\theta/(1 - \cos\theta)^2$ the determinant is $\sin^2\theta$ (@prp-sphere-gram):

{{< sage exr-sphere-gram-transform >}}
:::
::::

#### The Gram matrix of $SU(2)$

The matrix @eq-su2-gram has nine entries, each a sum of four products of derivatives of half-angle trigonometric
functions, and it is worth stating once and for all. The proposition records it; each entry follows by
differentiating the four components of the Euler-angle parametrisation and simplifying with the double-angle
identity for $\cos\theta$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-su2-gram}
#### The Gram matrix of the Euler angles

The Gram matrix of the Euler-angle parametrisation of $SU(2)$ is @eq-su2-gram.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2_gram`, which identifies the Gram matrix with the metric `su2` of
@sec-induced-metrics; each entry is proved by differentiating the four components and closing with `ring` after
the double-angle identity for $\cos\theta$.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The off-diagonal entry disappears at one latitude, and the first example evaluates the matrix there. At $\theta =
\pi/2$ the three coordinate velocities are orthogonal and equally long, and the Euler chart is as faithful as it
ever gets.

::: {#exm-su2-gram-equator}
#### The Gram matrix at $\theta = \pi/2$

At $\theta = \pi/2$, $\cos\theta = 0$ and $G = \tfrac14\, 1$: the three coordinate velocities are mutually
orthogonal, each of length $\tfrac12$. A step $d\psi$ or $d\varphi$ moves the point of $S^3$ by $\tfrac12 d\psi$,
which is why $\psi$ needs the range $(0, 4\pi)$ to go once around a great circle of length $2\pi$. Away from
$\theta = \pi/2$ the $\varphi$- and $\psi$-velocities tilt towards each other.
:::

The volume of the three-sphere is the second example, computed from $\sqrt{\det G}$ exactly as the area of the
two-sphere was. The answer, $2\pi^2$, is checked by an independent chart in the integrative exercises.

::: {#exm-su2-gram-volume}
#### The volume of $SU(2)$

$\sqrt{\det G} = \sin\theta/8$, so the volume of $SU(2) = S^3$ is $\int_0^{4\pi}\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi
\frac{\sin\theta}{8}\, d\theta\, d\varphi\, d\psi = \frac{2}{8} \cdot 2\pi \cdot 4\pi = 2\pi^2$, the volume of the
unit three-sphere (@exr-su2-gram-volume, @exr-cm-s3-volume). The set where the chart degenerates has zero volume
and is harmlessly left out.
:::

The eigenvalues of the Gram matrix measure the stretching of the parametrisation in its principal directions, and
the third example computes them. Two of them degenerate at the poles of the Euler chart, exactly as the sphere's
$\sin^2\theta$ does, and the eigenvectors $\partial_\varphi \pm \partial_\psi$ are the combinations that survive
there.

::: {#exm-su2-gram-eigenvalues}
#### Eigenvalues of the Gram matrix

The eigenvalues of $4G$ are $1$, $1 + \cos\theta$ and $1 - \cos\theta$, with eigenvectors $\partial_\theta$,
$\partial_\varphi + \partial_\psi$ and $\partial_\varphi - \partial_\psi$ (@def-eigenvalue); their product is
$\sin^2\theta$, confirming $\det G = \sin^2\theta/64$. At $\theta \to 0$ the eigenvalue $1 - \cos\theta$ vanishes:
the direction $\partial_\varphi - \partial_\psi$ collapses, which is the statement that only $\varphi + \psi$ matters
there (@exr-su2-det-euler). The metric with these components is the bi-invariant metric of $SU(2)$ in
@sec-induced-metrics.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The lengths and angles encoded in @eq-su2-gram can be read off directly, and the first exercise asks for them.
The angle between the $\varphi$- and $\psi$-curves turns out to be $\theta$ itself, a neat way to remember why the
chart degenerates at $\theta = 0$ and $\pi$.

::: {#exr-su2-gram-angle}
#### Lengths and angles of the Euler coordinate curves

From @eq-su2-gram, find the lengths of the three coordinate velocities of the Euler-angle parametrisation and the
angle $\alpha$ between the $\varphi$- and $\psi$-velocities; what happens to $\alpha$ as $\theta \to 0$ and $\theta
\to \pi$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The diagonal entries are all $\tfrac14$, so the three velocities have length $\tfrac12$. The cosine of the angle
between the $\varphi$- and $\psi$-velocities is $G_{\varphi\psi}/\sqrt{G_{\varphi\varphi}G_{\psi\psi}} =
(\cos\theta/4)/(1/4) = \cos\theta$, so $\alpha = \theta$: the two velocities are orthogonal at $\theta = \pi/2$,
become parallel as $\theta \to 0$ and antiparallel as $\theta \to \pi$. In both limits the three velocities span
only a plane, the rank drops and the chart degenerates, which is $\det G = \sin^2\theta/64 \to 0$.
:::

The second exercise computes @eq-su2-gram with Sage from the four real components of @exm-parametrisation-su2 and
finds the determinant. The computation rederives @prp-su2-gram symbolically and needs the half-angle identities,
handled by Sage's trigonometric simplification.

::: {#exr-su2-gram-sage}
#### The Gram matrix of $SU(2)$ in Sage

Write the four real components of the Euler-angle parametrisation of $SU(2)$, compute $J^{\mathsf{T}} J$ with
Sage and show that it equals @eq-su2-gram; compute the determinant and the cosine of the angle between the
$\varphi$- and $\psi$-velocities.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $E = (\cos\tfrac\theta2\cos\tfrac{\varphi + \psi}2,\ -\cos\tfrac\theta2\sin\tfrac{\varphi + \psi}2,\
\sin\tfrac\theta2\sin\tfrac{\varphi - \psi}2,\ -\sin\tfrac\theta2\cos\tfrac{\varphi - \psi}2)$, which lies on
$S^3$, the Jacobian is a $4 \times 3$ matrix and $J^{\mathsf{T}} J$ simplifies to $\tfrac14\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0
& 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \cos\theta \\ 0 & \cos\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ after `trig_reduce`; the determinant is
$\sin^2\theta/64$ and the cosine of the angle is $\cos\theta$ (@exr-su2-gram-angle):

{{< sage exr-su2-gram-sage >}}
:::

The volume integral of @exm-su2-gram-volume is the third exercise, with a twist: halving the range of $\psi$
halves the volume, and the result is the volume of the rotation group, which $SU(2)$ covers twice. The
computation is the same as for the area of the sphere, with one more angle.

::: {#exr-su2-gram-volume}
#### The volume of $SU(2)$ and of $SO(3)$

Compute $\int \sqrt{\det G}\, d\theta\, d\varphi\, d\psi$ over the Euler chart $(0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi) \times
(0, 4\pi)$, and over the same chart with $\psi \in (0, 2\pi)$. Explain why the second number is the volume of the
rotation group $SO(3)$ with the metric inherited from $SU(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sqrt{\det G} = \sin\theta/8$ on the chart, and $\int_0^\pi \sin\theta\, d\theta = 2$, so the volume is $\tfrac28
\cdot 2\pi \cdot 4\pi = 2\pi^2$ with $\psi \in (0, 4\pi)$ and $\pi^2$ with $\psi \in (0, 2\pi)$. The matrices $g$
and $-g$ are the same rotation (@sec-lie-groups), and in Euler angles $-g = g(\theta, \varphi, \psi + 2\pi)$ by
@exr-su2-det-euler, so the range $\psi \in (0, 2\pi)$ covers each rotation exactly once: $SO(3) = SU(2)/\{\pm 1\}$
has half the volume, $\pi^2$. The independent check of $2\pi^2$ through a stereographic chart is
@exr-cm-s3-volume.
:::
::::

### Exercises {#sec-charts-manifolds-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the sections of this chapter: the volume of the three-sphere computed in two atlases,
the Mercator chart of the sphere with its transition map and Gram matrix, and the length of a closed curve on the
torus.

The first integrative exercise returns to the stereographic atlas of $S^3$ built in @exr-manifold-s3-charts and
computes its Gram matrix, which turns out to be conformal like that of $S^2$. Integrating the area factor over
$\mathbb{R}^3$ must reproduce the volume $2\pi^2$ found with the Euler angles, a check that two unrelated charts
of the same manifold agree on a global quantity.

::: {#exr-cm-s3-volume}
#### The volume of $S^3$ in two charts

Compute the Gram matrix of the north stereographic parametrisation of $S^3$, $(u, v, w) \mapsto (2u, 2v, 2w,
\rho^2 - 1)/(1 + \rho^2)$, show that it is $4/(1 + \rho^2)^2$ times the identity, and integrate $\sqrt{\det G}$
over $\mathbb{R}^3$. Compare with the volume computed from the Euler-angle Gram matrix @eq-su2-gram.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The three coordinate velocities are orthogonal with common length $2/(1 + \rho^2)$, as in
@exr-velocity-stereographic one dimension up, so $G = 4/(1 + \rho^2)^2\, 1_3$ and $\sqrt{\det G} = 8/(1 +
\rho^2)^3$. Integrating over spherical shells of $\mathbb{R}^3$, the volume is $\int_0^\infty 4\pi\rho^2 \cdot 8/(1 +
\rho^2)^3\, d\rho = 32\pi \cdot \pi/16 = 2\pi^2$, and the Euler-angle chart gives $\int \sin\theta/8 = 2\pi^2$ as
well (@exm-su2-gram-volume). The chart of @exr-manifold-s3-charts misses one point and the Euler chart misses two
circles, both of volume zero:

{{< sage exr-cm-s3-volume >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise introduces a fourth chart on the sphere, the Mercator chart of navigators, and
runs it through the whole chapter: domain, transition map to spherical coordinates with its Jacobian, Gram matrix,
and finally its relation to the stereographic chart, which is a complex logarithm. Everything can be done by hand.

::: {#exr-cm-mercator}
#### The Mercator chart

The Mercator parametrisation of the sphere is $(\lambda, y) \mapsto (\cos\lambda/\cosh y,\ \sin\lambda/\cosh y,\
\tanh y)$ with $\lambda \in (0, 2\pi)$, $y \in \mathbb{R}$. Show that it lands on the sphere and find its image;
compute the transition map from spherical coordinates and its Jacobian determinant; compute the Gram matrix and
show that the chart is conformal; and show that the stereographic coordinate $w = u + iv$ of the same point is
$e^{y + i\lambda}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1/\cosh^2 y + \tanh^2 y = (1 + \sinh^2 y)/\cosh^2 y = 1$. As $y \to \pm\infty$, $Z \to \pm 1$,
so the image is the sphere minus the poles and the half-meridian $\lambda = 0$: the same domain as the spherical
chart. Comparing with @eq-sphere-embedding, $\lambda = \varphi$ and $\tanh y = \cos\theta$, that is $y =
\operatorname{artanh}(\cos\theta) = \ln\cot(\theta/2)$, and $1/\cosh y = \sin\theta$; the Jacobian of $(\theta,
\varphi) \mapsto (\lambda, y)$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1/\sin\theta & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ with determinant
$1/\sin\theta \neq 0$, so the Mercator chart is compatible with the spherical atlas. The velocities
$\partial_\lambda E = (-\sin\lambda, \cos\lambda, 0)/\cosh y$ and $\partial_y E = (-\cos\lambda\sinh y, -
\sin\lambda\sinh y, 1)/\cosh^2 y$ are orthogonal with equal length $1/\cosh y$, so $G = \cosh^{-2} y\, 1$:
conformal, which is why Mercator maps preserve compass bearings. Finally $u + iv = (X + iY)/(1 - Z) = e^{i\lambda}
/(\cosh y - \sinh y) = e^{y + i\lambda}$, so $y + i\lambda = \log w$: the Mercator chart is the complex logarithm of
the stereographic one, and its conformality follows from that of the stereographic chart and the holomorphy of the
logarithm (@exr-stereographic-complex).
:::

The third integrative exercise measures the closed curve $(t, 2t)$ of @exm-torus-curve with the Gram matrix of the
torus, combining the product chart, the curve and the metric. The speed is a trigonometric expression whose
integral is not elementary, so Sage evaluates it numerically and checks it against the speed computed directly in
$\mathbb{R}^3$.

::: {#exr-cm-torus-curve-length}
#### The length of a curve on the torus

For the torus with $R = 2$, $r = 1$, use the Gram matrix $G = \operatorname{diag}(r^2, (R + r\cos a)^2)$ to find
the lengths of a tube circle and of the axis circles at $a = 0$ and $a = \pi$, then compute the speed
$\sqrt{G_{ij}\dot x^i \dot x^j}$ of the curve $\gamma(t) = (t, 2t)$, check it against $|dE/dt|$ in
$\mathbb{R}^3$, and evaluate the length of the closed curve numerically with bounds.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A tube circle has length $\int_0^{2\pi} r\, da = 2\pi$; the axis circles have lengths $2\pi(R + r) = 6\pi$ at $a =
0$ and $2\pi(R - r) = 2\pi$ at $a = \pi$. For $\gamma(t) = (t, 2t)$, $\dot x = (1, 2)$ and the speed squared is
$G_{aa} + 4G_{bb} = 1 + 4(2 + \cos t)^2$, which agrees with $|dE/dt|^2$ computed from the embedding; since $2 +
\cos t$ ranges over $[1, 3]$ the speed lies between $\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt{37}$, so the length lies between $2\pi\sqrt5
\approx 14.05$ and $2\pi\sqrt{37} \approx 38.22$. Numerically it is $26.01$:

{{< sage exr-cm-torus-curve-length >}}
:::
::::

## Vector fields, forms and tensors {#sec-vector-fields-forms-tensors}

Tangent vectors are the velocities of curves, vector fields assign one to every point, one-forms are their duals, tensor fields combine them, and differential forms are the antisymmetric tensors that can be integrated and differentiated. Five sections.

### Tangent vectors {#sec-tangent-vectors}

The derivative of a function along a curve, @eq-velocity, is a number that does not depend on the chart, although
every term on its right-hand side does. The object that produces this number, the velocity of the curve, is a
tangent vector. This chapter defines tangent vectors as directional derivatives, their coordinate basis and
components, and the tangent space, and shows how components change when the chart changes.

#### Tangent vectors and velocities

On a curved surface there are no arrows that can be slid from point to point, but there is still a way to say "in
which direction and how fast": differentiate functions. The definition below takes this operation, a directional
derivative at one point, as the tangent vector itself, and the picture to keep is an arrow on the tangent plane that
acts on functions by measuring their rate of change.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-tangent-vector}
#### Tangent vector

A **tangent vector** at a point $p$ of a manifold is a linear map $X : f \mapsto X(f) \in \mathbb{R}$ on smooth
functions (@def-smooth-function) satisfying the **Leibniz rule** $X(fg) = X(f)\, g(p) + f(p)\, X(g)$: a
directional derivative at $p$. In a chart, every such map is of the form $X(f) = X^i\, \partial_i f(p)$ for some
numbers $X^i$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest directional derivatives at a point of the sphere are the two partial derivatives of the spherical chart.
The first example checks the two defining properties on them and on their combinations, which already exhaust all
tangent vectors at the point.

::: {#exm-tangent-partial}
#### Partial derivatives

$f \mapsto \partial_\theta f(p)$ and $f \mapsto \partial_\varphi f(p)$ on the sphere are tangent vectors at $p$:
linear, and obeying the Leibniz rule because partial derivatives do. So is any combination $f \mapsto
a\,\partial_\theta f(p) + b\,\partial_\varphi f(p)$.
:::

A definition by properties is best understood through the operations that fail them. The second example shows that
linearity alone is not enough: evaluation and second derivatives are linear maps on functions, and the Leibniz rule
is what excludes them.

::: {#exm-tangent-not}
#### What is not a tangent vector

$f \mapsto f(p)$ (evaluation) is linear but violates the Leibniz rule, since $f(p)g(p) \neq 2 f(p) g(p)$ in
general; $f \mapsto \partial_\theta^2 f(p)$ violates it too, as second derivatives of products produce cross
terms. Tangent vectors are exactly the first-order operators.
:::

In Euclidean space arrows and directional derivatives can be compared directly. The third example identifies them,
which explains why the definition is phrased through functions: it is the part of the familiar notion that survives on
a manifold, where only charts are available.

::: {#exm-tangent-rn}
#### In $\mathbb{R}^n$

At a point $p$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$, the tangent vector with components $X^i$ is the directional derivative along the
arrow $X$, $f \mapsto \frac{d}{dt} f(p + tX)|_{t = 0} = X^i \partial_i f(p)$ (@exm-jacobian-function); arrows at
$p$ and tangent vectors at $p$ are the same thing, and the definition above is what survives when there are no
arrows, only charts.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The examples above checked the Leibniz rule by hand for coordinate derivatives. The first exercise asks for the same
check on a concrete combination and two concrete functions, so that the cross terms of the product rule can be seen
to cancel.

::: {#exr-tv-leibniz-check}
#### The Leibniz rule on two functions

For $X = 2\,\partial_\theta - \partial_\varphi$ at the point $p = (\theta, \varphi) = (\pi/3, \pi/4)$ of the sphere and
$f = \cos\theta$, $g = \sin\varphi$, compute $X(f)$, $X(g)$ and $X(fg)$, and check that $X(fg) = X(f)\,g(p) +
f(p)\,X(g)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$X(f) = 2\,\partial_\theta\cos\theta = -2\sin\theta = -\sqrt3$ and $X(g) = -\partial_\varphi\sin\varphi = -\cos\varphi
= -\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ at $p$. For the product $fg = \cos\theta\sin\varphi$,
$$
X(fg) = -2\sin\theta\sin\varphi - \cos\theta\cos\varphi = -2 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} -
\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} = -\tfrac{\sqrt6}{2} - \tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}.
$$
On the other side, $X(f)\,g(p) + f(p)\,X(g) = -\sqrt3\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} + \tfrac12\cdot(-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2})$, the
same number: each term of $X(fg)$ differentiates one factor and evaluates the other at $p$.
:::

Two consequences of the axioms are used constantly: a tangent vector kills constants, and it is determined by what it
does to the coordinate functions. The second exercise derives both from linearity and the Leibniz rule alone.

::: {#exr-tv-constants}
#### Constants and coordinate functions

Show from the definition that a tangent vector $X$ at $p$ satisfies $X(c) = 0$ for every constant function $c$, and
that in a chart its components are $X^i = X(x^i)$, the values on the coordinate functions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the constant function $1$, the Leibniz rule gives $X(1) = X(1 \cdot 1) = X(1) \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot X(1) = 2X(1)$,
so $X(1) = 0$, and by linearity $X(c) = cX(1) = 0$. Writing $X(f) = X^j\,\partial_j f(p)$ and taking $f = x^i$, a
coordinate function, gives $X(x^i) = X^j\,\delta^i_j = X^i$: the components are the rates of change of the
coordinates along $X$, and two tangent vectors that agree on the $n$ coordinate functions are equal.
:::

The last exercise in this group generalises the second example to arbitrary components and arbitrary functions, a
computation that SageManifolds does symbolically. It also measures exactly how a second derivative fails the
Leibniz rule.

::: {#exr-tv-derivations}
#### Derivations with SageManifolds

With SageManifolds, take a vector field $X = a\,\partial_\theta + b\,\partial_\varphi$ with arbitrary component
functions $a, b$ and two arbitrary functions $f, g$ on the sphere; check the Leibniz rule, $X(1) = 0$ and $X(\theta)
= a$, $X(\varphi) = b$, and compute the defect $D(fg) - D(f)g - fD(g)$ of $D = \partial_\theta^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All three properties hold identically, and the defect of the second derivative is $2\,\partial_\theta f\,
\partial_\theta g$, the cross term of the product rule applied twice, which is not zero in general:

{{< sage exr-tv-derivations >}}
:::
::::

The most important source of tangent vectors is motion: a point moving along a curve has a velocity at every
instant. The next definition makes this precise as a directional derivative along the curve, and it is the reason the
abstract definition above is the right one.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-velocity}
#### Velocity of a curve

The **velocity** of a curve $\gamma$ at the parameter value $t$ is the tangent vector $\dot\gamma(t) : f \mapsto
\frac{d}{dt} f(\gamma(t))$ at the point $\gamma(t)$; in a chart its components are $\dot x^i(t)$, by @eq-velocity.
Every tangent vector is the velocity of some curve.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coordinate curves of the spherical chart are the parallels and the meridians. Their velocities are the two
partial derivatives, which is the first example and the bridge between curves and the coordinate basis of the next
subsection.

::: {#exm-velocity-parallel}
#### Parallel and meridian

The velocity of the parallel $\gamma(t) = (\theta_0, \varphi_0 + t)$ is $f \mapsto \partial_\varphi f$, components
$(0, 1)$; the velocity of the meridian $(t, \varphi_0)$ is $f \mapsto \partial_\theta f$, components $(1, 0)$
(@exm-parallel-curve, @exm-meridian-curve).
:::

A curve that moves in both coordinates at once has a velocity with two non-zero components. The second example reads
them off for a straight line in the chart and applies the resulting vector to the height function.

::: {#exm-velocity-general}
#### A slanted curve

The velocity of $t \mapsto (\pi/3 + t, \pi/4 + 2t)$ is $f \mapsto \partial_\theta f + 2\,\partial_\varphi f$,
components $(1, 2)$; applied to the height $Z = \cos\theta$ it gives $-\sin(\pi/3) = -\sqrt3/2$ at $t = 0$
(@exr-curve-velocity, @prp-velocity-height).
:::

For a surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$ the velocity is also an ordinary arrow, the derivative of the ambient position. The
third example connects the two descriptions through the Jacobian of the embedding, and the figure shows the tangent
plane in which all such arrows lie.

::: {#exm-velocity-ambient}
#### Velocities seen in the ambient space

For an embedded surface the velocity of a curve, as a vector in $\mathbb{R}^N$, is $\dot x^i\partial_i E$, a
combination of the coordinate velocities of @def-coordinate-velocity; it lies in the plane spanned by them, the
**tangent plane** of the surface at the point (@fig-tangent-vectors).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![Tangent vectors on the sphere at $(\theta, \varphi) = (\pi/3, \pi/4)$: the tangent plane (grey), the coordinate
basis vectors $\partial_\theta$ (red, tangent to the meridian) and $\partial_\varphi$ (green, tangent to the
parallel), and a general tangent vector $X = 0.4\,\partial_\theta + 0.5\,\partial_\varphi$ (blue). Generated by
`figures/tangent_vectors.sage`.](figures/tangent_vectors.png){#fig-tangent-vectors width=55%}

The slanted curve of the examples is the subject of the first exercise, now computed with SageManifolds' curves. It
checks that the chart formula for the velocity reproduces the rate of change of the height along the curve.

::: {#exr-curve-velocity}
#### The velocity of a curve

With SageManifolds, define the curve $\gamma(t) = (\pi/3 + t, \pi/4 + 2t)$ on the sphere, compute its velocity as
a tangent vector field along it, and check @eq-velocity on the height function.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-curve-velocity >}}
:::

A great circle that is not a coordinate curve has a velocity whose components change along it. The second exercise
computes them at one point, from the chart coordinates of the curve, and compares with the ambient derivative.

::: {#exr-tv-great-circle}
#### The velocity of a great circle

The great circle $E(t) = (\cos t, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin t, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin t)$ lies on the unit sphere. Find
its spherical coordinates $(\theta(t), \varphi(t))$ for $0 < t < \pi/2$, the components of its velocity at
$t = \pi/4$, and the value of the velocity on the height $Z$; compare with $\frac{d}{dt}Z(E(t))$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\cos\theta = Z = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin t$ and $\tan\varphi = Y/X = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\tan t$. At $t = \pi/4$ the point
is $(\theta, \varphi) = (\pi/3, \arctan\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})$ and the velocity has components $(\dot\theta, \dot\varphi)
= (-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}, \tfrac{2\sqrt2}{3})$. On the height it gives $-\sin\theta\,\dot\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}
\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} = \tfrac12$, which is $\frac{d}{dt}\big(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin t\big) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos t$
at $t = \pi/4$:

{{< sage exr-tv-great-circle >}}
:::

The velocity depends on the parametrisation, not only on the path. The third exercise shows how it rescales under a
change of parameter, and deduces from a straight line in a chart that every tangent vector is a velocity.

::: {#exr-tv-reparametrisation}
#### Reparametrisation and every vector as a velocity

Let $\gamma$ be a curve and $\tilde\gamma(s) = \gamma(t(s))$ a reparametrisation. Show that $\dot{\tilde\gamma}(s) =
t'(s)\,\dot\gamma(t(s))$. Then show that every tangent vector $X$ at $p$ is the velocity at $t = 0$ of the curve
with coordinates $x^i(t) = x^i(p) + tX^i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the chain rule, $\dot{\tilde\gamma}(s)(f) = \frac{d}{ds}f(\gamma(t(s))) = t'(s)\,\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))
\big|_{t = t(s)}$, so the velocity is rescaled by $t'(s)$ and reversed when $t' < 0$; the path is the same. For the
second statement, the curve stays in the chart domain for small $|t|$ because the domain is open, and by
@eq-velocity its velocity at $t = 0$ has components $\dot x^i(0) = X^i$, hence equals $X = X^i\partial_i$.
:::
::::

#### Coordinate basis and components

Every tangent vector at a point is a combination of finitely many special ones, and a chart supplies them: the
velocities of its coordinate curves. The definition below names this basis, which turns tangent vectors into columns
of numbers and makes calculations possible.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-coordinate-basis}
#### Coordinate basis

In a chart the **coordinate basis** vectors at $p$ are $\partial_i = \partial/\partial x^i$, the velocities of the
coordinate curves (@def-coordinate-curve): $\partial_i$ sends $f$ to its partial derivative $\partial f/\partial
x^i$ at $p$. They are linearly independent and every tangent vector at $p$ is a combination of them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the sphere the coordinate basis consists of the vectors tangent to the meridian and to the parallel. The first
example identifies them with the columns of the Jacobian of the embedding and notes the length of each.

::: {#exm-basis-sphere}
#### The basis on the sphere

$\partial_\theta$ and $\partial_\varphi$, tangent to the meridian and the parallel through the point
(@fig-tangent-vectors); as ambient vectors they are the columns @eq-sphere-jacobian, and $\partial_\varphi$ has
ambient length $\sin\theta$.
:::

The coordinate basis belongs to the chart, not only to the point. The second example compares the Cartesian and polar
bases of the plane at the same point, where they are different pairs of arrows of different lengths.

::: {#exm-basis-polar}
#### The basis in polar coordinates

On the plane in polar coordinates, $\partial_r$ points radially outward with unit length and $\partial_\varphi$
points along the circle through the point with length $r$ (@fig-jacobian-polar): the basis depends on the chart,
not only on the point, while in Cartesian coordinates $\partial_x, \partial_y$ are the same two arrows everywhere.
:::

A chart that covers the sphere near its south pole gives a third coordinate basis. The third example describes it in
the stereographic chart, where the two basis vectors are orthogonal and of equal length but the length varies from
point to point.

::: {#exm-basis-stereographic}
#### The stereographic basis

In the stereographic chart the basis vectors $\partial_u$, $\partial_v$ are orthogonal with equal ambient length
$2/(1 + u^2 + v^2)$ (@exr-stereographic-gram); at the point with $u^2 + v^2 = 1$ (the equator) they have length
$1$ and far from the origin they shrink, since the chart compresses the neighbourhood of the north pole.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The lengths quoted in the third example are best checked by computing the ambient vectors directly. The first exercise
does this with the Jacobian of the inverse stereographic map and finds where the chart stretches or compresses the
sphere.

::: {#exr-tv-stereo-basis}
#### The stereographic basis in $\mathbb{R}^3$

With the embedding $E(u, v) = (2u, 2v, u^2 + v^2 - 1)/(1 + u^2 + v^2)$ of the stereographic chart, compute with
SageManifolds the ambient vectors $\partial_u E$ and $\partial_v E$, check that they are tangent to the sphere and
orthogonal, and find their common length at the origin, on the unit circle and at $(u, v) = (3, 0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both vectors are orthogonal to the position vector and to each other, with $|\partial_uE|^2 = |\partial_vE|^2 =
4/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$: the length is $2$ at the south pole $u = v = 0$, $1$ on the equator $u^2 + v^2 = 1$ and
$\tfrac15$ at $(3, 0)$, where a unit step in the chart covers a short distance on the sphere:

{{< sage exr-tv-stereo-basis >}}
:::

The torus is the third running surface, and its chart has a coordinate basis that can be found in two lines. The second
exercise asks for its ambient vectors and their lengths, which differ on the outer and inner equators.

::: {#exr-tv-torus-basis}
#### The coordinate basis of the torus

For the torus $E(a, b) = ((R + r\cos a)\cos b, (R + r\cos a)\sin b, r\sin a)$ with $R > r > 0$, compute $\partial_aE$
and $\partial_bE$, show that they are orthogonal, and find their lengths. Where is $\partial_b$ longest?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_aE = (-r\sin a\cos b, -r\sin a\sin b, r\cos a)$ and $\partial_bE = (-(R + r\cos a)\sin b, (R + r\cos a)\cos
b, 0)$. Their dot product is $r\sin a(R + r\cos a)(\cos b\sin b - \sin b\cos b) = 0$. The lengths are $|\partial_a| =
r$ and $|\partial_b| = R + r\cos a$: the $b$-circles are horizontal circles of radius $R + r\cos a$, longest on the
outer equator $a = 0$ (radius $R + r$) and shortest on the inner one $a = \pi$ (radius $R - r$).
:::

The definition asserts that the coordinate basis vectors are linearly independent. The third exercise proves it by
letting a vanishing combination act on the coordinate functions, the argument of @exr-tv-constants.

::: {#exr-tv-basis-independence}
#### Independence of the coordinate basis

Show that if $a^i\partial_i = 0$ at $p$ then all $a^i = 0$, and deduce that $T_pM$ has dimension exactly $n$ once
it is known that every tangent vector is a combination of the $\partial_i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Apply the zero vector $a^i\partial_i$ to the coordinate function $x^j$: $0 = a^i\,\partial_ix^j = a^i\delta^j_i =
a^j$. So the $n$ vectors $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_n$ are independent, and since they span the tangent vectors at
$p$ they form a basis: the dimension is $n$, the number of coordinates, in every chart (@def-dimension).
:::
::::

Having a basis, each tangent vector becomes a list of numbers, its components. The next definition records how these
numbers change when the chart changes, the transformation law that every later object of the chapter generalises.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-components}
#### Components of a tangent vector

Every tangent vector at $p$ is a unique combination
$$
X = X^i\, \partial_i, \qquad X(f) = X^i\, \partial_i f ,
$$ {#eq-tangent-vector}
and the $n$ numbers $X^i$ are its **components** in the chart. Under a change of chart $x \to x'$ the chain rule
(@thm-chain-rule) gives
$$
\partial_i = \frac{\partial x'^j}{\partial x^i}\, \partial'_j, \qquad X'^j = \frac{\partial x'^j}{\partial x^i}\, X^i :
$$ {#eq-vector-transformation}
the components transform with the Jacobian of the transition map while the vector itself does not change.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The rotation field of the sphere has the simplest possible components in the spherical chart and less simple ones in
the stereographic chart. The first example applies the transformation law to it and finds the generator of rotations
of the chart plane.

::: {#exm-components-sphere}
#### Components in spherical and stereographic coordinates

The vector $\partial_\varphi$ has components $(0, 1)$ in spherical coordinates and, by @eq-vector-transformation
with $\partial u/\partial\varphi = -v$, $\partial v/\partial\varphi = u$ (@prp-dphi-stereographic), components
$(-v, u)$ in stereographic coordinates: $\partial_\varphi = -v\,\partial_u + u\,\partial_v$, the generator of
rotations of the $(u, v)$-plane.
:::

When the transition map is a translation, the Jacobian is the identity and components do not change. The second
example is the circle with its two angle charts, the simplest case of the law.

::: {#exm-components-circle}
#### Components on the circle

$\partial_\varphi$ has component $1$ in both angle charts, since $\varphi' = \varphi + \text{const}$ on each
piece of the overlap (@exm-transition-circle): the Jacobian of the transition map is $1$.
:::

The third example goes the other way, writing the polar basis vectors of the plane in Cartesian components. The
columns of the Jacobian appear directly as the answer, a pattern used throughout the chapter.

::: {#exm-components-polar}
#### From polar to Cartesian
