With $x = r\cos\varphi$, $y = r\sin\varphi$, the Jacobian @exm-jacobian-polar gives $\partial_r = \cos\varphi\,
\partial_x + \sin\varphi\,\partial_y$ and $\partial_\varphi = -r\sin\varphi\,\partial_x + r\cos\varphi\,\partial_y$:
the columns of the Jacobian are the components of the polar basis vectors in the Cartesian basis
(@exr-components-polar).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The rotation field of the first example is the subject of the first exercise, worked first by hand from the
transformation law and then displayed with SageManifolds in the stereographic frame. The two partial derivatives
of the transition map that enter are the ones computed in @exm-transition-spherical.

::: {#exr-dphi-stereographic}
#### A vector in another chart

Using @eq-vector-transformation, find the components of $\partial_\varphi$ in the north stereographic chart, and
confirm with SageManifolds by displaying the vector field in the stereographic frame.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $X^\theta = 0$, $X^\varphi = 1$: $X^u = \partial u/\partial\varphi = -\sin\theta\sin\varphi/(1 - \cos\theta)
= -v$ and $X^v = \partial v/\partial\varphi = u$, so $\partial_\varphi = -v\,\partial_u + u\,\partial_v$. In
SageManifolds:

{{< sage exr-dphi-stereographic >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The two derivatives $\partial u/\partial\varphi = -v$ and $\partial v/\partial\varphi = u$ are proved in Lean.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.dphi_v >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second exercise runs the transformation law in both directions on the plane. Inverting the Jacobian brings out
the factor $1/r$ that marks the failure of polar coordinates at the origin.

::: {#exr-components-polar}
#### Polar basis vectors in Cartesian components

Express $\partial_r$ and $\partial_\varphi$ in terms of $\partial_x$ and $\partial_y$, and conversely $\partial_x$
in terms of $\partial_r$ and $\partial_\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @eq-vector-transformation with $x' = (x, y)$, $x = (r, \varphi)$: $\partial_r = \frac{\partial x}{\partial r}
\partial_x + \frac{\partial y}{\partial r}\partial_y = \cos\varphi\,\partial_x + \sin\varphi\,\partial_y$ and
$\partial_\varphi = -r\sin\varphi\,\partial_x + r\cos\varphi\,\partial_y$. Inverting the Jacobian (@exm-chain-inverse),
$\partial_x = \cos\varphi\,\partial_r - \frac{\sin\varphi}{r}\,\partial_\varphi$: the inverse Jacobian has the
$1/r$ that makes $\partial_x$ well defined only away from the origin, where polar coordinates fail.
:::

The gradient field of the height has a surprisingly simple form in the stereographic chart. The third exercise finds
it from the transformation law with SageManifolds, which turns a computation with half-angle formulas into one line.

::: {#exr-tv-gradient-stereographic}
#### The gradient field in the stereographic chart

Find the stereographic components of $X = -\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ from @eq-vector-transformation, using $u =
\cot(\theta/2)\cos\varphi$, $v = \cot(\theta/2)\sin\varphi$, and confirm with SageManifolds. What do its integral
curves look like in the chart plane?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial u/\partial\theta = -\cos\varphi/(2\sin^2(\theta/2))$, so $X^u = -\sin\theta\,\partial u/\partial\theta =
2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)\cos\varphi/(2\sin^2(\theta/2)) = \cot(\theta/2)\cos\varphi = u$, and likewise $X^v = v$:
$X = u\,\partial_u + v\,\partial_v$, the radial field of the plane. Its integral curves are rays leaving the origin
(the south pole), the images of the meridians, which run towards the north pole at infinity:

{{< sage exr-tv-gradient-stereographic >}}
:::
::::

All the tangent vectors at one point form a vector space, and the next definition gives it a name. The picture is the
tangent plane of an embedded surface, but the definition needs no ambient space.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-tangent-space}
#### Tangent space

The tangent vectors at $p$ form an $n$-dimensional vector space (@def-vector-space), the **tangent space**
$T_pM$, with basis $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_n$. Its dimension equals that of the manifold, and tangent spaces
at different points are different vector spaces: there is no canonical way to add a vector at $p$ to a vector at
$q$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$ the tangent space is a plane through the origin parallel to the tangent plane at the
point. The first example identifies it and its dimension.

::: {#exm-tangent-space-sphere}
#### $T_pS^2$ is the tangent plane

For the embedded sphere, $T_pS^2$ is identified with the plane through $p$ spanned by $\partial_\theta E$ and
$\partial_\varphi E$, the plane perpendicular to the position vector $p$ (@fig-tangent-vectors), of dimension $2$.
:::

Groups of matrices are manifolds, and their tangent spaces at the identity are spaces of matrices. The second example
describes the one of $SU(2)$, which is the Lie algebra studied later in the book.

::: {#exm-tangent-space-group}
#### The tangent space of $SU(2)$ at the identity

$T_eSU(2)$ is three-dimensional; its elements are the velocities $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}|_{t=0} = A$ of one-parameter
families of matrices, the traceless anti-Hermitian matrices $A$: this tangent space is the Lie algebra
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ of @sec-lie-algebras.
:::

Euclidean space is the one manifold whose tangent spaces are all canonically the same. The third example explains the
identification and why it fails elsewhere, which is the motivation for connections.

::: {#exm-tangent-space-rn}
#### $T_p\mathbb{R}^n$

Every tangent space of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a copy of $\mathbb{R}^n$ itself, with $\partial_i$ corresponding to the
$i$-th standard basis vector $e_i$; it is only in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that vectors at different points can be compared
without further structure. On a general manifold that comparison needs a connection (@sec-covariant-derivative).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A change of chart acts on a single tangent space as a change of basis of a two-dimensional vector space. The first
exercise carries it out at one point of the plane with numbers, in both directions.

::: {#exr-tv-basis-change-tangent}
#### A change of basis in one tangent space

At the point $(x, y) = (1, 1)$ of the plane, express $\partial_r$ and $\partial_\varphi$ in the Cartesian basis, write
$X = 3\,\partial_x + \partial_y$ in the polar basis, and check the result.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At $(1, 1)$, $r = \sqrt2$ and $\varphi = \pi/4$, so by @exm-components-polar $\partial_r = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}
(\partial_x + \partial_y)$ and $\partial_\varphi = -\partial_x + \partial_y$. By the inverse law, $X^r = (xX^x +
yX^y)/r = 4/\sqrt2 = 2\sqrt2$ and $X^\varphi = (-yX^x + xX^y)/r^2 = (-3 + 1)/2 = -1$. Check: $2\sqrt2 \cdot
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\partial_x + \partial_y) - (-\partial_x + \partial_y) = 3\,\partial_x + \partial_y$.
:::

The second exercise computes the tangent spaces of two matrix groups, $SO(2)$ and $SO(3)$, at the identity. It shows
that the defining equation of the group becomes, after differentiation, a linear condition on the velocity.

::: {#exr-tv-so-tangent}
#### Tangent spaces of rotation groups

Differentiate $R(t)^{\mathsf T}R(t) = 1$ at $t = 0$ for a curve of rotation matrices with $R(0) = 1$, and conclude
that $T_1SO(n)$ consists of antisymmetric matrices. Give a basis for $n = 2$ and the dimension for $n = 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $A = \dot R(0)$, the derivative of $R^{\mathsf T}R = 1$ at $t = 0$ is $A^{\mathsf T} + A = 0$: velocities at
the identity are antisymmetric. Conversely $R(t) = e^{tA}$ is a curve of rotations with velocity $A$ for every
antisymmetric $A$. For $n = 2$ the space is spanned by $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, the
velocity of the rotation by the angle $t$, so $SO(2)$ is one-dimensional; for $n = 3$ an antisymmetric matrix has
three free entries, and $\dim SO(3) = 3$, the three generators $L_a$ of @sec-lie-algebras.
:::

The definition stresses that tangent spaces at different points are different spaces. The third exercise shows what
goes wrong if one adds vectors at two points by adding their components: the answer depends on the chart.

::: {#exr-tv-no-addition}
#### Adding vectors at different points

Take $p = (1, 0)$ and $q = (-1, 0)$ in the plane and the vector $\partial_\varphi$ at each. Add their components in the
polar chart and in the Cartesian chart, and compare the two "sums".
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In polar components both vectors are $(0, 1)$, so the polar "sum" is $(0, 2)$, that is $2\partial_\varphi$, which has
length $2$ at either point. In Cartesian components, $\partial_\varphi = -y\,\partial_x + x\,\partial_y$ is $\partial_y$
at $p$ and $-\partial_y$ at $q$, so the Cartesian "sum" is $0$. The two procedures disagree, so neither defines an
operation on vectors: comparing vectors at different points needs extra structure, a connection
(@sec-covariant-derivative), which in $\mathbb{R}^n$ happens to be the Cartesian one.
:::
::::

The two propositions that close the section record, as general statements, the two computations used most often
above: a tangent vector acting on the height function, and the stereographic components of the rotation field. The first one
is the general-point version of @exm-velocity-general.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-velocity-height}
#### A velocity acting on the height

For $X = \partial_\theta + 2\,\partial_\varphi$, $X(Z) = -\sin\theta$ with $Z = \cos\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.velocity_on_height`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.velocity_on_height >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Since $X(Z) = -\sin\theta$ does not depend on $\varphi$, it can be read off on any meridian. The first example
evaluates it at a few latitudes and finds where the vector moves horizontally.

::: {#exm-tv-height-points}
#### The value at a few points

At $\theta = \pi/3$, $X(Z) = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, the number of @exm-velocity-general; on the equator $\theta =
\pi/2$ it is $-1$, the largest possible rate of descent for a vector whose $\theta$-component is $1$; near the poles
it tends to $0$, since the height is stationary there. The component $2$ along $\partial_\varphi$ never contributes,
because $Z$ is constant on parallels.
:::

The proposition is a sum over components, and writing the sum out term by term shows which entries matter and
which drop out. The second example does so for an arbitrary tangent vector, not only for the one of the proposition.

::: {#exm-tv-height-lean}
#### The value as a sum over components

For $X = X^\theta\partial_\theta + X^\varphi\partial_\varphi$, @eq-tangent-vector gives $X(Z) =
X^\theta\,\partial_\theta Z + X^\varphi\,\partial_\varphi Z$. With $Z = \cos\theta$ the partial derivatives are
$\partial_\theta Z = -\sin\theta$ and $\partial_\varphi Z = 0$ (@prp-dZ), so $X(Z) = -X^\theta\sin\theta$ for every
$X$. For the components $(1, 2)$ of the proposition this is $-\sin\theta$; for $(3, -5)$ it is $-3\sin\theta$; and
for any multiple of $\partial_\varphi$ it is $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** In the Lean statement `velocity_on_height`, a chart point is `x : Fin 2 → ℝ` with `x 0` $= \theta$ and `x 1` $=
\varphi$, and the sum `∑ i, pd i heightZ x * ![1, 2] i` equals `-Real.sin (x 0)`. Here `heightZ x = Real.cos (x 0)`
is the height in the chart, `pd i` is the partial derivative with respect to the $i$-th coordinate, and `![1, 2]` is
the component vector of $X$: the sum is $X^i\partial_iZ$. The proof rewrites with the two partial derivatives of
`dZ_components` (@prp-dZ) and sums.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The number $X(Z)$ depends on $X$ only through a linear function of its components, which will be the differential of
$Z$. The third example anticipates this and the gradient field that it produces with a metric.

::: {#exm-tv-height-dz}
#### Towards the differential of the height

For any $X = a\,\partial_\theta + b\,\partial_\varphi$, $X(Z) = -a\sin\theta$: a linear function of $(a, b)$ with
coefficients $(-\sin\theta, 0)$. These two numbers are the components of the differential $dZ$ (@prp-dZ), the
cotangent vector of @sec-one-forms, and raising its index with the round metric gives the gradient field
$-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ of @fig-sphere-vector-fields (@prp-raise-lower).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The general vector at a point acts on the height through its $\theta$-component alone. The first exercise makes this
explicit and finds the vectors that leave the height unchanged.

::: {#exr-tv-height-general}
#### Which vectors preserve the height?

For $X = a\,\partial_\theta + b\,\partial_\varphi$ compute $X(Z)$ and $X(Z^2)$, and describe the tangent vectors with
$X(Z) = 0$ at a point that is not a pole.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$X(Z) = -a\sin\theta$ and, by the Leibniz rule, $X(Z^2) = 2Z\,X(Z) = -2a\sin\theta\cos\theta$. Away from the poles
$\sin\theta \neq 0$, so $X(Z) = 0$ exactly when $a = 0$: the vectors tangent to the parallel through the point,
multiples of $\partial_\varphi$, along which the height is constant.
:::

The height is one of three ambient coordinate functions, and the same vector acts on all three. The second exercise
computes the three values with SageManifolds and recognises them as the ambient components of the vector.

::: {#exr-tv-height-ambient}
#### The vector acting on the three ambient coordinates

With SageManifolds, apply $X = \partial_\theta + 2\,\partial_\varphi$ to the functions $X_{\rm amb} =
\sin\theta\cos\varphi$, $Y_{\rm amb} = \sin\theta\sin\varphi$ and $Z = \cos\theta$, and compare the three results with
the ambient vector $\partial_\theta E + 2\,\partial_\varphi E$ of @exm-velocity-ambient.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The three numbers are exactly the components of the ambient vector, since $X(E^k) = X^i\partial_iE^k$; the third is
$-\sin\theta$, the proposition:

{{< sage exr-tv-height-ambient >}}
:::

The proposition concerns one function of the height. The third exercise generalises it to every function of the
height, which is the chain rule in the language of tangent vectors.

::: {#exr-tv-height-function}
#### Functions of the height

Let $h$ be a smooth function of one variable. Show that $X(h(Z)) = h'(Z)\,X(Z) = -h'(\cos\theta)\sin\theta$ for $X =
\partial_\theta + 2\,\partial_\varphi$, and evaluate it for $h(Z) = Z^3$ at $\theta = \pi/3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the chart $h(Z) = h(\cos\theta)$, so $X(h(Z)) = \partial_\theta h(\cos\theta) + 2\,\partial_\varphi h(\cos\theta)
= -h'(\cos\theta)\sin\theta$, which is $h'(Z)X(Z)$ by the proposition. For $h(Z) = Z^3$, $h' = 3Z^2$, and at $\theta
= \pi/3$: $-3 \cdot \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = -\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{8}$.
:::
::::

The second proposition records the stereographic components of the rotation field as two partial derivatives of the
transition map. It is the computation behind @exm-components-sphere and @exr-dphi-stereographic.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-dphi-stereographic}
#### The rotation field in stereographic coordinates

$\partial u/\partial\varphi = -v$ and $\partial v/\partial\varphi = u$ for $u = \sin\theta\cos\varphi/(1 -
\cos\theta)$, $v = \sin\theta\sin\varphi/(1 - \cos\theta)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.dphi_u` and `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.dphi_v`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.dphi_u >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two derivatives can be evaluated at a point of the equator, where the chart is easiest to picture. The first
example does this at two points a quarter turn apart.

::: {#exm-tv-dphi-point}
#### Two points of the equator

At $(\theta, \varphi) = (\pi/2, 0)$, $u = 1$ and $v = 0$, so $(\partial u/\partial\varphi, \partial v/\partial\varphi)
= (-v, u) = (0, 1)$: there $\partial_\varphi = \partial_v$. At $(\pi/2, \pi/2)$, $(u, v) = (0, 1)$ and $\partial_\varphi
= -\partial_u$. In both cases the vector is tangent to the unit circle of the chart plane, the image of the equator.
:::

The two derivatives are short enough to be computed by hand, and doing so shows why the factor $1/(1 - \cos\theta)$
plays no role. The second example differentiates and draws a consequence for the distance from the chart origin.

::: {#exm-tv-dphi-lean}
#### The derivatives by hand

In $u = \sin\theta\cos\varphi/(1 - \cos\theta)$ only $\cos\varphi$ depends on $\varphi$, so $\partial u/\partial\varphi
= -\sin\theta\sin\varphi/(1 - \cos\theta) = -v$; likewise $\partial v/\partial\varphi = \sin\theta\cos\varphi/(1 -
\cos\theta) = u$. Consequently $\partial_\varphi(u^2 + v^2) = 2u(-v) + 2v\,u = 0$: the rotation field does not change
the distance $\sqrt{u^2 + v^2} = \cot(\theta/2)$ from the chart origin, and its flow lines are the circles about
it, the images of the parallels. The formulas hold wherever the chart is defined, $\theta \neq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** In Lean, `stereoU x` is `Real.sin (x 0) * Real.cos (x 1) / (1 - Real.cos (x 0))`, the coordinate $u$ as a function of
$(\theta, \varphi)$ = (`x 0`, `x 1`), and `stereoV x` is the same with `Real.sin (x 1)`. `dphi_u` states `pd 1
stereoU x = -stereoV x`, the derivative with respect to the second coordinate $\varphi$, and `dphi_v` states `pd 1
stereoV x = stereoU x`. There is no hypothesis: at $\theta = 0$, where the chart fails, Lean's convention that
division by zero gives zero makes both sides vanish.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The field $-v\,\partial_u + u\,\partial_v$ generates rotations of the chart plane about its origin. The third example
connects this to the rotations of the sphere and to the two other rotation fields, whose stereographic form is found in
@exr-tv-rotation-stereographic.

::: {#exm-tv-dphi-rotation}
#### Rotations of the chart plane

The integral curves of $-v\,\partial_u + u\,\partial_v$ are the circles $u^2 + v^2 = \text{const}$, the images of the
parallels, traversed at unit angular speed: rotating the sphere about its axis rotates the stereographic plane about
the origin. Rotations about the other two axes do not preserve the chart's centre, and their generators $K_1, K_2$
(@sec-killing) have quadratic components in $(u, v)$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proposition differentiates the transition map in $\varphi$. The first exercise differentiates it in $\theta$ and
finds the stereographic components of $\partial_\theta$, which point radially in the chart plane.

::: {#exr-tv-dtheta-stereographic}
#### The meridian vector in the stereographic chart

Show that $\partial_\theta = -\dfrac{1 + \rho^2}{2\rho}\,(u\,\partial_u + v\,\partial_v)$ with $\rho^2 = u^2 + v^2$,
using $\rho = \cot(\theta/2)$, and confirm with SageManifolds.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$u = \rho\cos\varphi$, $v = \rho\sin\varphi$ with $\rho = \cot(\theta/2)$, so $\partial_\theta u = \rho'\cos\varphi$
with $\rho' = -1/(2\sin^2(\theta/2)) = -(1 + \rho^2)/2$. Hence $\partial_\theta = \rho'(\cos\varphi\,\partial_u +
\sin\varphi\,\partial_v) = -\tfrac{1 + \rho^2}{2\rho}(u\,\partial_u + v\,\partial_v)$, pointing towards the origin, the
south pole, as $\theta$ increases. On the equator $\rho = 1$ and at $(u, v) = (1, 0)$ this is $-\partial_u$:

{{< sage exr-tv-dtheta-stereographic >}}
:::

The stereographic chart is centred at the south pole, and the rotation fields about horizontal axes move that point.
The second exercise finds their components with SageManifolds and checks that they are regular where the spherical
chart is not.

::: {#exr-tv-rotation-stereographic}
#### The three rotation fields in the stereographic chart

The rotation fields $K_1 = -\sin\varphi\,\partial_\theta - \cot\theta\cos\varphi\,\partial_\varphi$, $K_2 =
\cos\varphi\,\partial_\theta - \cot\theta\sin\varphi\,\partial_\varphi$ and $K_3 = \partial_\varphi$ are singular at the
poles in the spherical chart. Compute their stereographic components with SageManifolds.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$K_1 = uv\,\partial_u + \tfrac12(1 - u^2 + v^2)\,\partial_v$, $K_2 = -\tfrac12(1 + u^2 - v^2)\,\partial_u -
uv\,\partial_v$ and $K_3 = -v\,\partial_u + u\,\partial_v$: polynomial components, smooth at the south pole $u = v =
0$, where $K_1 = \tfrac12\partial_v$ and $K_2 = -\tfrac12\partial_u$ do not vanish, while $K_3$ does:

{{< sage exr-tv-rotation-stereographic >}}
:::

The north stereographic chart misses the north pole; the south one, projecting from the south pole, misses the south
pole. The third exercise repeats the proposition in that chart and explains why the answer has the same form.

::: {#exr-tv-south-chart}
#### The south stereographic chart

For $u' = \sin\theta\cos\varphi/(1 + \cos\theta)$, $v' = \sin\theta\sin\varphi/(1 + \cos\theta)$, compute $\partial
u'/\partial\varphi$ and $\partial v'/\partial\varphi$ and write $\partial_\varphi$ in the south chart.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The factor $\sin\theta/(1 + \cos\theta)$ does not depend on $\varphi$, so $\partial u'/\partial\varphi = -\sin\theta
\sin\varphi/(1 + \cos\theta) = -v'$ and $\partial v'/\partial\varphi = u'$: again $\partial_\varphi = -v'\partial_{u'} +
u'\partial_{v'}$. Any chart of the form $(\rho(\theta)\cos\varphi, \rho(\theta)\sin\varphi)$ gives this answer, because
$\varphi$ enters only through $(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$, which rotates at unit speed.
:::
::::

### Vector fields {#sec-vector-fields}

A tangent vector lives at one point; a vector field chooses one at every point, smoothly. Vector fields are the
infinitesimal motions of a manifold: the rotation field of the sphere generates rotations about an axis, and the
three rotation fields together generate the whole rotation group, which is the mechanism behind the gauge
symmetries of later chapters. This chapter defines vector fields, their commutator, their integral curves
and frames.

#### Vector fields and their brackets

A single tangent vector is a directional derivative at one point; choosing one at every point gives an operator that
differentiates functions everywhere at once. The definition below asks that the choice be smooth, and the picture is a
field of arrows on the surface, as in the figure after the examples.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vector-field}
#### Vector field

A **vector field** $X$ assigns a tangent vector $X(p) \in T_pM$ to every point $p$, with smooth components
$X^i(x)$ in every chart. It acts on a smooth function $f$ by $X(f) = X^i\partial_i f$, giving a new smooth
function, and this action is linear and obeys the Leibniz rule $X(fg) = X(f)g + fX(g)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the field of the sphere that generates rotations about its axis. Its components are constant in
the spherical chart, yet it vanishes at the poles, a first sign that components alone can mislead.

::: {#exm-vector-field-rotation}
#### The rotation field on the sphere

$\partial_\varphi$, tangent to the parallels, is a vector field on the sphere minus the poles that extends to the
poles by zero, since its ambient length is $\sin\theta$ (@fig-sphere-vector-fields): it generates rotations about
the $Z$-axis. In @sec-killing it is one of three fields generating all rotations, and in Part IV those fields
become the gauge fields of $SU(2)$.
:::

The second field points along the meridians and is the gradient of the height. It also vanishes at both poles, and the
example quotes the theorem saying that some zero is unavoidable on the sphere.

::: {#exm-vector-field-gradient}
#### A field with a zero

$-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ points along the meridians towards the north pole and vanishes at both poles
(@fig-sphere-vector-fields); it is the gradient of the height $Z$, obtained from $dZ$ by raising the index with the
metric (@sec-metric). Every vector field on $S^2$
vanishes somewhere (the hairy ball theorem, @exr-hairy-ball), unlike on the circle or the torus.
:::

On the plane and the circle there are fields without zeros as well as fields with them. The third example lists the
constant, radial and rotation fields of the plane, which serve as test cases for every later notion.

::: {#exm-vector-field-rn}
#### Fields on the plane and the circle

$\partial_x$ (a constant field), $x\partial_x + y\partial_y$ (the radial field, vanishing at the origin) and
$-y\partial_x + x\partial_y$ (the rotation field of the plane, which is $\partial_\varphi$ in polar coordinates)
are vector fields on $\mathbb{R}^2$; $\partial_\varphi$ is a nowhere-vanishing field on the circle.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![Two vector fields on the sphere, defined in the spherical chart with SageManifolds and plotted on the embedded
sphere: the rotation field $\partial_\varphi$ (blue) and the gradient of the height $-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$
(red); both vanish at the poles. Generated by
`figures/sphere_vector_fields.sage`.](figures/sphere_vector_fields.png){#fig-sphere-vector-fields width=55%}

{{< interactive sphere_vector_fields 460 >}}

The two fields of the figure vanish at the poles although their spherical components never vanish together. The first
exercise asks why, and why no combination of them can avoid zeros.

::: {#exr-hairy-ball}
#### Fields that must vanish

Explain why $\partial_\varphi$ and $-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ both vanish at the poles although their
components in the spherical chart are $(0, 1)$ and $(-\sin\theta, 0)$, and why a nowhere-vanishing field on the
sphere cannot be built from them.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The components are chart quantities and the chart degenerates at the poles; the ambient length of
$\partial_\varphi$ is $\sin\theta$, which vanishes there, and the length of $-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ is
$\sin\theta$ as well. A combination $a\,\partial_\varphi + b\,\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ with constant $a, b$
still vanishes at both poles. The hairy ball theorem states that *every* continuous vector field on $S^2$ has a
zero; the two fields above are instances, and the circle and the torus, which admit $\partial_\varphi$ and
$\partial_a, \partial_b$, show that the obstruction is specific to the sphere's topology.
:::

The rotation field $\partial_\varphi$ has two partners that generate rotations about the other two axes. The second
exercise pushes all three to $\mathbb{R}^3$ with SageManifolds and identifies them with the familiar velocity fields of
rigid rotations.

::: {#exr-vf-rotation-fields}
#### The three rotation fields in $\mathbb{R}^3$

Let $K_1 = -\sin\varphi\,\partial_\theta - \cot\theta\cos\varphi\,\partial_\varphi$, $K_2 = \cos\varphi\,\partial_\theta -
\cot\theta\sin\varphi\,\partial_\varphi$ and $K_3 = \partial_\varphi$. With SageManifolds, compute their ambient
vectors through the Jacobian of the embedding and show that $K_a$ is the cross product $e_a \times p$ of the $a$-th
axis with the position vector $p$. Where does each field vanish?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each ambient vector equals $e_a \times p$, the velocity of a rigid rotation about the $a$-th axis at unit angular
speed; it is orthogonal to $p$, hence tangent, and its squared length $1 - (p \cdot e_a)^2$ vanishes exactly at the two
points $\pm e_a$ where the axis meets the sphere:

{{< sage exr-vf-rotation-fields >}}
:::

A vector field acts on functions, and the Leibniz rule holds pointwise everywhere. The third exercise applies the
rotation field of the plane to a product and sees one factor drop out because it is invariant.

::: {#exr-vf-leibniz-field}
#### The rotation field on a product

For $X = -y\,\partial_x + x\,\partial_y$, $f = x^2 + y^2$ and $g = x$, compute $X(f)$, $X(g)$ and $X(fg)$, and
explain why $X(fg) = f\,X(g)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$X(f) = -y \cdot 2x + x \cdot 2y = 0$, $X(g) = -y$, and $X(fg) = X(x^3 + xy^2) = -y(3x^2 + y^2) + x \cdot 2xy = -
x^2y - y^3 = -(x^2 + y^2)\,y$. By the Leibniz rule $X(fg) = X(f)\,g + f\,X(g) = f\,X(g)$ because $X(f) = 0$: the
squared radius is constant along the circles that the rotation field follows, so it behaves as a constant factor.
:::
::::

Two vector fields can be applied one after the other, but the result is a second-order operator. The next definition
shows that the commutator of the two orders is again a vector field, and this bracket measures how far the two flows
fail to commute.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lie-bracket}
#### Lie bracket

The **Lie bracket** (or **commutator**) of two vector fields is the vector field $[X, Y]$ acting on functions as
$[X, Y](f) = X(Y(f)) - Y(X(f))$; the second derivatives cancel, and in a chart
$$
[X, Y]^k = X^l\, \partial_l Y^k - Y^l\, \partial_l X^k .
$$ {#eq-lie-bracket}
It is antisymmetric, $[Y, X] = -[X, Y]$, and satisfies the Jacobi identity $[X, [Y, Z]] + [Y, [Z, X]] + [Z, [X, Y]]
= 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** In the Lean library the bracket is `KaluzaKlein.lieBracket`, defined by the chart formula @eq-lie-bracket.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Coordinate fields always commute, because partial derivatives do. The first example notes this and finds a pair of
non-coordinate fields that commute as well.

::: {#exm-bracket-commuting}
#### Commuting fields

$[\partial_\theta, \partial_\varphi] = 0$, as for any two coordinate fields (partial derivatives commute); and
$[\partial_\varphi, -\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta] = 0$, since neither field's components depend on $\varphi$
and $\partial_\varphi$ has constant components (@prp-brackets-sphere, @exr-bracket-fields).
:::

Multiplying a field by a function changes its brackets. The second example computes the simplest non-zero bracket on
the sphere from the chart formula, which the proposition at the end of the section records.

::: {#exm-bracket-nonzero}
#### A non-zero bracket

$[\partial_\theta, \sin\theta\,\partial_\varphi] = \cos\theta\,\partial_\varphi$: by @eq-lie-bracket only the term
$\partial_\theta(\sin\theta)$ survives (@prp-brackets-sphere). Rescaling a field by a function changes its
brackets.
:::

The three rotation fields of the sphere do not commute, and their brackets reproduce those of the rotation generators.
The third example states this, the first appearance of a Lie algebra of vector fields.

::: {#exm-bracket-rotations}
#### The rotation fields close into a Lie algebra

The three rotation fields of the sphere, $K_1, K_2, K_3$ with $K_3 = \partial_\varphi$, satisfy $[K_a, K_b] = -
\epsilon_{abc} K_c$ (@sec-killing): their brackets reproduce the structure constants of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, the
first example of a Lie algebra of vector fields.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The brackets of the examples are computed in the first exercise with SageManifolds, which also tests that the chart
formula agrees with the definition as a commutator of derivations. The same two brackets return as a proposition at
the end of the section.

::: {#exr-bracket-fields}
#### Brackets with SageManifolds

Compute $[\partial_\varphi, -\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta]$ and $[\partial_\theta, \sin\theta\,\partial_\varphi]$
with SageManifolds' `bracket`, and check on a generic function that $[X, Y](f) = X(Y(f)) - Y(X(f))$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-bracket-fields >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The first bracket is also proved in Lean.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.bracket_dphi_gradZ >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

How does the bracket react when the fields are rescaled by functions? The second exercise derives the general rule
from @eq-lie-bracket, which explains @exm-bracket-nonzero at once.

::: {#exr-vf-function-rescaling}
#### Brackets of rescaled fields

Show that $[fX, gY] = fg\,[X, Y] + f\,X(g)\,Y - g\,Y(f)\,X$ for functions $f, g$, and deduce $[\partial_\theta,
\sin\theta\,\partial_\varphi] = \cos\theta\,\partial_\varphi$ from $[\partial_\theta, \partial_\varphi] = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On a function $h$: $fX(gY(h)) = fX(g)\,Y(h) + fg\,X(Y(h))$ by the Leibniz rule, and $gY(fX(h)) = gY(f)\,X(h) +
gf\,Y(X(h))$. Subtracting, $[fX, gY](h) = fg\,[X, Y](h) + fX(g)\,Y(h) - gY(f)\,X(h)$. With $f = 1$, $X =
\partial_\theta$, $g = \sin\theta$, $Y = \partial_\varphi$: $[\partial_\theta, \sin\theta\,\partial_\varphi] = 0 +
\partial_\theta(\sin\theta)\,\partial_\varphi - 0 = \cos\theta\,\partial_\varphi$.
:::

The third example claimed that the rotation fields close under the bracket with the structure constants of
$\mathfrak{so}(3)$. The third exercise checks the three brackets and the Jacobi identity with SageManifolds, signs
included.

::: {#exr-vf-so3-brackets}
#### The rotation algebra

With SageManifolds, compute $[K_1, K_2]$, $[K_2, K_3]$, $[K_3, K_1]$ for the fields of @exr-vf-rotation-fields and
verify the Jacobi identity for $K_1, K_2, K_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[K_1, K_2] = -K_3$ and cyclically, that is $[K_a, K_b] = -\epsilon_{abc}K_c$, as stated in @exm-bracket-rotations; the
Jacobi identity holds:

{{< sage exr-vf-so3-brackets >}}
:::
::::

#### Integral curves and frames

A vector field prescribes a velocity at every point, so one can ask for the curves that follow it. The definition below
turns this into a system of ordinary differential equations and names the resulting motion of the whole manifold.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-integral-curve}
#### Integral curve

An **integral curve** of a vector field $X$ is a curve $\gamma$ whose velocity at every parameter value is the
value of the field there, $\dot\gamma(t) = X(\gamma(t))$; in a chart, $\dot x^i = X^i(x)$, a system of ordinary
differential equations with a unique solution through every point. The map sending a point to its position
after time $t$ along the integral curve is the **flow** of $X$ (@sec-flows).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The rotation field has the parallels as integral curves, and its flow is a rigid rotation. The first example is the
case where the differential equations integrate at sight.

::: {#exm-integral-parallel}
#### Parallels

The integral curves of $\partial_\varphi$ are the parallels $t \mapsto (\theta_0, \varphi_0 + t)$: $\dot\theta =
0$, $\dot\varphi = 1$. Its flow by time $t$ is the rotation about the $Z$-axis by the angle $t$.
:::

The gradient field of the height moves points along the meridians towards a zero of the field. The second example
shows that such a point is approached but never reached.

::: {#exm-integral-gradient}
#### Meridians

The integral curves of $-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ solve $\dot\theta = -\sin\theta$, $\dot\varphi = 0$: they
run along meridians towards the north pole, which they approach as $t \to \infty$ without reaching it (the pole
is a zero of the field, a fixed point of the flow).
:::

The three fields of the plane have lines, circles and rays as integral curves. The third example collects them, and the
exercises below compute their flows explicitly.

::: {#exm-integral-plane}
#### Straight lines and circles

The integral curves of $\partial_x$ on the plane are horizontal lines; those of $-y\partial_x + x\partial_y$ are
circles about the origin, traversed at angular speed $1$; those of the radial field $x\partial_x + y\partial_y$
are rays $t \mapsto e^t p$ leaving the origin.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The second example asserted that the meridian flow never reaches the pole. The first exercise solves the differential
equation exactly and confirms it.

::: {#exr-integral-curves}
#### Integral curves of the gradient field

Solve $\dot\theta = -\sin\theta$ with $\theta(0) = \pi/2$ and describe the integral curve.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Separating variables, $\int d\theta/\sin\theta = \log\tan(\theta/2)$, so $\tan(\theta(t)/2) = e^{-t}$ and
$\theta(t) = 2\arctan e^{-t}$: the curve starts on the equator, moves up the meridian, and tends to the north
pole $\theta = 0$ as $t \to \infty$ without reaching it in finite time, since the field vanishes there.
:::

A flow is a family of maps, and for the plane's fields these maps are explicit. The second exercise finds them and
checks the group property, that flowing for time $s$ and then for time $t$ is flowing for time $s + t$.

::: {#exr-vf-flows-plane}
#### Flows on the plane

Find the flows $\phi_t$ of the radial field $x\,\partial_x + y\,\partial_y$ and of the rotation field $-y\,\partial_x +
x\,\partial_y$, and verify $\phi_t \circ \phi_s = \phi_{t + s}$ and $\phi_0 = \mathrm{id}$ for both.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the radial field $\dot x = x$, $\dot y = y$ give $\phi_t(x, y) = e^t(x, y)$, a dilation, and $\phi_t\circ\phi_s =
e^te^s = e^{t + s}$. For the rotation field $\dot x = -y$, $\dot y = x$ give $\ddot x = -x$, so $\phi_t(x, y) =
(x\cos t - y\sin t, x\sin t + y\cos t)$, the rotation by the angle $t$, and the composition of rotations by $s$ and $t$
is the rotation by $s + t$ (the addition formulas of sine and cosine). In both cases $\phi_0$ is the identity: the flows
are one-parameter groups of diffeomorphisms.
:::

The integral curves of $K_1$ are rotations about the $X$-axis, which cut across the spherical chart in a complicated
way. The third exercise checks with Sage that an explicit rotation solves the chart equations of $K_1$.

::: {#exr-vf-integral-k1}
#### An integral curve of $K_1$

The rotation about the $X$-axis moves the equator point $(\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, 0)$ along $(\tfrac12,
\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cos t, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin t)$. Write this curve in spherical coordinates and verify with Sage that
it solves $\dot\theta = -\sin\varphi$, $\dot\varphi = -\cot\theta\cos\varphi$, the equations of $K_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\theta(t) = \arccos(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin t)$ and $\varphi(t) = \arctan(\sqrt3\cos t)$, starting at $(\pi/2, \pi/3)$.
Both residuals simplify to $0$: the curve is the integral curve of $K_1$, so the flow of $K_1$ is the rotation about
the $X$-axis, as @exr-vf-rotation-fields predicted from $K_1 = e_1 \times p$:

{{< sage exr-vf-integral-k1 >}}
:::
::::

The coordinate basis is one way of choosing a basis of every tangent space at once; there are others, often better
adapted to the geometry. The next definition names such a choice, and the examples show that it need not come from any
chart.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-frame}
#### Frame

A **frame** on an open set is a family of $n$ vector fields $e_1, \dots, e_n$ that form a basis of $T_pM$ at
every point of the set. The coordinate basis is a frame; a frame that is not the coordinate basis of any chart
is a **non-coordinate frame**, and the components of a vector in a frame are written $X = X^a e_a$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coordinate vectors of the sphere are orthogonal but $\partial_\varphi$ has length $\sin\theta$. Rescaling it gives
an orthonormal frame, and the first example shows that this frame belongs to no chart.

::: {#exm-frame-orthonormal}
#### The orthonormal frame of the sphere

$e_1 = \partial_\theta$, $e_2 = \sin^{-1}\theta\,\partial_\varphi$ have unit ambient length and are orthogonal
(@fig-coordinate-velocities); they are not a coordinate basis, since $[e_1, e_2] = -\cot\theta\, e_2 \neq 0$ by
@exm-bracket-nonzero, while coordinate fields always commute.
:::

The plane has its own orthonormal non-coordinate frame. The second example compares it with the Cartesian frame and
relates the two by a rotation.

::: {#exm-frame-polar}
#### Polar frames

$\partial_r$, $r^{-1}\partial_\varphi$ is an orthonormal frame on the punctured plane; the Cartesian basis
$\partial_x, \partial_y$ is a coordinate frame; both are frames, and the matrix relating them is a rotation by
$\varphi$ (@exr-components-polar).
:::

Some manifolds carry frames defined everywhere, and Lie groups are the main examples. The third example describes the
left-invariant frames of $SU(2)$, which reappear as vielbeins later in the book.

::: {#exm-frame-group}
#### Left-invariant frames

On $SU(2)$ the three fields obtained by transporting a basis of $T_eSU(2)$ by left multiplication form a frame
defined on the whole group (@sec-maurer-cartan); its existence is why the three-sphere, unlike the two-sphere,
carries nowhere-vanishing vector fields. Coset vielbeins (@sec-coset-vielbeins) are frames of this kind.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The orthonormal frame of the sphere is described through ambient lengths and a bracket. The first exercise checks both
with SageManifolds, on vector fields and on a test function.

::: {#exr-vf-orthonormal-frame}
#### The orthonormal frame of the sphere

With SageManifolds, check that $e_1 = \partial_\theta$ and $e_2 = \sin^{-1}\theta\,\partial_\varphi$ have unit ambient
length and are orthogonal, compute $[e_1, e_2]$, and check the result on an arbitrary function.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The ambient Gram matrix of the frame is the identity, and $[e_1, e_2] = -\cos\theta/\sin^2\theta\,\partial_\varphi = -
\cot\theta\,e_2$, also as a commutator of derivations:

{{< sage exr-vf-orthonormal-frame >}}
:::

Components of a vector field depend on the frame as much as on the chart. The second exercise rewrites one field in
the orthonormal frame and compares the two sets of components.

::: {#exr-vf-frame-components}
#### Components in the orthonormal frame

Write $X = \partial_\theta + 2\,\partial_\varphi$ in the frame $e_1, e_2$ of @exm-frame-orthonormal, and compute its
ambient length from either description.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_\varphi = \sin\theta\,e_2$, so $X = e_1 + 2\sin\theta\,e_2$, with frame components $(1, 2\sin\theta)$. Since
the frame is orthonormal its squared length is $1 + 4\sin^2\theta$; in the coordinate basis the same number is $1
\cdot 1 + 4\,|\partial_\varphi|^2 = 1 + 4\sin^2\theta$, using the lengths of @exm-basis-sphere.
:::

Why can a frame with a non-zero bracket not be a coordinate frame? The third exercise proves the criterion used in
@exm-frame-orthonormal and applies it to the polar frame of the plane.

::: {#exr-vf-frame-noncoordinate}
#### Brackets detect non-coordinate frames

Show that the fields of a coordinate frame commute, so a frame with $[e_a, e_b] \neq 0$ for some $a, b$ is not the
coordinate frame of any chart. Compute $[\partial_r, r^{-1}\partial_\varphi]$ for the polar frame of @exm-frame-polar.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $e_a = \partial/\partial y^a$ for a chart $y$, then $[e_a, e_b](f) = \partial_a\partial_bf - \partial_b\partial_af =
0$ because mixed partial derivatives of a smooth function commute. For the polar frame, by @exr-vf-function-rescaling
with $f = 1$, $g = r^{-1}$: $[\partial_r, r^{-1}\partial_\varphi] = \partial_r(r^{-1})\,\partial_\varphi = -
r^{-2}\,\partial_\varphi = -r^{-1}\,(r^{-1}\partial_\varphi)$, non-zero, so the orthonormal polar frame is not a
coordinate frame. (The converse, that commuting frames are locally coordinate frames, is also true but is not needed
here.)
:::
::::

The section closes with the two brackets of the examples stated as a proposition. Both are computed from the chart
formula @eq-lie-bracket, which only needs the components of the fields and their first derivatives.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-brackets-sphere}
#### Two brackets on the sphere

$[\partial_\varphi, -\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta] = 0$ and $[\partial_\theta, \sin\theta\,\partial_\varphi] =
\cos\theta\,\partial_\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.bracket_dphi_gradZ` and `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.bracket_dtheta_sinDphi`, from the chart
formula @eq-lie-bracket.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.bracket_dtheta_sinDphi >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The second bracket is a vector field whose length varies with the latitude. The first example evaluates it at a few
points and reads off where the two fields do commute.

::: {#exm-vf-brackets-point}
#### The bracket at a few points

$[\partial_\theta, \sin\theta\,\partial_\varphi] = \cos\theta\,\partial_\varphi$ is $\tfrac12\partial_\varphi$ at
$\theta = \pi/3$, $0$ on the equator and $-\tfrac12\partial_\varphi$ at $\theta = 2\pi/3$, with ambient length
$|\cos\theta|\sin\theta$. On the equator the two fields commute to first order: there $\sin\theta$ is stationary, so
moving along the meridian does not change the second field.
:::

The chart formula makes both brackets a two-line computation, since one field of each pair has constant components.
The second example carries out the two computations component by component.

::: {#exm-vf-brackets-lean}
#### The two brackets by components

In the chart $(\theta, \varphi)$, $\partial_\varphi$ has components $(0, 1)$ and $-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ has
components $(-\sin\theta, 0)$. In @eq-lie-bracket the second term vanishes because the components of $\partial_\varphi$
are constant, and the first is $\partial_\varphi(-\sin\theta, 0) = (0, 0)$: the bracket is zero. For $X =
\partial_\theta$, components $(1, 0)$, and $Y = \sin\theta\,\partial_\varphi$, components $(0, \sin\theta)$, again only
the first term survives and gives $\partial_\theta(0, \sin\theta) = (0, \cos\theta)$, that is $\cos\theta\,
\partial_\varphi$. In both cases the bracket is the derivative of the non-constant field along the constant one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** In Lean, a vector field is a family of component functions `Fin 2 → (Fin 2 → ℝ) → ℝ`, and `lieBracket X Y k x` is
`∑ l, (X l x * pd l (Y k) x - Y l x * pd l (X k) x)`, @eq-lie-bracket at the chart point `x`. The fields are `dphi = ![fun _ => 0,
fun _ => 1]`, `gradZ = ![fun x => -Real.sin (x 0), fun _ => 0]` and their analogues `dtheta`, `sinDphi`.
`bracket_dphi_gradZ` states that every component `k` of the bracket vanishes at every `x`; `bracket_dtheta_sinDphi`
states that component `0` (the $\theta$-component) is $0$ and component `1` is `Real.cos (x 0)`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

That $\partial_\varphi$ commutes with the gradient of the height has a geometric meaning: rotations about the axis do
not change the gradient field. The third example explains this through flows.

::: {#exm-vf-brackets-symmetry}
#### Commuting fields and symmetry

The flow of $\partial_\varphi$ is the rotation about the $Z$-axis (@exm-integral-parallel). Since the height is
invariant under it, so is its gradient field, and an invariant field commutes with the generator: $[\partial_\varphi, -
\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta] = 0$. In general $[X, Y] = 0$ exactly when the flows of $X$ and $Y$ commute, and $[X, Y]$
is the rate of change of $Y$ along the flow of $X$, the Lie derivative of @sec-flows.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proposition concerns two specific functions $\pm\sin\theta$. The first exercise replaces them by an arbitrary
function of $\theta$ and checks the general rule with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-vf-brackets-general}
#### Arbitrary functions of the latitude

With SageManifolds, show that $[\partial_\varphi, f(\theta)\,\partial_\theta] = 0$ and $[\partial_\theta,
f(\theta)\,\partial_\varphi] = f'(\theta)\,\partial_\varphi$ for an arbitrary function $f$, and recover the proposition.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both identities hold for arbitrary $f$, and $f = \mp\sin\theta$ gives the two brackets of the proposition:

{{< sage exr-vf-brackets-general >}}
:::

A bracket is a vector field, so it can be computed in any chart. The second exercise recomputes the first bracket in
the stereographic chart, where both fields have linear components.

::: {#exr-vf-brackets-stereographic}
#### The first bracket in the stereographic chart

Using $\partial_\varphi = -v\,\partial_u + u\,\partial_v$ and $-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta = u\,\partial_u +
v\,\partial_v$ (@exr-tv-gradient-stereographic), compute their bracket from @eq-lie-bracket in the stereographic
chart.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $X = (-v, u)$ and $Y = (u, v)$: $[X, Y]^u = X^l\partial_lY^u - Y^l\partial_lX^u = (-v)\cdot 1 + u \cdot 0 - (u
\cdot 0 + v \cdot (-1)) = 0$ and $[X, Y]^v = (-v) \cdot 0 + u \cdot 1 - (u \cdot 1 + v \cdot 0) = 0$. The rotation and
radial fields of the plane commute: rotating and then dilating is dilating and then rotating. The bracket vanishes in
both charts, as it must for a tensorial object.
:::

The orthonormal frame contains a rescaled $\partial_\varphi$, and its bracket is a case of the second identity. The
third exercise generalises to any rescaling and finds the frames whose fields commute.

::: {#exr-vf-brackets-frame}
#### Rescaled frames

For $e_1 = \partial_\theta$ and $e_2 = h(\theta)\,\partial_\varphi$ with $h$ nowhere zero, show that $[e_1, e_2] =
(h'/h)\,e_2$. Recover $[e_1, e_2] = -\cot\theta\,e_2$ for $h = 1/\sin\theta$, and find all $h$ for which the two fields
commute.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the proposition's rule, $[\partial_\theta, h\,\partial_\varphi] = h'\,\partial_\varphi = (h'/h)\,e_2$. For $h =
1/\sin\theta$, $h' = -\cos\theta/\sin^2\theta$ and $h'/h = -\cot\theta$. The fields commute iff $h' = 0$, so $h$ is a
non-zero constant: the only commuting rescalings are constant multiples of the coordinate field, consistent with
@exr-vf-frame-noncoordinate.
:::
::::

### Cotangent vectors and one-forms {#sec-one-forms}

A tangent vector eats a function and returns a number; a cotangent vector eats a tangent vector and returns a
number. The differential of a function is the basic example, and one-forms, fields of cotangent vectors, are the
objects that gauge potentials turn out to be: the electromagnetic potential $A = A_\mu dx^\mu$ of Part II is a
one-form, which is why its components carry a lower index.

#### Cotangent vectors

Many quantities attached to a point are linear functions of a tangent vector there: a rate of change, a work done
along a displacement, a flux. The definition below gives them a home, the dual space of the tangent space, and the
picture to keep is a family of parallel level lines that a vector crosses.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-cotangent-vector}
#### Cotangent vector

A **cotangent vector** (or **covector**) at $p$ is a linear functional (@def-linear-functional) $\omega : T_pM \to
\mathbb{R}$ on the tangent space. The cotangent vectors at $p$ form the **cotangent space** $T_p^*M$, the dual
space (@def-dual-space) of $T_pM$, of dimension $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A linear functional on a two-dimensional space is fixed by two numbers. The first example fixes them on the coordinate
basis of the sphere and evaluates the covector on the vector of @fig-tangent-vectors.

::: {#exm-cotangent-evaluation}
#### Reading off a cotangent vector

On the sphere, the covector that sends $\partial_\theta$ to $3$ and $\partial_\varphi$ to $-1$ sends the vector
$X = 0.4\,\partial_\theta + 0.5\,\partial_\varphi$ of @fig-tangent-vectors to $1.2 - 0.5 = 0.7$
(@exr-differential-height); a covector is determined by its values on a basis.
:::

Rates of change are the covectors met in practice. The second example names the one attached to the height, which the
next subsection defines as a differential.

::: {#exm-cotangent-rate}
#### Rates of change

"The rate of change of the height along $X$" is a linear function of the tangent vector $X$, hence a cotangent
vector at each point; it is the differential $dZ$ of @def-differential, and @fig-height-levels pictures it
through the level sets of $Z$.
:::

In $\mathbb{R}^n$ covectors are rows and vectors are columns, and pairing is matrix multiplication. The third example
records this and the identification with dot products that holds only in Euclidean space.

::: {#exm-cotangent-rn}
#### Rows at a point

At a point of $\mathbb{R}^n$ a cotangent vector is a row $(\omega_1, \dots, \omega_n)$ acting on the column of
components of a tangent vector, $\omega(X) = \omega_i X^i$ (@exm-dual-space-rows); the dot product with a fixed
vector $a$, $X \mapsto a \cdot X$, is one, and in $\mathbb{R}^n$ every covector is of this form.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A covector given by its values on a basis can be applied to any vector by linearity. The first exercise practises this
on the sphere and writes the result as a row times a column.

::: {#exr-of-covector-evaluate}
#### Evaluating a covector

At a point of the sphere let $\omega$ be the covector with $\omega(\partial_\theta) = 2$ and $\omega(\partial_\varphi) =
5$. Evaluate it on $\partial_\theta - \partial_\varphi$, on $3\,\partial_\theta + \partial_\varphi$ and on the vector
of @fig-tangent-vectors, and find a non-zero vector on which it vanishes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\omega(X) = (2, 5)\begin{pmatrix} X^\theta \\ X^\varphi \end{pmatrix} = 2X^\theta + 5X^\varphi$: the three values are
$2 - 5 = -3$, $6 + 5 = 11$ and $0.8 + 2.5 = 3.3$. It vanishes on $5\,\partial_\theta - 2\,\partial_\varphi$ and its
multiples, a one-dimensional kernel, as for every non-zero covector on a two-dimensional space.
:::

A basis of tangent vectors determines a dual basis of covectors, also for non-coordinate frames. The second exercise
finds the dual of the orthonormal frame of the sphere with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-of-dual-frame}
#### The dual of the orthonormal frame

Find the covectors $e^1, e^2$ with $e^a(e_b) = \delta^a_b$ for the orthonormal frame $e_1 = \partial_\theta$, $e_2 =
\sin^{-1}\theta\,\partial_\varphi$ of @exm-frame-orthonormal, by hand and with SageManifolds' `coframe`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d\theta$ takes the values $1, 0$ on $e_1, e_2$, so $e^1 = d\theta$; for $e^2 = a\,d\theta + b\,d\varphi$ the
conditions $e^2(e_1) = a = 0$ and $e^2(e_2) = b/\sin\theta = 1$ give $e^2 = \sin\theta\,d\varphi$. The coordinate
differential is rescaled by the inverse of the factor that rescaled the vector:

{{< sage exr-of-dual-frame >}}
:::

The pairing $\omega(X)$ is defined without coordinates, so it cannot depend on them. The third exercise proves that
the component formula respects this and that a covector is determined by its values on any basis.

::: {#exr-of-pairing-invariant}
#### The pairing does not depend on the basis

Let $e_a$ and $f_b = M^a{}_be_a$ be two bases of $T_pM$ with dual bases $e^a$, $f^b$. Show that $f^b = (M^{-1})^b{}_a
e^a$, and that $\omega_aX^a$ computed in either basis gives the same number. Conclude that a covector vanishing on a
basis is zero.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Write $f^b = N^b{}_ce^c$; then $\delta^b_d = f^b(f_d) = N^b{}_ce^c(M^a{}_de_a) = N^b{}_cM^c{}_d$, so $N = M^{-1}$. The
components in the new bases are $\omega'_b = \omega(f_b) = M^a{}_b\omega_a$ and $X'^b = (M^{-1})^b{}_aX^a$, hence
$\omega'_bX'^b = \omega_aM^a{}_b(M^{-1})^b{}_cX^c = \omega_aX^a$. If $\omega$ vanishes on a basis, all its components
vanish and $\omega(X) = \omega_aX^a = 0$ for every $X$.
:::
::::

A chart provides a basis of covectors as well as of vectors: the dual basis of the coordinate basis. The next
definition introduces it and derives the transformation law of covector components, the inverse of the law for
vectors.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-coordinate-differentials}
#### Coordinate differentials

In a chart the **coordinate differentials** $dx^1, \dots, dx^n$ are the covectors defined by $dx^i(\partial_j) =
\delta^i_j$: the dual basis (@def-dual-basis) of the coordinate basis. Every covector is $\omega = \omega_i\,dx^i$
with components $\omega_i = \omega(\partial_i)$, and $\omega(X) = \omega_i X^i$. Under a change of chart,
$$
\omega'_j = \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^j}\, \omega_i ,
$$ {#eq-covector-transformation}
the inverse Jacobian of @eq-vector-transformation, so that $\omega_i X^i$ is chart independent.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the sphere the coordinate differentials read off the two components of a vector. The first example applies them to
the vector of the first example of the section.

::: {#exm-differentials-sphere}
#### $d\theta$ and $d\varphi$

$d\theta$ reads off the $\theta$-component of a tangent vector and $d\varphi$ the $\varphi$-component: $d\theta(X)
= 0.4$ and $d\varphi(X) = 0.5$ for the vector of @exm-cotangent-evaluation, and the covector there is $3\,d\theta -
d\varphi$.
:::

The transformation law is tested on $d\varphi$, moved to the stereographic chart. The second example checks that its
pairing with $\partial_\varphi$ stays equal to $1$, as the cancellation of Jacobians requires.

::: {#exm-differentials-transformation}
#### $d\varphi$ in stereographic coordinates

The components of $d\varphi$ in the stereographic chart are $(\partial\varphi/\partial u, \partial\varphi/\partial
v) = (-v, u)/(u^2 + v^2)$ by @eq-covector-transformation, the rotation field divided by $u^2 + v^2$; paired with
$\partial_\varphi = -v\,\partial_u + u\,\partial_v$ (@prp-dphi-stereographic) this gives $(v^2 + u^2)/(u^2 + v^2) = 1$,
as it must.
:::

The polar differentials of the plane are the rows of the inverse Jacobian. The third example writes them in Cartesian
form and pairs them with the rotation field, and the figure shows the level sets that picture a differential.

::: {#exm-differentials-polar}
#### $dr$ and $d\varphi$ on the plane

$dr = (x\,dx + y\,dy)/r$ and $d\varphi = (-y\,dx + x\,dy)/r^2$: the rows of the inverse of the polar Jacobian
(@exm-chain-inverse). On the rotation field $-y\partial_x + x\partial_y$, $d\varphi$ gives $1$ and $dr$ gives
$0$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The differential of the height. Left: in the stereographic chart the level sets of $Z$ are circles, and the
arrows show the direction in which $Z$ increases; $dZ$ measures how many level lines a vector crosses. Right: in a
meridian plane of the sphere the level sets are the parallels; $dZ(\partial_\varphi) = 0$ and $dZ(\partial_\theta)
= -\sin\theta$. Generated by `figures/height_levels.sage`.](figures/height_levels.svg){#fig-height-levels width=85%}

The second example is worked out in the first exercise, from the transformation law and with the pairing checked in
both charts. The answer is the row of partial derivatives of the angle, divided by the squared radius of the chart plane.

::: {#exr-covector-transformation}
#### Transforming a covector

Find the components of $d\varphi$ in the stereographic chart from @eq-covector-transformation, and check that
$d\varphi(\partial_\varphi) = 1$ in both charts.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\varphi = \operatorname{atan2}(v, u)$ on the overlap, so $\partial\varphi/\partial u = -v/(u^2 + v^2)$ and
$\partial\varphi/\partial v = u/(u^2 + v^2)$, the components of $d\varphi$. Paired with $\partial_\varphi = -
v\,\partial_u + u\,\partial_v$: $(-v)(-v)/(u^2 + v^2) + u \cdot u/(u^2 + v^2) = 1$, the same as $d\varphi(\partial_\varphi)
= 1$ in the spherical chart. The Jacobian factors of @eq-vector-transformation and @eq-covector-transformation cancel.
:::

SageManifolds performs the change of coframe automatically. The second exercise displays both spherical differentials
in the stereographic chart and checks two pairings.

::: {#exr-of-coframe-stereographic}
#### The spherical coframe in the stereographic chart

With SageManifolds, display $d\theta$ and $d\varphi$ in the coframe $(du, dv)$ of the stereographic chart, and evaluate
both on $\partial_\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d\varphi = (-v\,du + u\,dv)/(u^2 + v^2)$ as in @exm-differentials-transformation, and $d\theta = -2(u\,du +
v\,dv)/\big((1 + \rho^2)\rho\big)$ with $\rho^2 = u^2 + v^2$, the dual statement of @exr-tv-dtheta-stereographic.
Paired with $\partial_\varphi = -v\,\partial_u + u\,\partial_v$ they give $1$ and $0$:

{{< sage exr-of-coframe-stereographic >}}
:::

The transformation law of covector components was stated; it can also be derived from the differentials themselves.
The third exercise does this and shows that the two laws are each other's inverse.

::: {#exr-of-dual-transform}
#### Deriving the covector law

Show that $dx'^j = \dfrac{\partial x'^j}{\partial x^i}\,dx^i$ by evaluating both sides on $\partial_k$, and deduce
@eq-covector-transformation from $\omega = \omega_i\,dx^i = \omega'_j\,dx'^j$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $\partial_k$, the left side gives $dx'^j(\partial_k) = \partial_k(x'^j) = \partial x'^j/\partial x^k$ (a coordinate
differential reads off the rate of change of its coordinate), and the right side gives $\frac{\partial x'^j}{\partial
x^i}\delta^i_k$, the same. Symmetrically $dx^i = \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^j}dx'^j$, and substituting into
$\omega_i\,dx^i$ gives $\omega = \omega_i\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^j}\,dx'^j$, whose coefficients are
$\omega'_j$. The vector law uses $\partial x'/\partial x$, the covector law its inverse $\partial x/\partial x'$.
:::
::::

#### Differentials and one-forms

Every smooth function produces a covector at each point, its rate of change in every direction. The next definition
introduces this differential, the main source of covectors and the reason they are written $dx^i$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-differential}
#### Differential of a function

The **differential** $df$ of a smooth function is the covector $df(X) = X(f)$ at each point; in a chart $df =
\partial_i f\, dx^i$, with components $(\partial_1 f, \dots, \partial_n f)$. Its value on a velocity is the rate
of change of $f$ along the curve, @eq-velocity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The height of the sphere has the simplest non-trivial differential. The first example computes it and evaluates it on
the two coordinate vectors, which the figure above draws.

::: {#exm-height-differential}
#### The differential of the height function

On the sphere $dZ = d(\cos\theta) = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$: components $(-\sin\theta, 0)$ (@prp-dZ). On
$\partial_\varphi$ it gives zero (moving along a parallel does not change the height) and on $\partial_\theta$ it
gives $-\sin\theta$ (@fig-height-levels).
:::

The coordinate differentials of the previous definition are differentials of functions, the coordinates. The second
example checks the consistency and notes the subtlety of the angle on the circle.

::: {#exm-differential-coordinate}
#### Differentials of the coordinates

$d\theta$ and $d\varphi$ are the differentials of the coordinate functions $\theta$ and $\varphi$, consistent with
@def-coordinate-differentials; $d\varphi$ is a well-defined covector field on the circle even though $\varphi$ is
not a function (@exm-angle-not-function), since the jumps of $\varphi$ are constant (@exr-dphi-closed).
:::

The same differential looks different in the stereographic chart, because its components transform. The third
example computes it there and checks that it still vanishes on the rotation field.

::: {#exm-differential-stereographic}
#### $dZ$ in the stereographic chart

$Z = (u^2 + v^2 - 1)/(u^2 + v^2 + 1)$ gives $dZ = 4(u\,du + v\,dv)/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$, which vanishes on the rotation
field $-v\partial_u + u\partial_v$: the same covector field as $-\sin\theta\,d\theta$, in other components.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/height_levels.sage`).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the differential of the height with SageManifolds and evaluates it on several vectors,
including the one of @fig-tangent-vectors. The last part evaluates the covector of @exm-cotangent-evaluation, written now as a one-form.

::: {#exr-differential-height}
#### Differentials with SageManifolds

Compute $dZ$ for $Z = \cos\theta$ with SageManifolds' `differential`, evaluate it on $\partial_\theta$,
$\partial_\varphi$ and $X = 0.4\,\partial_\theta + 0.5\,\partial_\varphi$, and evaluate the one-form $3\,d\theta -
d\varphi$ on $X$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-differential-height >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.dZ_on_fields >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The radius of the plane is a function whose differential is simple in polar coordinates and less simple in Cartesian
ones. The second exercise computes it in both and checks the chain rule on its square.

::: {#exr-of-dr-polar}
#### The differential of the radius

With SageManifolds, compute $dr$ for $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ on the punctured plane in Cartesian and polar coordinates,
evaluate it on $\partial_r$ and $\partial_\varphi$, and check $d(r^2) = 2r\,dr$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dr = (x\,dx + y\,dy)/\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$, which is simply $dr$ in polar coordinates, with $dr(\partial_r) = 1$ and
$dr(\partial_\varphi) = 0$; and $d(r^2) = 2r\,dr$, the chain rule:

{{< sage exr-of-dr-polar >}}
:::

The differential obeys the rules of calculus because tangent vectors do. The third exercise derives the product and
chain rules from the definition $df(X) = X(f)$.

::: {#exr-of-leibniz-chain}
#### Product and chain rules

Show that $d(fg) = f\,dg + g\,df$ and $d(h \circ f) = h'(f)\,df$ for smooth $f, g$ and a smooth function $h$ of one
variable. Apply the second to $d(\cos\theta)$ and to $d(Z^2)$ on the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On any vector $X$: $d(fg)(X) = X(fg) = X(f)\,g + f\,X(g) = (g\,df + f\,dg)(X)$ by the Leibniz rule. In a chart,
$X(h(f)) = X^i\partial_i h(f) = h'(f)X^i\partial_if = h'(f)\,df(X)$. Hence $d(\cos\theta) = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$,
the differential of the height of @exm-height-differential, and $d(Z^2) = 2Z\,dZ = -2\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta$.
:::
::::

A covector at every point, varying smoothly, is a one-form; differentials are examples, but not all one-forms are
differentials. The next definition introduces one-forms and the distinction between exact and arbitrary ones.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-one-form}
#### One-form

A **one-form** is a smooth field of cotangent vectors, $\omega = \omega_i(x)\,dx^i$ with smooth components in every
chart; it pairs with a vector field to give a function, $\omega(X) = \omega_i X^i$. The differential $df$ of a
smooth function is a one-form, called **exact**; not every one-form is exact.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example compares two one-forms on the sphere, one exact and one that cannot be extended to the poles. The
second will return as the connection of the Hopf fibration.

::: {#exm-one-form-sphere}
#### One-forms on the sphere

$dZ = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$ and $\cos\theta\,d\varphi$ are one-forms on the sphere minus the poles; the first
extends smoothly to the poles, the second cannot (it is the Hopf connection of @sec-hopf).
:::

On the circle the angle form is defined everywhere but is not the differential of a function. The second example
proves this with an integral, the first appearance of topology in the chapter.

::: {#exm-one-form-circle}
#### The one-form $d\varphi$ on the circle

$d\varphi$ is a globally defined one-form on $S^1$ whose integral around the circle is $2\pi$
(@exr-dphi-closed); it is not the differential of any smooth function on the circle, since the integral of $df$
around a closed curve is $f(\text{end}) - f(\text{start}) = 0$. It is exact on each chart domain but not globally.
:::

The third example is the physical one: the electromagnetic potential is a one-form, and gauge transformations add
exact one-forms to it. Their difference from the geometric one-forms above is only in the manifold, spacetime instead of a surface.

::: {#exm-one-form-gauge}
#### Gauge potentials

The electromagnetic potential $A = A_\mu\,dx^\mu$ on spacetime is a one-form (@sec-abelian-gauge); a gauge
transformation adds the exact one-form $d\lambda$, and the field strength of @sec-forms measures how far $A$ is
from being exact.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The claims of the second example are the first exercise, with the integral computed in SageManifolds. It turns the argument of the second example into a computation.

::: {#exr-dphi-closed}
#### $d\varphi$ is not exact

Show that the one-form $d\varphi$ on the circle has integral $2\pi$ around the circle and conclude that it is not
the differential of a function on the circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the angle chart $\omega = d\varphi$ has component $1$, and $\int_0^{2\pi} 1\, d\varphi = 2\pi$. If $\omega = df$
for a smooth $f$ on the circle, the integral along the closed curve $\gamma(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$ would be
$\int_0^{2\pi} \frac{d}{dt} f(\gamma(t))\, dt = f(\gamma(2\pi)) - f(\gamma(0)) = 0$. In SageManifolds:

{{< sage exr-dphi-closed >}}
:::

The rotation field of the plane has a dual one-form with the same components, $-y\,dx + x\,dy$. The second exercise
writes it in polar coordinates and integrates it around the unit circle by pulling it back along a parametrisation.

::: {#exr-of-rotation-form-polar}
#### The rotation one-form of the plane

With SageManifolds, show that $\omega = -y\,dx + x\,dy$ is $r^2\,d\varphi$ in polar coordinates, compute its pullback
along $\gamma(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$ and its integral around the circle. Is $\omega$ exact on the plane?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\omega = r^2\,d\varphi$, the pullback along the unit circle is $dt$, and the integral is $2\pi$. A non-zero integral
around a closed curve rules out $\omega = df$, as in @exm-one-form-circle; equivalently $d\omega = 2\,dx \wedge dy
\neq 0$ (@sec-forms), while exact forms have $d(df) = 0$:

{{< sage exr-of-rotation-form-polar >}}
:::

The circle has one non-exact one-form; the torus has two independent ones. The third exercise identifies them and
uses integrals around the two cycles to show that no combination of them is exact.

::: {#exr-of-torus-forms}
#### One-forms on the torus

On the torus with angle coordinates $(a, b)$, show that $da$ and $db$ are globally defined one-forms, compute their
integrals around the circles $b = \text{const}$ and $a = \text{const}$, and show that $\lambda\,da + \mu\,db$ is
exact only for $\lambda = \mu = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the overlaps of the angle charts $a' = a + \text{const}$, so $da' = da$ and likewise for $b$: both forms are global
although $a$ and $b$ are not global functions. Around the $a$-circle ($b$ fixed, $a$ from $0$ to $2\pi$) $da$
integrates to $2\pi$ and $db$ to $0$; around the $b$-circle the values are swapped. If $\lambda\,da + \mu\,db = df$, both
integrals would vanish, giving $2\pi\lambda = 2\pi\mu = 0$.
:::
::::

The section ends with the differential of the height stated as a proposition. It is the covector behind every
earlier computation of $X(Z)$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-dZ}
#### The differential of the height

$dZ$ has components $(-\sin\theta, 0)$, $dZ(\partial_\varphi) = 0$ and $dZ(\partial_\theta) = -\sin\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.dZ_components` and `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.dZ_on_fields`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.dZ_components >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The components $(-\sin\theta, 0)$ depend only on the latitude. The first example evaluates the covector at one point
and on a vector met earlier.

::: {#exm-of-dz-point}
#### At one point

At $\theta = \pi/3$, $dZ = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,d\theta$. On $X = 0.4\,\partial_\theta + 0.5\,\partial_\varphi$ it gives
$-0.2\sqrt3 \approx -0.346$, and on $\partial_\theta + 2\,\partial_\varphi$ it gives $-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, the value of
@prp-velocity-height: the covector ignores the $\partial_\varphi$-component of every vector.
:::

The proposition gives the components of $dZ$, and pairing them with the components of a vector is a finite sum. The
second example writes that sum out for the two coordinate fields and for a general vector, so that the proposition's
two pairings appear as special cases.

::: {#exm-of-dz-lean}
#### Pairing by components

A covector $\omega = \omega_\theta\,d\theta + \omega_\varphi\,d\varphi$ pairs with $X = X^\theta\partial_\theta +
X^\varphi\partial_\varphi$ as $\omega(X) = \omega_iX^i = \omega_\theta X^\theta + \omega_\varphi X^\varphi$. For $dZ$, with
components $(\partial_\theta Z, \partial_\varphi Z) = (-\sin\theta, 0)$, this is $dZ(X) = -X^\theta\sin\theta$. The field
$\partial_\varphi$ has components $(0, 1)$ and gives $0$; the field $\partial_\theta$ has components $(1, 0)$ and gives
$-\sin\theta$; the field $\cos\theta\,\partial_\theta - \partial_\varphi$ gives $-\sin\theta\cos\theta$. No new object is
needed: the differential is the pair of partial derivatives and the pairing is the sum.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** In Lean, `dZ_components` states that `pd 0 heightZ x = -Real.sin (x 0)` and `pd 1 heightZ x = 0` for every chart point `x`,
where `heightZ x = Real.cos (x 0)`: the components $\partial_\theta Z$ and $\partial_\varphi Z$ of $dZ$.
`dZ_on_fields` states that `∑ i, pd i heightZ x * dphi i x = 0` and `∑ i, pd i heightZ x * dtheta i x = -Real.sin (x
0)`: the pairings $\omega_iX^i$ of $dZ$ with $\partial_\varphi$ and $\partial_\theta$.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A covector becomes a vector once a metric is available. The third example raises the index of $dZ$ with the round
metric and recovers the gradient field of the previous section.

::: {#exm-of-dz-gradient}
#### From the differential to the gradient

With the round metric $g = \operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$, the vector with components $g^{ij}(dZ)_j$ is
$(1 \cdot (-\sin\theta), \sin^{-2}\theta \cdot 0) = (-\sin\theta, 0)$: the gradient field $-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$
of @exm-vector-field-gradient (@prp-raise-lower). The differential needs no metric; the gradient does.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The height is one of three ambient coordinates, and each has a differential on the sphere. The first exercise computes
all three with SageManifolds and evaluates them on the three rotation fields.

::: {#exr-of-ambient-differentials}
#### Differentials of the ambient coordinates

With SageManifolds, compute $dX$, $dY$, $dZ$ for the restrictions of the ambient coordinates to the sphere and the
nine numbers $dX_b(K_a)$ for the rotation fields of @exr-vf-rotation-fields. Show that $dX_b(K_a) = -
\epsilon_{abc}X_c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dZ = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$ is the proposition; $dX$ and $dY$ have both components. The table of $dX_b(K_a) = K_a(X_b)$
is $-\epsilon_{abc}X_c$, the infinitesimal form of $K_a = e_a \times p$: for instance $dY(K_1) = -Z$ and $dZ(K_1) = Y$:

{{< sage exr-of-ambient-differentials >}}
:::

The differential of the height in the stereographic chart was quoted in @exm-differential-stereographic. The second
exercise derives it from the proposition by the transformation law, through the radius $\rho$ of the chart plane.

::: {#exr-of-dz-stereographic}
#### The height differential in the stereographic chart

Using $\rho = \cot(\theta/2)$ and $Z = (\rho^2 - 1)/(\rho^2 + 1)$, derive $dZ = 4\rho\,d\rho/(1 + \rho^2)^2 =
4(u\,du + v\,dv)/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$ and check that it equals $-\sin\theta\,d\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the chain rule, $dZ = \frac{d}{d\rho}\frac{\rho^2 - 1}{\rho^2 + 1}\,d\rho = \frac{2\rho(\rho^2 + 1) - 2\rho(\rho^2 -
1)}{(1 + \rho^2)^2}\,d\rho = \frac{4\rho}{(1 + \rho^2)^2}\,d\rho$, and $\rho\,d\rho = u\,du + v\,dv$. Conversely
$d\rho = -d\theta/(2\sin^2(\theta/2))$ and $1 + \rho^2 = 1/\sin^2(\theta/2)$, so $4\rho\,d\rho/(1 + \rho^2)^2 = -
2\cot(\theta/2)\sin^2(\theta/2)\,d\theta = -2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)\,d\theta = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$.
:::

Integrating a differential along a curve gives the change of the function. The third exercise proves this fundamental
theorem for one-forms and applies it to the height along a meridian and a parallel.

::: {#exr-of-height-ftc}
#### Integrating the differential of the height
