shows why: the coordinate vector $\partial_\varphi$ grows with the distance from the origin.

::: {#exm-metric-euclidean}
#### The Euclidean metric

On $\mathbb{R}^n$ in Cartesian coordinates, $g_{ij} = \delta_{ij}$: $g(X, Y)$ is the dot product. In polar
coordinates on the plane the same metric has components $g_{rr} = 1$, $g_{\varphi\varphi} = r^2$, $g_{r\varphi} = 0$
(@fig-polar-grid, @prp-polar-metric): the components depend on the chart, the metric does not.
:::

![The plane in polar coordinates: circles $r = \text{const}$ (red) and rays $\varphi = \text{const}$ (blue), with
the coordinate basis vectors $\partial_r$ (black, unit length) and $\partial_\varphi$ (green, length $r$) at two
points. The rays spread, so $g_{\varphi\varphi} = r^2$ grows, although the plane is flat. Generated by
`figures/polar_grid.sage`.](figures/polar_grid.svg){#fig-polar-grid width=45%}

Nothing in the definition requires the inner product to be positive, only that it be non-degenerate. The metric of
special relativity is the standard example of a metric that is not: it assigns positive, zero and negative norms to
different vectors, and it is the metric of every spacetime factor in later chapters.

::: {#exm-metric-minkowski}
#### The Minkowski metric

On $\mathbb{R}^4$, $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$ is a metric: non-degenerate (@prp-minkowski-metric),
but $\eta(X, X)$ can be positive (for $X = \partial_t$), zero (for $X = \partial_t + \partial_x$) or negative (for
$X = \partial_x$). It
is the metric of special relativity, and of the spacetime factor of every Kaluza-Klein product.
:::

The third example is a metric on a manifold that is not a vector space, the sphere. Its components are the Gram
matrix of the spherical chart computed in @sec-manifolds, and they show the typical behaviour of a metric in a
chart that does not cover the whole manifold: a component degenerates exactly where the chart does.

::: {#exm-metric-sphere}
#### The round metric

On the sphere, $g = d\theta \otimes d\theta + \sin^2\theta\, d\varphi \otimes d\varphi$, the Gram matrix of the
spherical chart (@prp-sphere-gram): $g_{\theta\theta} = 1$, $g_{\varphi\varphi} = \sin^2\theta$, non-degenerate on
the chart domain. Its unit vectors are drawn in @fig-metric-ellipses of @sec-lengths-volumes.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The polar components of the Euclidean metric can be produced by SageManifolds rather than by hand: one declares
the metric in the Cartesian chart and asks for its components in the polar one. The first exercise does this and
reads off the determinant and the inverse, which anticipate the two notions defined below.

::: {#exr-polar-metric}
#### The polar metric with SageManifolds

Declare the Euclidean metric of the plane in Cartesian coordinates, display it in polar coordinates, and compute
its determinant, inverse and volume element there.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1/r^2)$, $\det g = r^2$, $\sqrt{\det g} = r$, the Jacobian of polar coordinates
(@sec-lengths-volumes):

{{< sage exr-polar-metric >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.polar_det >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The two conditions of the definition, symmetry and non-degeneracy, are best learned on candidates that fail them
in different ways. Four symmetric tensor fields on the plane follow; the reader should find a point where the
determinant vanishes, or conclude that there is none, and classify the survivors by the sign of $g(X, X)$.

::: {#exr-metric-which-are-metrics}
#### Which symmetric tensor fields are metrics?

Decide which of $dx \otimes dx + dy \otimes dy$, $dx \otimes dy + dy \otimes dx$, $x^2\,dx \otimes dx + dy \otimes
dy$ and $dx \otimes dx - dy \otimes dy$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and for those that are, say whether
$g(X, X)$ can be negative.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All four are symmetric. The matrices are $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix} x^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1
\end{pmatrix}$ with determinants $1$, $-1$, $x^2$ and $-1$. The third is degenerate along the line $x = 0$, where
$\partial_x$ has zero length, so it is not a metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$ (it is one on either half-plane). The other
three are metrics: the first is positive, $g(X, X) = (X^x)^2 + (X^y)^2 > 0$ for $X \neq 0$; the second gives
$g(X, X) = 2X^xX^y$, negative for $X = \partial_x - \partial_y$; the fourth gives $(X^x)^2 - (X^y)^2$, negative for
$X = \partial_y$. The last two are the two-dimensional Minkowski metric in different coordinates.
:::

The definition says that non-degeneracy must hold "in every chart", which would be a lot to check if it were not
automatic. The third exercise asks for the transformation law of the components under a change of chart and for the
consequence that the determinant can only vanish in all charts at once.

::: {#exr-metric-chart-independence}
#### Non-degeneracy does not depend on the chart

Derive the transformation law $g'_{kl} = \dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^k}\dfrac{\partial x^j}{\partial x'^l}\,
g_{ij}$ of the components under a change of chart $x \mapsto x'$, deduce that $\det g' = (\det J)^2\det g$ with
$J = \partial x/\partial x'$ the Jacobian, and conclude that $\det g \neq 0$ in one chart implies $\det g' \neq 0$ in
every overlapping chart. Check the formula on the polar chart of the plane.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $g$ is a tensor field, $g = g_{ij}\,dx^i \otimes dx^j$ and $dx^i = (\partial x^i/\partial x'^k)\,dx'^k$;
substituting gives the components $g'_{kl}$ as stated, which in matrix form reads $g' = J^{\mathsf{T}} g J$. Taking
determinants, $\det g' = (\det J)^2\det g$, and $\det J \neq 0$ on the overlap of two charts because the transition
map is a diffeomorphism. So $\det g'$ and $\det g$ vanish at the same points: non-degeneracy is a property of the
metric. For the polar chart, $J = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\varphi & -r\sin\varphi \\ \sin\varphi & r\cos\varphi
\end{pmatrix}$ has $\det J = r$, so $\det g_{\text{polar}} = r^2 \cdot 1$, as @prp-polar-metric states; the zero at
$r = 0$ belongs to the chart, not to the metric.
:::
::::

Since a metric is non-degenerate, its eigenvalues at a point are all non-zero, and what remains to classify is how
many are positive and how many negative. The signature of @sec-linear-algebra records exactly this, and the next
definition applies it pointwise and names the two cases that physics uses.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-signature-metric}
#### Signature of a metric

The **signature** of a metric is the signature (@def-signature) of the symmetric bilinear form $g_p$ on each
tangent space; it is the same at every point of a connected manifold. A **Riemannian** metric is positive
definite, $g(X, X) > 0$ for $X \neq 0$; a **Lorentzian** metric has one positive sign, the time direction, and the
rest negative, written $(+, -, -, -)$ in our conventions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Riemannian metrics are the ones that measure genuine lengths, and the first example shows that every surface
sitting inside Euclidean space carries one. The argument is a single line: the Gram matrix is positive because it
computes the squared Euclidean length of an ambient velocity.

::: {#exm-signature-riemannian}
#### Riemannian examples

The Euclidean metric, the Gram matrix of any embedding into Euclidean space (its eigenvalues are positive since
$v^{\mathsf{T}}Gv = |Jv|^2 > 0$), and every internal space of these lectures: the circle, the sphere, the torus,
$SU(2)$.
:::

Lorentzian metrics are the metrics of spacetime, and the second example collects those that appear later. It also
shows how the sign convention for a product metric is fixed: the internal directions are counted negative so that
the enlarged metric still has exactly one positive direction.

::: {#exm-signature-lorentzian}
#### Lorentzian examples

The Minkowski metric and the de Sitter metric of @sec-einstein-equations; a Kaluza-Klein metric on
$M_4 \times S^1$, with the circle direction counted negative, has five eigenvalues of signs $(+, -, -, -, -)$,
Lorentzian in five dimensions.
:::

A zero eigenvalue of the component matrix does not necessarily mean a degenerate metric, because the matrix belongs
to a chart. The third example makes this distinction on the sphere, where a second chart shows the metric to be
perfectly regular at the point where the first chart gives up.

::: {#exm-metric-signature-degenerate}
#### Where a chart fails

At $\theta = 0$ the matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$ has a zero eigenvalue: the round metric is not
degenerate there, the spherical chart is. In a chart valid at the pole (stereographic) the components are
$4\,\delta_{ij}/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$ (@exr-stereographic-gram), positive definite everywhere.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Vectors of zero norm are the hallmark of indefinite signature, and in Minkowski space they form the light cone. The
first exercise finds them in the $(t, x)$ plane and asks why a Riemannian metric has none, which is the content of
positive definiteness.

::: {#exr-null-vectors}
#### Null vectors of the Minkowski metric

Find all vectors $X = a\,\partial_t + b\,\partial_x$ with $\eta(X, X) = 0$, and show that a Riemannian metric has
no non-zero null vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\eta(X, X) = a^2 - b^2 = 0$ iff $b = \pm a$: the two null lines $X = a(\partial_t \pm \partial_x)$, the light
cone of @fig-minkowski-cone. For a Riemannian metric $g(X, X) > 0$ whenever $X \neq 0$, by positive definiteness,
so $g(X, X) = 0$ forces $X = 0$.
:::

For a constant metric the signature is a matter of linear algebra, and Sage computes it from the matrix. The second
exercise runs this on the Minkowski metric, on its five-dimensional extension and on three $2 \times 2$ matrices
with cross terms, one of which turns out not to be a metric at all.

::: {#exr-signature-sage}
#### Signatures with Sage

Compute with Sage the signature of $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$, of $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -
1, -1)$ and of the matrices $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2
\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, and classify each as Riemannian, Lorentzian or
degenerate.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`QuadraticForm(QQ, 2*G).signature_vector()` returns the numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues. The
Minkowski metric has signature $(1, 3, 0)$ and the five-dimensional one $(1, 4, 0)$, both Lorentzian. The matrix
with entries $1, 2, 2, 1$ has eigenvalues $3$ and $-1$, signature $(1, 1, 0)$: a two-dimensional Lorentzian metric
in disguise. The matrix with entries $2, 1, 1, 2$ has eigenvalues $1, 3$ and is Riemannian. The last has
determinant $0$ and signature $(1, 0, 1)$: degenerate, not a metric.

{{< sage exr-signature-sage >}}
:::

The definition asserts that the signature is the same at every point of a connected manifold, and the third
exercise asks for the proof. The idea is that eigenvalues move continuously with the point and cannot cross zero
without the determinant vanishing.

::: {#exr-signature-constant}
#### The signature is constant

Prove that the number of positive eigenvalues of $g_{ij}(p)$ is the same at every point $p$ of a connected
manifold. Use that the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix depend continuously on its entries and that
$\det g_{ij} \neq 0$ everywhere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Order the eigenvalues $\lambda_1(p) \leq \dots \leq \lambda_n(p)$ of the component matrix; each is a continuous
function of $p$ within a chart, and none vanishes since their product is $\det g \neq 0$. A continuous function
that never vanishes keeps its sign on a connected set, so each $\lambda_k$ has a constant sign on the chart domain,
and the number $p$ of positive eigenvalues is constant there. On an overlap, $g' = J^{\mathsf{T}}gJ$ has the same
signature as $g$ by Sylvester's law (@def-signature), so the count agrees between charts. The set of points where
the count equals a given value is therefore open, and its complement is a union of such open sets; on a connected
manifold a set that is open and closed is everything or nothing, so the count is constant.
:::
::::

#### Line element and inverse metric

Writing a metric as a tensor with $\otimes$ signs is precise but cumbersome, and the physics literature almost
always writes it as a quadratic expression in the coordinate differentials instead. The next definition fixes what
this shorthand means, in particular how a cross term is to be read.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-line-element}
#### Line element

The **line element** $ds^2 = g_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$ is the shorthand for the metric that lists its components as
the coefficients of the quadratic expression in the coordinate differentials, with $dx^i dx^j$ standing for the
symmetrised product $\tfrac12(dx^i \otimes dx^j + dx^j \otimes dx^i)$, so that a cross term $2g_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$
($i \neq j$) counts both orderings.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the Euclidean plane again, now written in the new notation in both charts. Comparing the two
expressions is a good way to see that the line element encodes the metric, not the coordinates: the same object
appears with constant coefficients in one chart and with $r^2$ in the other.

::: {#exm-line-element-polar}
#### Polar coordinates

$ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2d\varphi^2$ encodes $g_{rr} = 1$, $g_{\varphi\varphi} = r^2$, $g_{r\varphi} = 0$; in Cartesian
coordinates the same metric reads $ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2$.
:::

The line elements of the sphere, of a sphere of any radius and of Minkowski space are the three that will be
written most often in this book. Note in the last one the signs of our convention: one plus for time, three minus
signs for space.

::: {#exm-line-element-sphere}
#### Spheres and Minkowski space

$ds^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$ is the unit sphere, $ds^2 = R^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,
d\varphi^2)$ the sphere of radius $R$, and $ds^2 = dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 - dz^2$ Minkowski space.
:::

A line element with a cross term is where the convention about symmetrised products matters, and the metric of
$SU(2)$ in Euler angles provides one. The example reads off the matrix entries from it, with the factor of $2$ in
the cross term split between the two off-diagonal positions.

::: {#exm-line-element-cross}
#### A cross term

$ds^2 = \tfrac14(d\theta^2 + d\varphi^2 + d\psi^2 + 2\cos\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi)$, the $SU(2)$ metric of
@sec-induced-metrics, encodes $g_{\varphi\varphi} = g_{\psi\psi} = \tfrac14$ and $g_{\varphi\psi} = g_{\psi\varphi}
= \tfrac14\cos\theta$: the cross term $2g_{\varphi\psi}\,d\varphi\,d\psi$ counts both orderings.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Translating between a line element and a matrix of components is the first thing to practise, and the two
directions should become automatic. The first exercise gives two line elements with cross terms, one Riemannian and
one Lorentzian, and asks for their matrices, determinants and signatures.

::: {#exr-line-element-read-off}
#### Reading off the components

Write down the component matrices of $ds^2 = 4\,du^2 + 6\,du\,dv + 9\,dv^2$ and of $ds^2 = dt^2 - 2\,dt\,dx$,
compute their determinants and decide whether each is Riemannian or Lorentzian.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The cross term $6\,du\,dv = 2g_{uv}\,du\,dv$ gives $g_{uv} = 3$, so the first matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\
3 & 9 \end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $36 - 9 = 27 > 0$; both eigenvalues are positive (their sum is $13$ and
their product $27$), so it is Riemannian. The second has $g_{tt} = 1$, $g_{tx} = -1$, $g_{xx} = 0$, matrix
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $-1 < 0$: one eigenvalue of each sign,
Lorentzian, although no $dx^2$ term appears. Both are inverted in @exr-inverse-metric-check.
:::

A change of coordinates is carried out on a line element by substituting the differentials, and SageManifolds does
the substitution as a pullback. The second exercise applies this to the parabolic coordinates of the plane, where
the result is a conformal multiple of the flat line element, like the stereographic chart of the sphere.

::: {#exr-line-element-parabolic}
#### Parabolic coordinates

With SageManifolds, find the line element of the Euclidean plane in the parabolic coordinates $x = uv$, $y =
\tfrac12(u^2 - v^2)$, and its determinant and inverse. Is the chart orthogonal?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dx = v\,du + u\,dv$ and $dy = u\,du - v\,dv$ give $dx^2 + dy^2 = (u^2 + v^2)(du^2 + dv^2)$: the chart is
orthogonal and even conformal, with $\det g = (u^2 + v^2)^2$ and inverse $(u^2 + v^2)^{-1}\delta^{ij}$. The chart
degenerates at the origin only.

{{< sage exr-line-element-parabolic >}}
:::

Why is the symmetrised product the right reading of $dx^i dx^j$, and why does the line element determine the metric
at all? The third exercise asks for both facts, and for the substitution rule that underlies the previous exercise;
together they justify the use of $ds^2$ as a complete description of a metric.

::: {#exr-line-element-symmetrised}
#### The line element determines the metric

Show that $ds^2$ evaluated on a vector $X$, that is, $g_{ij}X^iX^j$, is $g(X, X)$; that two symmetric tensors
with the same values $g(X, X)$ for all $X$ are equal; and that an antisymmetric part of $g_{ij}$ would be invisible
in $ds^2$. Then show that substituting $dx^i = (\partial x^i/\partial x'^k)\,dx'^k$ into $ds^2$ reproduces the
transformation law of @exr-metric-chart-independence.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $dx^i(X) = X^i$, the symmetrised product gives $\tfrac12(X^iX^j + X^jX^i) = X^iX^j$, so $ds^2(X) =
g_{ij}X^iX^j = g(X, X)$. For symmetric $g$ the polarisation identity $g(X, Y) = \tfrac12\big(g(X + Y, X + Y) -
g(X, X) - g(Y, Y)\big)$ recovers all values from the diagonal ones, so the quadratic form determines the tensor. An
antisymmetric $a_{ij}$ gives $a_{ij}X^iX^j = 0$ for every $X$, so it contributes nothing to $ds^2$; this is why the
line element can only describe symmetric tensors, and why $dx^i dx^j$ must be read symmetrically. Substituting the
differentials, $g_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j = g_{ij}\,\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^k}\dfrac{\partial x^j}{\partial x'^l}
\,dx'^k dx'^l$, whose coefficients are $g'_{kl}$ as in @exr-metric-chart-independence.
:::
::::

Non-degeneracy was built into the definition of a metric for one purpose: to be able to invert it. The inverse
matrix of the components is itself a tensor, of the opposite type, and it is the tool that converts one-forms back
into vectors in the next section.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-inverse-metric}
#### Inverse metric

The **inverse metric** $g^{ij}$ is the inverse matrix of $g_{ij}$, $g^{ik}g_{kj} = \delta^i_j$; it exists because
the metric is non-degenerate, and it is a symmetric tensor field of type $(2, 0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** In Lean, `(metricAt g x)⁻¹` is the matrix inverse, equal to the inverse metric wherever the determinant is
non-zero.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Most metrics met in practice are diagonal in a well-chosen chart, and then the inverse is immediate. The first
example lists the inverses of the three running metrics, including the Minkowski metric, which is its own inverse
because its entries are $\pm 1$.

::: {#exm-inverse-diagonal}
#### Diagonal metrics

For a diagonal metric the inverse is the diagonal of reciprocals: $g^{rr} = 1$, $g^{\varphi\varphi} = 1/r^2$ for
polar coordinates (@prp-polar-metric), $g^{\theta\theta} = 1$, $g^{\varphi\varphi} = 1/\sin^2\theta$ for the sphere
(@prp-sphere-metric), $\eta^{\mu\nu} = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$ for Minkowski space.
:::

With a cross term the inverse mixes components, and the $2 \times 2$ formula shows how: the off-diagonal entries
change sign and everything is divided by the determinant. The example inverts the lower block of the $SU(2)$ metric
and notes where the inverse ceases to exist.

::: {#exm-inverse-cross}
#### A $2 \times 2$ block with a cross term

For $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \cos\theta \\ \cos\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ the inverse is $\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\cos\theta \\ -\cos\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, which exists where $\sin\theta \neq 0$; this is
the lower block of the $SU(2)$ inverse metric of @sec-induced-metrics.
:::

A metric proportional to the identity is the simplest non-constant case, and its inverse is the reciprocal
multiple. The example records this for the stereographic chart of the sphere, whose conformal factor will matter
when angles are discussed.

::: {#exm-inverse-conformal}
#### A conformal metric

For $g_{ij} = \Omega^2 \delta_{ij}$ (the stereographic metric, with $\Omega = 2/(1 + u^2 + v^2)$) the inverse is
$g^{ij} = \Omega^{-2}\delta^{ij}$: the inverse of a multiple of the identity is the reciprocal multiple.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The $2 \times 2$ block of the $SU(2)$ metric comes with a factor $\tfrac14$, and the first exercise asks for the
inverse with that factor included. Besides the formula, the point is to locate the values of $\theta$ where the
inverse does not exist and to interpret them.

::: {#exr-cross-term-inverse}
#### Inverting a cross term

Invert $g = \tfrac14\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \cos\theta \\ \cos\theta & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and state where the inverse
exists.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\det g = \tfrac{1}{16}(1 - \cos^2\theta) = \tfrac{1}{16}\sin^2\theta$, and $g^{-1} = \frac{4}{\sin^2\theta}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\cos\theta \\ -\cos\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, which exists for $\sin\theta \neq 0$; at
$\theta = 0$ the two rows coincide and the Euler chart of $SU(2)$ degenerates.
:::

SageManifolds inverts a metric with `.inverse()` and checks the result by multiplying back. The second exercise
applies it to the two constant metrics of @exr-line-element-read-off, the Lorentzian one being instructive because
its inverse has a non-zero $xx$ entry although the metric itself has none.

::: {#exr-inverse-metric-check}
#### Inverses with SageManifolds

Declare $ds^2 = 4\,du^2 + 6\,du\,dv + 9\,dv^2$ and $ds^2 = dt^2 - 2\,dt\,dx$ as metrics in SageManifolds, compute
their inverses, and check $g^{ik}g_{kj} = \delta^i_j$ for both.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the first, $g^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{27}\begin{pmatrix} 9 & -3 \\ -3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$. For the second, $g^{-1} =
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$: the inverse acquires an $xx$ entry. The eigenvalues
$(1 \pm \sqrt5)/2$ of the second matrix have opposite signs, confirming the Lorentzian signature.

{{< sage exr-inverse-metric-check >}}
:::

The definition claims that the inverse components form a tensor of type $(2, 0)$, and the third exercise proves it
from the transformation law of $g_{ij}$. It also establishes the block-diagonal rule that makes product metrics
easy to invert in @sec-induced-metrics.

::: {#exr-inverse-metric-tensor}
#### The inverse metric is a $(2, 0)$ tensor

From $g' = J^{\mathsf{T}} g J$ under a change of chart (@exr-metric-chart-independence), derive the transformation
law of $g^{-1}$ and identify it as that of a tensor of type $(2, 0)$. Show also that the inverse of a block-diagonal
metric is block diagonal, with the inverses of the blocks.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Inverting $g' = J^{\mathsf{T}} g J$ gives $g'^{-1} = J^{-1}g^{-1}J^{-\mathsf{T}}$, that is, $g'^{kl} =
\dfrac{\partial x'^k}{\partial x^i}\dfrac{\partial x'^l}{\partial x^j}\,g^{ij}$, since $J^{-1} = \partial x'/\partial
x$. Two factors of the inverse Jacobian is the transformation law of a tensor with two upper indices
(@def-tensor-field). For $g = \begin{pmatrix} A & 0 \\ 0 & B \end{pmatrix}$ with $A$, $B$ invertible,
$\begin{pmatrix} A^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & B^{-1} \end{pmatrix}$ multiplies $g$ to the identity block by block, and the
inverse is unique.
:::
::::

The three propositions that close this section record the component matrices, determinants and inverses of the
polar, Minkowski and round metrics. They are the facts every later computation on these spaces relies on, and each
is followed by examples that evaluate the matrices and extend them, and by exercises that redo the computation in
other charts.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-polar-metric}
#### The polar metric

The polar metric has matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1, r^2)$, determinant $r^2$ and inverse $\operatorname{diag}(1,
1/r^2)$ for $r \neq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.polar_metricAt`, `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.polar_det` and
`KaluzaKlein.Geometry.polar_invMetric`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.polar_invMetric >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1, r^2)$ is best understood by evaluating it at a few radii and comparing with the
unit ellipses of @fig-metric-ellipses. The first example does this and watches the determinant shrink to zero at
the origin, where the polar chart fails.

::: {#exm-polar-metric-points}
#### The polar metric at a few points

At $r = 1$ the matrix is the identity and the unit vectors of $g$ form a round circle in the chart plane; at
$r = 2$ it is $\operatorname{diag}(1, 4)$, with $|\partial_\varphi| = 2$, so the unit vectors form an ellipse of
$\varphi$ semi-axis $\tfrac12$; at $r = \tfrac12$ the ellipse is elongated along $\varphi$. The determinant $r^2$
tends to zero as $r \to 0$, where the rays of @fig-polar-grid meet and the chart stops being one-to-one.
:::

The inverse in the proposition carries the hypothesis $r \neq 0$, and it is worth seeing exactly what goes wrong
without it. The second example checks the inverse by multiplication and shows that at the origin no inverse exists.

::: {#exm-polar-metric-lean}
#### The inverse and the origin

For $r \neq 0$, $\operatorname{diag}(1, r^2)\operatorname{diag}(1, 1/r^2) = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1)$, so the
proposition's inverse is correct, and the determinant $r^2$ is the product of the diagonal entries. At $r = 0$ the
matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(1, 0)$: for every matrix $M$ the product $M\operatorname{diag}(1, 0)$ has zero second
column, so it is never the identity and no inverse exists. Geometrically, $|\partial_\varphi| = r$ vanishes at the
origin, where all values of $\varphi$ label the same point, and the inverse component $1/r^2$, the squared length of
$d\varphi$, blows up.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `polar_metricAt` states that `metricAt polar x` is the matrix `!![1, 0; 0, x 0 ^ 2]`, that is,
$\operatorname{diag}(1, r^2)$ with $r =$ `x 0` (a chart point is `x : Fin 2 → ℝ`); `polar_det` states that its
determinant is `x 0 ^ 2`; and `polar_invMetric` states, under the hypothesis `x 0 ≠ 0`, that the matrix inverse is
`!![1, 0; 0, 1 / x 0 ^ 2]`. The hypothesis is needed because Lean's `⁻¹` of a singular matrix is the zero matrix.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The polar metric reappears inside every metric that has an axis of symmetry. The third example embeds it in
cylindrical coordinates on $\mathbb{R}^3$, where a constant $dz^2$ is added and the determinant and inverse change
in the obvious way; spherical coordinates follow in @exr-polar-metric-spherical.

::: {#exm-polar-metric-cylindrical}
#### Cylindrical coordinates

In cylindrical coordinates $(r, \varphi, z)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ the Euclidean metric is $ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2d\varphi^2 +
dz^2$, with matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1, r^2, 1)$, determinant $r^2$ and inverse $\operatorname{diag}(1, 1/r^2,
1)$ for $r \neq 0$: the polar block of @prp-polar-metric sits inside, and the $z$-direction contributes a constant
block. The volume element $r\,dr\,d\varphi\,dz$ is the familiar one of cylindrical integrals.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Spherical coordinates on $\mathbb{R}^3$ are the next case after cylindrical ones, and the metric is again diagonal
with two non-constant entries. The first exercise obtains it with SageManifolds by pulling back the Cartesian
metric, and compares with the cylindrical result.

::: {#exr-polar-metric-spherical}
#### Spherical coordinates with SageManifolds

Compute with SageManifolds the Euclidean metric of $\mathbb{R}^3$ in spherical coordinates $(\rho, \theta,
\varphi)$, with $x = \rho\sin\theta\cos\varphi$, $y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\varphi$, $z = \rho\cos\theta$, and in
cylindrical coordinates; give the matrices, determinants and inverses.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$ds^2 = d\rho^2 + \rho^2d\theta^2 + \rho^2\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$, with $\det g = \rho^4\sin^2\theta$ and inverse
$\operatorname{diag}(1, \rho^{-2}, \rho^{-2}\sin^{-2}\theta)$; the angular block is $\rho^2$ times the round metric
of @prp-sphere-metric. In cylindrical coordinates $ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2d\varphi^2 + dz^2$ with $\det g = r^2$.

{{< sage exr-polar-metric-spherical >}}
:::

Replacing the radius by its logarithm turns the polar metric into a conformal one, a trick that is used whenever
the plane minus the origin is to be compared with a cylinder. The second exercise carries out the substitution by
hand and recomputes the determinant and the inverse.

::: {#exr-log-polar}
#### Log-polar coordinates

With $r = e^u$, write the polar metric in the coordinates $(u, \varphi)$, and find its determinant and inverse.
Which metric on the cylinder $\mathbb{R} \times S^1$ does it become after dividing by $e^{2u}$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dr = e^u\,du$, so $ds^2 = e^{2u}du^2 + e^{2u}d\varphi^2 = e^{2u}(du^2 + d\varphi^2)$: a conformal multiple of
the flat metric of the cylinder, with $\det g = e^{4u}$ and inverse $e^{-2u}\delta^{ij}$, both defined for every
$u$, since $r = e^u$ never reaches the origin. Dividing by $e^{2u}$ gives $du^2 + d\varphi^2$, the flat cylinder
metric of @exm-flat-circle: the punctured plane and the cylinder are conformally equivalent.
:::

The three metrics of this section are all diagonal, and the pattern of their determinants and inverses is general.
The third exercise formulates it for an arbitrary orthogonal chart in terms of scale factors, and asks the reader to
identify those factors in the examples met so far.

::: {#exr-orthogonal-chart-scale-factors}
#### Orthogonal charts and scale factors

For a metric that is diagonal in a chart, $ds^2 = h_1^2\,(dx^1)^2 + \dots + h_n^2\,(dx^n)^2$ with positive
functions $h_i$ (the **scale factors**), give the determinant, the volume element and the inverse, and identify the
scale factors of the polar, cylindrical, spherical and round metrics.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\det g = h_1^2\cdots h_n^2$, so $\sqrt{\det g} = h_1\cdots h_n$, and $g^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(h_1^{-2}, \dots,
h_n^{-2})$, since the inverse of a diagonal matrix is the diagonal of reciprocals. Polar: $(h_r, h_\varphi) = (1,
r)$; cylindrical: $(1, r, 1)$; spherical: $(1, \rho, \rho\sin\theta)$; round metric: $(1, \sin\theta)$. The scale
factor $h_i$ is the length $|\partial_i|$ of the coordinate vector, and the volume element is the product of these
lengths, the volume of the coordinate box.
:::
::::

The Minkowski metric is constant, so its determinant is a single number, but that number carries information: its
sign records the signature. The proposition fixes it, and the examples that follow explain what the sign means,
why isometries preserve it, and what changes in five dimensions.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-minkowski-metric}
#### The Minkowski metric is non-degenerate

$\det \eta = -1$ for $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$ as a metric on $\mathbb{R}^4$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.minkowski_det`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of its entries, and here three of them are $-1$. The first
example draws the general conclusion that the sign of the determinant counts the negative directions, which is why
the volume element of a four-dimensional spacetime is written with $-g$ under the root.

::: {#exm-minkowski-det-sign}
#### The sign of the determinant

$\det\eta = 1 \cdot (-1)^3 = -1$: the determinant of a diagonal metric is the product of its entries, and its sign
is $(-1)^q$ with $q$ the number of negative eigenvalues. For a Lorentzian metric in four dimensions $q = 3$ and
$\det g < 0$ in every chart (@exr-minkowski-det-sign), so the volume element is $\sqrt{-\det g}\,d^4x$, written
$\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$ in @sec-lengths-volumes.
:::

A Lorentz transformation preserves $\eta$, and taking the determinant of the defining relation constrains its own
determinant. The second example does this for a boost and verifies the result on the explicit matrix, where the
hyperbolic identity $\cosh^2 - \sinh^2 = 1$ appears.

::: {#exm-minkowski-boost}
#### Boosts preserve the determinant

A Lorentz transformation satisfies $\Lambda^{\mathsf{T}}\eta\Lambda = \eta$; taking determinants gives
$(\det\Lambda)^2\det\eta = \det\eta$, so $\det\Lambda = \pm1$. For the boost $\Lambda = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh\xi &
\sinh\xi \\ \sinh\xi & \cosh\xi \end{pmatrix}$ in the $(t, x)$ plane, $\det\Lambda = \cosh^2\xi - \sinh^2\xi = 1$,
and the transformed metric $\Lambda^{\mathsf{T}}\eta\Lambda$ is $\eta$ again (@exr-isometry-boost), with the same
determinant $-1$.
:::

Adding a fifth, spacelike direction flips the sign of the determinant, and this has a notational consequence that
is easy to overlook. The third example computes the determinant of the five-dimensional product metric and explains
why its volume element must be written with an absolute value.

::: {#exm-minkowski-five}
#### Five dimensions

The metric $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1, -R^2)$ on $M_4 \times S^1$ has determinant $(-1)^3 \cdot (-R^2) =
R^2 > 0$: with four negative directions the determinant is positive, and $\sqrt{-g}$ would be imaginary. The
volume element in odd Lorentzian dimension is $\sqrt{|\det g|}\,d^5x = R\,d^4x\,d\varphi$, which is why the general
definition of @sec-lengths-volumes carries an absolute value.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage computes determinants and signatures of constant metrics exactly, and symbolic entries are no obstacle. The
first exercise checks the determinant of $\eta$, of a boosted $\eta$ and of the five-dimensional product metric
with a symbolic radius, together with their signatures.

::: {#exr-minkowski-det-sage}
#### Determinants with Sage

Compute with Sage $\det\eta$ and the signature of $\eta$; check that $\Lambda^{\mathsf{T}}\eta\Lambda = \eta$ for
the boost of @exm-minkowski-boost and that $\det\Lambda = 1$; and compute the determinant and signature of
$\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1, -R^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\det\eta = -1$ with signature $(1, 3, 0)$; the boosted metric is $\eta$ exactly, after simplifying
$\cosh^2\xi - \sinh^2\xi$, and $\det\Lambda = 1$; the five-dimensional metric has determinant $R^2$, so
$\sqrt{|\det g|} = R$, and signature $(1, 4, 0)$.

{{< sage exr-minkowski-det-sage >}}
:::

Non-degeneracy does not require any diagonal entry to be non-zero, as the light-cone coordinates of Minkowski
space show. The second exercise rewrites the two-dimensional Minkowski metric in them, finds a matrix with zeros on
the diagonal, and inverts it.

::: {#exr-minkowski-lightcone}
#### Light-cone coordinates

With $u = t - x$ and $v = t + x$, write $ds^2 = dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 - dz^2$ in the coordinates $(u, v, y, z)$, give
the component matrix, its determinant and its inverse, and check that the determinant agrees with
@exr-metric-chart-independence.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dt^2 - dx^2 = (dt - dx)(dt + dx) = du\,dv$, so $ds^2 = du\,dv - dy^2 - dz^2$ with $g_{uv} = g_{vu} = \tfrac12$,
$g_{uu} = g_{vv} = 0$. The matrix is block diagonal with blocks $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & \tfrac12 \\ \tfrac12 & 0
\end{pmatrix}$ and $-1_2$, so $\det g = (-\tfrac14)(1) = -\tfrac14$ and the inverse has blocks $\begin{pmatrix} 0 &
2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $-1_2$. The Jacobian of $(t, x) \mapsto (u, v)$ has determinant $2$, so $J =
\partial(t, x)/\partial(u, v)$ has $\det J = \tfrac12$ and $\det g' = \tfrac14 \cdot (-1) = -\tfrac14$, as found.
The coordinate vectors $\partial_u$ and $\partial_v$ are null: the light cone of @exr-null-vectors has become the
coordinate axes.
:::

The sign of the determinant was read off from the diagonal form of $\eta$, but the claim that it is the same in
every chart needs the transformation law. The third exercise proves the general statement for a metric of any
signature and spells out the consequence for even and odd dimensions.

::: {#exr-minkowski-det-sign}
#### The sign of the determinant in any chart

Show that a metric of signature $(p, q)$ has $\operatorname{sign}\det g = (-1)^q$ in every chart. Deduce that a
Lorentzian metric has negative determinant in even dimension and positive determinant in odd dimension, and
identify the two cases in @exm-minkowski-det-sign and @exm-minkowski-five.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At a point, Sylvester's law (@def-signature) gives a basis in which the matrix of $g$ is $\operatorname{diag}(1,
\dots, 1, -1, \dots, -1)$ with $q$ entries $-1$, so in that basis $\det g = (-1)^q$. Any other basis is related by
an invertible $P$, and $\det(P^{\mathsf{T}}gP) = (\det P)^2\det g$ has the same sign. A Lorentzian metric has
$q = n - 1$: $\det g < 0$ for $n$ even ($n = 4$: $\det\eta = -1$) and $\det g > 0$ for $n$ odd ($n = 5$: $R^2$).
This is why $\sqrt{-g}$ is correct in four dimensions and $\sqrt{|g|}$ is needed in general.
:::
::::

The round metric is the first non-constant metric of the section, and its inverse requires a hypothesis, since the
component $\sin^2\theta$ vanishes at the poles. The proposition records the three facts, and the examples evaluate
the matrix at a few latitudes, rescale it and compare it with the stereographic chart, where no hypothesis is
needed.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sphere-metric}
#### The round metric, its determinant and its inverse

On the chart domain $\sin\theta \neq 0$ the metric matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$, its determinant
is $\sin^2\theta$, and its inverse is $\operatorname{diag}(1, 1/\sin^2\theta)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.sphere_metricAt`, `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.sphere_det` and
`KaluzaKlein.Geometry.sphere_invMetric`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.sphere_invMetric >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The component $\sin^2\theta$ is $1$ on the equator and shrinks towards the poles, and the inverse component grows
correspondingly. The first example evaluates both at two latitudes and relates them to the lengths of the parallels,
which is how the picture of @fig-metric-ellipses arises.

::: {#exm-sphere-metric-latitudes}
#### The round metric at a few latitudes

On the equator $\theta = \pi/2$ the matrix is the identity: $\partial_\theta$ and $\partial_\varphi$ are
orthonormal there, and the parallel has length $2\pi$. At $\theta = \pi/6$ the matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(1,
\tfrac14)$ with inverse $\operatorname{diag}(1, 4)$: $|\partial_\varphi| = \tfrac12$ and the parallel has length
$\pi$. The determinant $\sin^2\theta$ takes the values $1$ and $\tfrac14$, and tends to zero at the poles, where
the chart degenerates (@exm-metric-signature-degenerate).
:::

Multiplying a metric by a constant is the simplest modification, and it changes determinant and inverse by fixed
powers of that constant. The second example applies this to the sphere of radius $R$, where the rule also predicts
how areas and lengths scale.

::: {#exm-sphere-metric-radius}
#### The sphere of radius $R$

The metric $R^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$ has matrix $R^2\operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$,
determinant $R^4\sin^2\theta$ and inverse $R^{-2}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1/\sin^2\theta)$. In general, multiplying
an $n$-dimensional metric by a constant $\lambda$ multiplies its determinant by $\lambda^n$ and its inverse by
$\lambda^{-1}$; here $\sqrt{\det g} = R^2\sin\theta$ gives the area $4\pi R^2$ of @exr-sphere-area.
:::

The hypothesis $\sin\theta \neq 0$ in the proposition belongs to the chart, not to the metric, and the cleanest
way to see this is to compute the same metric in a chart that covers a pole. The third example quotes the
stereographic components and checks that their determinant and inverse are regular there.

::: {#exm-sphere-metric-stereographic}
#### The same metric in the stereographic chart

In the stereographic chart the round metric is $g_{ij} = 4\,\delta_{ij}/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$
(@exr-stereographic-gram), with determinant $16/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^4$ and inverse $\tfrac14(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2\,
\delta^{ij}$, both finite and non-zero at every point of the chart, including $u = v = 0$, the pole the spherical
chart misses. The two component matrices describe the same tensor field, and @exr-sphere-metric-stereographic
computes the second one.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The stereographic components are quoted in @exm-sphere-metric-stereographic; the first exercise derives them. The
derivation is a pullback of the Euclidean metric through the inverse stereographic projection, which SageManifolds
performs and simplifies, and it confirms the regularity at the pole.

::: {#exr-sphere-metric-stereographic}
#### The round metric in the stereographic chart

With the inverse stereographic projection $E(u, v) = \big(2u, 2v, u^2 + v^2 - 1\big)/(1 + u^2 + v^2)$, compute
with SageManifolds the induced metric, its determinant and its inverse, and evaluate the matrix at $u = v = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The induced metric is $4\,\delta_{ij}/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$, with determinant $16/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^4$ and inverse
$\tfrac14(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2\delta^{ij}$; at $u = v = 0$, the image of which is the pole $(0, 0, -1)$, the matrix is
$\operatorname{diag}(4, 4)$ with determinant $16$: perfectly regular.

{{< sage exr-sphere-metric-stereographic >}}
:::

Another chart of the sphere uses the height $z = \cos\theta$ in place of the colatitude, and in it the round metric
has a remarkable determinant. The second exercise asks for the transformation by hand and for the interpretation
of the result, a theorem of Archimedes about the area of a zone.

::: {#exr-sphere-metric-height-chart}
#### The height chart

Write the round metric in the coordinates $(z, \varphi)$ with $z = \cos\theta$, and compute its determinant and
inverse. What does the determinant say about the area of the zone between the heights $z_1$ and $z_2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dz = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sin^2\theta = 1 - z^2$, so $d\theta^2 = dz^2/(1 - z^2)$ and
$$
ds^2 = \frac{dz^2}{1 - z^2} + (1 - z^2)\,d\varphi^2 , \qquad \det g = 1 , \qquad g^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(1 - z^2,
1/(1 - z^2)) .
$$
The volume element is $dz\,d\varphi$, so the area of the zone $z_1 \leq z \leq z_2$ is $2\pi(z_2 - z_1)$,
proportional to its height alone (Archimedes); for $z_1 = -1$, $z_2 = 1$ this is $4\pi$. The chart is valid for
$-1 < z < 1$, degenerating at the poles like the spherical one.
:::

The sphere is one of many surfaces obtained by rotating a profile curve about an axis, and all of them have
metrics of the same shape. The third exercise derives the general formula with SageManifolds using symbolic profile
functions and specialises it to four surfaces, two of which are flat.

::: {#exr-surface-of-revolution}
#### Surfaces of revolution

For the surface $(t, \varphi) \mapsto (f(t)\cos\varphi, f(t)\sin\varphi, h(t))$ obtained by rotating the profile
curve $(f, h)$ about the $z$-axis, compute with SageManifolds the induced metric, its determinant and its inverse
for symbolic $f$ and $h$, and specialise to the sphere ($f = \sin t$, $h = \cos t$), the cylinder ($f = R$, $h =
t$), the cone ($f = h = t$) and the torus ($f = R + r\cos t$, $h = r\sin t$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$ds^2 = (f'^2 + h'^2)\,dt^2 + f^2\,d\varphi^2$: the chart is orthogonal, $\det g = f^2(f'^2 + h'^2)$, and the
inverse is $\operatorname{diag}(1/(f'^2 + h'^2), 1/f^2)$. The sphere gives $dt^2 + \sin^2 t\,d\varphi^2$, the
cylinder $dt^2 + R^2d\varphi^2$, the cone $2\,dt^2 + t^2\,d\varphi^2$ and the torus $r^2dt^2 + (R + r\cos t)^2
d\varphi^2$ of @exm-torus-metric. Parametrising the profile by arc length, $f'^2 + h'^2 = 1$, puts every surface
of revolution in the form $dt^2 + f(t)^2d\varphi^2$.

{{< sage exr-surface-of-revolution >}}
:::
::::

### Lengths, angles and volumes {#sec-lengths-volumes}

With a metric in hand one can measure: lengths of curves, angles between vectors, areas and volumes. The metric
also converts vectors into one-forms and back, the index gymnastics that every physics formula uses. This section
defines these operations and computes them on the plane, the sphere and the torus, and closes with one proposition
on lowering and raising indices on the sphere.

#### Lengths and angles

A curve has a velocity vector at each instant, and the metric assigns that vector a norm; adding up the norms along
the curve gives its length. The definition below writes this as an integral and records the two facts that make it
geometrically meaningful, independence of the chart and of the parametrisation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-curve-length}
#### Length of a curve

The **length** of a curve $\gamma : [a, b] \to M$ with respect to a metric is
$$
L(\gamma) = \int_a^b \sqrt{|g(\dot\gamma, \dot\gamma)|}\, dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{|g_{ij}\,\dot x^i \dot x^j|}\, dt ,
$$ {#eq-curve-length}
the integral of the length of the velocity; it does not depend on the chart or on the parametrisation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first lengths to compute are those of coordinate curves in the plane, where the answer is known in advance and
serves as a check of the formula. Along a circle only $g_{\varphi\varphi} = r^2$ contributes, along a ray only
$g_{rr} = 1$.

::: {#exm-length-circle}
#### Circles in the plane

For the circle $r = r_0$, $\varphi = t$ in polar coordinates, $g(\dot\gamma, \dot\gamma) = r_0^2$ and $L =
\int_0^{2\pi} r_0\, dt = 2\pi r_0$; a ray $r = t$, $\varphi = \varphi_0$, $t \in [0, R]$, has length $R$.
:::

On the sphere the coordinate curves are parallels and meridians, and their lengths show the component
$\sin^2\theta$ at work. Two parallels that make the same full turn in $\varphi$ have different lengths, which is
the first measurable consequence of a non-constant metric component.

::: {#exm-length-sphere}
#### Parallels and meridians

On the unit sphere the parallel at colatitude $\theta_0$ has length $2\pi\sin\theta_0$ and a meridian has length
$\pi$ (@exr-sphere-area, @exr-curve-length); the parallel $\theta_0 = \pi/3$ has length $\sqrt3\,\pi$, shorter than
the equator, although both are full turns in $\varphi$.
:::

For a curve that is not a coordinate line both components enter and the integral is usually numerical. The third
example compares the length of a slanted curve with the Euclidean distance between its endpoints in the chart, and
finds the former smaller because the metric shrinks the $\varphi$ direction.

::: {#exm-length-slanted}
#### A slanted curve

The curve $(\theta, \varphi) = (\pi/2 + 0.3t, t)$, $t \in [0, 1]$, has length $\int_0^1 \sqrt{0.09 + \sin^2(\pi/2 + 0.
3t)}\, dt \approx 1.0297$, less than the chart distance $\sqrt{1.09} \approx 1.044$ because $g_{\varphi\varphi} < 1$
away from the equator (@exr-curve-length).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
SageManifolds represents curves as maps from an interval and provides their velocity fields, so @eq-curve-length
can be evaluated directly. The first exercise computes the three lengths quoted in the examples, one exactly and
two numerically.

::: {#exr-curve-length}
#### Lengths of curves on the sphere

With SageManifolds, compute the lengths of the parallel $\theta = \pi/3$, of a meridian, and of the curve
$(\pi/2 + 0.3t, t)$, $t \in [0, 1]$, from @eq-curve-length.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-curve-length >}}
:::

The torus has two families of coordinate circles of different lengths, visible in @fig-torus-embedding, and a
diagonal curve that winds once in each direction. The second exercise computes all of them from the induced metric
of @exm-torus-metric, the diagonal numerically.

::: {#exr-curve-length-torus}
#### Lengths on the torus

For the torus with $R = 2$, $r = \tfrac45$ and metric $r^2da^2 + (R + r\cos a)^2db^2$, compute with SageManifolds
the length of a tube circle $b = \text{const}$, of the outer and inner axis circles $a = 0$ and $a = \pi$, and of
the diagonal curve $a = b = t$, $t \in [0, 2\pi]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The tube circle has length $2\pi r = 8\pi/5$, the outer axis circle $2\pi(R + r) = 28\pi/5$ and the inner one
$2\pi(R - r) = 12\pi/5$. The diagonal has speed $\sqrt{r^2 + (R + r\cos t)^2}$, and numerical integration gives
$L \approx 13.605$, against the chart length $2\sqrt2\,\pi \approx 8.886$: the axis direction is stretched by the
factor $R + r\cos a > 1$.

{{< sage exr-curve-length-torus >}}
:::

The absolute value in @eq-curve-length is there for Lorentzian metrics, where the length of a timelike curve is the
proper time of the observer travelling along it. The third exercise computes it for uniform motion, obtaining time
dilation, and proves the independence of the parametrisation claimed in the definition.

::: {#exr-proper-time}
#### Proper time and reparametrisation

In Minkowski space compute the length of the worldline $(t, x) = (t, vt)$, $t \in [0, T]$, with $|v| < 1$; what
happens for $|v| = 1$? Then prove that $L(\gamma)$ is unchanged by a reparametrisation $t = t(s)$ with $dt/ds > 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dot\gamma = (1, v)$ and $\eta(\dot\gamma, \dot\gamma) = 1 - v^2 > 0$: the curve is timelike and $L = \int_0^T
\sqrt{1 - v^2}\,dt = T\sqrt{1 - v^2}$, the proper time elapsed for the moving observer, less than the coordinate
time $T$ (time dilation). For $|v| = 1$ the worldline is null and its length is zero: light experiences no proper
time. For the reparametrisation, $\tilde\gamma(s) = \gamma(t(s))$ has $\dot{\tilde\gamma} = \dot\gamma\,(dt/ds)$,
so $\sqrt{|g(\dot{\tilde\gamma}, \dot{\tilde\gamma})|} = \sqrt{|g(\dot\gamma, \dot\gamma)|}\,(dt/ds)$, and the
substitution rule gives $\int \sqrt{|g(\dot\gamma, \dot\gamma)|}\,(dt/ds)\,ds = \int \sqrt{|g(\dot\gamma,
\dot\gamma)|}\,dt$. Chart independence holds because $g(\dot\gamma, \dot\gamma)$ is a scalar.
:::
::::

Once vectors have norms, the Euclidean formula $\cos\angle = X \cdot Y/(|X||Y|)$ carries over verbatim to any
Riemannian metric. The definition below records it together with orthogonality, which makes sense for any
signature, and with the norm.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-angle}
#### Angle between vectors

For a Riemannian metric the **angle** between non-zero tangent vectors $X, Y$ at a point is given by
$\cos\angle(X, Y) = g(X, Y)/\sqrt{g(X, X)\, g(Y, Y)}$, and $X, Y$ are **orthogonal** if $g(X, Y) = 0$; the
**norm** of $X$ is $|X| = \sqrt{g(X, X)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In a chart with a diagonal metric the coordinate vectors are orthogonal, though not in general of unit length. The
first example records this for the sphere and the plane and names the property, which all the running metrics
except that of $SU(2)$ share.

::: {#exm-angle-coordinate}
#### Orthogonal coordinates

$\partial_\theta$ and $\partial_\varphi$ are orthogonal on the sphere since $g_{\theta\varphi} = 0$, with norms $1$
and $\sin\theta$; $\partial_r$ and $\partial_\varphi$ are orthogonal on the plane, with norms $1$ and $r$. A chart
with $g_{ij} = 0$ for $i \neq j$ is an **orthogonal** chart.
:::

An off-diagonal component means that two coordinate directions are not perpendicular, and the cosine of the angle
between them is the normalised cross term. The second example reads this off for $SU(2)$, where the angle varies
from a right angle to zero across the chart.

::: {#exm-angle-su2}
#### Non-orthogonal coordinates

For the $SU(2)$ metric of @sec-induced-metrics, $\cos\angle(\partial_\varphi, \partial_\psi) = \cos\theta$: the two
angle directions are orthogonal only on the "equator" $\theta = \pi/2$ and become parallel as $\theta \to 0$,
where the Euler chart degenerates.
:::

A conformal factor cancels from the formula for the cosine, so a chart in which the metric is a multiple of the
identity shows all angles correctly. The third example states this for the stereographic chart, where it is the
reason maps of the globe based on it preserve the shapes of small regions.

::: {#exm-angle-conformal}
#### Conformal charts preserve angles

In the stereographic chart $g_{ij} = \Omega^2\delta_{ij}$, so $\cos\angle(X, Y) = \delta_{ij}X^iY^j/(|X||Y|)$ is the
Euclidean angle of the chart plane: angles on the sphere equal angles in the chart, lengths do not
(@exr-stereographic-gram).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![A metric as a field of unit circles. Left: the vectors of unit polar length at points of the $(r, \varphi)$
chart plane form ellipses whose $\varphi$ semi-axis is $1/r$, since $|\partial_\varphi| = r$. Right: for the round
metric in the $(\theta, \varphi)$ chart the $\varphi$ semi-axis is $1/\sin\theta$, stretching near the poles.
Generated by `figures/metric_ellipses.sage`.](figures/metric_ellipses.svg){#fig-metric-ellipses width=90%}

{{< interactive metric_ellipses 460 >}}

Two vectors with constant components can have an angle that varies from point to point, because the metric varies.
The first exercise follows the angle between $\partial_\theta + \partial_\varphi$ and $\partial_\theta -
\partial_\varphi$ across the sphere and finds the one latitude where they are orthogonal.

::: {#exr-angle-sphere-vectors}
#### An angle that depends on the point

On the unit sphere, compute with SageManifolds the cosine of the angle between $X = \partial_\theta +
\partial_\varphi$ and $Y = \partial_\theta - \partial_\varphi$ as a function of $\theta$, evaluate it at $\theta =
\pi/6$, $\pi/4$, $\pi/2$, and find where $X$ and $Y$ are orthogonal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g(X, Y) = 1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta$ and $|X| = |Y| = \sqrt{1 + \sin^2\theta}$, so $\cos\angle(X, Y) =
\cos^2\theta/(1 + \sin^2\theta)$: $\tfrac35$ at $\pi/6$, $\tfrac13$ at $\pi/4$ and $0$ on the equator, the only
place where the two are orthogonal. In the chart plane they are orthogonal everywhere; the metric bends them.

{{< sage exr-angle-sphere-vectors >}}
:::

The cross term of the $SU(2)$ metric means $\partial_\varphi$ and $\partial_\psi$ are not orthogonal, but one can
always subtract the projection of one onto the other. The second exercise derives the angle quoted in
@exm-angle-su2 and constructs the orthogonal complement of $\partial_\psi$ in the $(\varphi, \psi)$ plane, together
with its norm.

::: {#exr-angle-su2-orthogonal}
#### Orthogonalising the Euler directions

From the $SU(2)$ metric @eq-su2-metric, derive $\cos\angle(\partial_\varphi, \partial_\psi) = \cos\theta$, find
the vector $H = \partial_\varphi + c\,\partial_\psi$ orthogonal to $\partial_\psi$, and compute $|H|$ and
$|\partial_\psi|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g(\partial_\varphi, \partial_\psi) = \tfrac14\cos\theta$ and $|\partial_\varphi| = |\partial_\psi| = \tfrac12$, so
the cosine is $\tfrac14\cos\theta/\tfrac14 = \cos\theta$. Orthogonality $g(H, \partial_\psi) = \tfrac14(\cos\theta +
c) = 0$ gives $c = -\cos\theta$, $H = \partial_\varphi - \cos\theta\,\partial_\psi$, and $|H|^2 =
\tfrac14(1 - 2\cos^2\theta + \cos^2\theta) = \tfrac14\sin^2\theta$, so $|H| = \tfrac12\sin\theta$. The vectors
$\partial_\theta$, $H$ span the directions orthogonal to the $\psi$-circles, on which the metric is
$\tfrac14(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$, a sphere of radius $\tfrac12$ (@exm-su2-metric-hopf,
@exr-raise-lower-su2).
:::

The observation about the stereographic chart is an instance of a general fact about conformal rescalings. The
third exercise proves it, with a lemma that the angle between curves is the angle between their velocities, and
draws the consequence for the Mercator chart of navigators.

::: {#exr-angle-conformal}
#### Conformal rescalings

Show that replacing $g$ by $\tilde g = \Omega^2 g$ with a positive function $\Omega$ leaves every angle unchanged
and multiplies the length of every curve by $\Omega$ along it. Deduce that in a chart with $g_{ij} =
\Omega^2\delta_{ij}$ the angle at which two curves cross on the manifold equals the angle at which their chart
images cross, and apply this to the Mercator chart $ds^2 = \operatorname{sech}^2 y\,(dx^2 + dy^2)$ of the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tilde g(X, Y)/\sqrt{\tilde g(X, X)\tilde g(Y, Y)} = \Omega^2 g(X, Y)/\big(\Omega^2\sqrt{g(X, X)g(Y, Y)}\big)$: the
factor cancels, so angles agree. For lengths, $\sqrt{\tilde g(\dot\gamma, \dot\gamma)} = \Omega\sqrt{g(\dot\gamma,
\dot\gamma)}$, so $\tilde L(\gamma) = \int \Omega(\gamma(t))\,|\dot\gamma|_g\,dt$. Two curves cross at the angle
between their velocities, and with $g = \Omega^2\delta$ that angle is the Euclidean angle between the velocities in
the chart, that is, the angle between the chart images. The Mercator metric is a multiple of $dx^2 + dy^2$, so a
course making a constant angle with the meridians $x = \text{const}$ is a straight line on the chart, which is why
it was drawn for navigation; the factor $\operatorname{sech}^2 y$ shows how much it exaggerates lengths and areas
near the poles.
:::
::::

#### Index gymnastics

A metric pairs a vector with every other vector, and fixing the first argument produces a linear functional, that
is, a one-form. The definition below names this operation and its effect on components, which is to multiply by the
metric matrix.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lowering}
#### Lowering an index

The metric converts a vector field into a one-form: $X_i = g_{ij}X^j$ **lowers** the index. The one-form
$X^\flat = X_i\,dx^i$ is $g(X, \cdot)$, the inner product with $X$, and the same contraction lowers any upper index
of a tensor field.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In Minkowski space lowering an index flips the sign of the spatial components, and this sign is responsible for the
different norms of timelike and spacelike unit vectors. The first example records the effect on a unit spacelike
vector and on the unit timelike one.

::: {#exm-lowering-minkowski}
#### Lowering with the Minkowski metric

For $X^\mu = (0, 1, 0, 0)$, $X_\mu = (0, -1, 0, 0)$: the signs of the space components flip, which is why
$\eta_{\mu\nu}X^\mu X^\nu = -1$ for a unit spacelike vector and $+1$ for the unit timelike vector $(1, 0, 0, 0)$
(@exm-nondegenerate-lowering).
:::

On the sphere lowering multiplies the $\varphi$ component by $\sin^2\theta$, so the one-form associated with the
rotation field is not $d\varphi$ but a rescaled version of it. The second example computes it and interprets the
value of the one-form on a vector as an inner product, as the definition says.

::: {#exm-lowering-rotation}
#### Lowering the rotation field

On the sphere, $\partial_\varphi$ with components $(0, 1)$ becomes the one-form $\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi$
(@prp-raise-lower, @exr-raise-index): its value on a vector $Y$ is $g(\partial_\varphi, Y) = \sin^2\theta\,Y^\varphi$.
:::

Why is the distinction between upper and lower indices invisible in elementary vector calculus? The third example
answers: with the identity metric the two sets of components coincide, and the moment one leaves Cartesian
coordinates they part ways.

::: {#exm-lowering-euclidean}
#### Euclidean space

With $g_{ij} = \delta_{ij}$ lowering does nothing to the numbers, $X_i = X^i$: this is why in Euclidean space the
position of an index is invisible, and why it matters as soon as the metric is not the identity, as in polar
coordinates, where $(\partial_\varphi)_\varphi = r^2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
SageManifolds lowers an index with `down`, and the first exercise does so in polar coordinates, where the
non-constant component $r^2$ enters. It also checks the defining property $X^\flat(Y) = g(X, Y)$ on an explicit
pair of vector fields.

::: {#exr-lowering-polar}
#### Lowering in polar coordinates

With SageManifolds and the polar metric, lower the indices of $\partial_\varphi$ and of $X = \partial_r +
\partial_\varphi$, and check that $X^\flat(Y) = g(X, Y)$ for $Y = r\,\partial_r - \partial_\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\partial_\varphi)^\flat = r^2\,d\varphi$ and $X^\flat = dr + r^2\,d\varphi$; on $Y$ both $X^\flat(Y)$ and
$g(X, Y)$ give $r - r^2$. The norm of $\partial_\varphi$ can be read from its lowered form,
$(\partial_\varphi)^\flat(\partial_\varphi) = r^2$.

{{< sage exr-lowering-polar >}}
:::

Lowering with $\eta$ is a sign flip of three components, and the invariant $X_\mu X^\mu$ then sorts vectors into
timelike, null and spacelike. The second exercise practises this on three explicit four-vectors, one of each kind.

::: {#exr-lowering-minkowski-components}
#### Lowering four-vectors

Lower the indices of $X^\mu = (3, 1, 2, 0)$, $Y^\mu = (1, 1, 0, 0)$ and $Z^\mu = (1, 2, 2, 0)$ with $\eta$, compute
$X_\mu X^\mu$, $Y_\mu Y^\mu$, $Z_\mu Z^\mu$ and classify the three vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$X_\mu = (3, -1, -2, 0)$, $Y_\mu = (1, -1, 0, 0)$, $Z_\mu = (1, -2, -2, 0)$. The invariants are $9 - 1 - 4 = 4 > 0$
(timelike), $1 - 1 = 0$ (null) and $1 - 4 - 4 = -7 < 0$ (spacelike). With the convention $(+, -, -, -)$, timelike
means positive norm, and the sign of $X_\mu X^\mu$ is independent of the frame, since boosts are isometries
(@exr-isometry-boost).
:::

The definition says that the same contraction lowers any index of any tensor, and the third exercise explores
this. Lowering an index of the identity tensor produces the metric itself, and the operation is injective because
the metric is non-degenerate.

::: {#exr-lowering-tensor}
#### Lowering indices of tensors

Lower the upper index of a tensor $T^i{}_j$ of type $(1, 1)$ to obtain $T_{ij}$, and compute the result for $T =
\delta^i{}_j$. Show that $X_iY^i = g(X, Y)$, and that $X \mapsto X^\flat$ is linear and injective.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T_{ij} = g_{ik}T^k{}_j$; for the identity, $T_{ij} = g_{ik}\delta^k{}_j = g_{ij}$: the metric is the identity with
one index lowered. $X_iY^i = g_{ij}X^jY^i = g(X, Y)$ by symmetry of $g$. Linearity is linearity of matrix
multiplication; if $X^\flat = 0$ then $g(X, Y) = 0$ for every $Y$, and non-degeneracy (@def-nondegenerate) forces
$X = 0$. So lowering is an isomorphism between tangent and cotangent space at each point, and raising is its
inverse.
:::
::::

The inverse metric undoes the lowering: multiplying the components of a one-form by $g^{ij}$ produces a vector
field. The definition below names this operation and notes that it is indeed the inverse of the previous one,
because the two matrices are inverse to each other.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-raising}
#### Raising an index

The inverse metric converts a one-form into a vector field: $\omega^i = g^{ij}\omega_j$ **raises** the index,
giving $\omega^\sharp$. Raising then lowering returns the original components, since $g^{ik}g_{kj} = \delta^i_j$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The most important one-form to raise is the differential of a function, whose raised version is the gradient
vector field. The first example computes the gradient of the height on the sphere and identifies it as a field
drawn in an earlier chapter.

::: {#exm-raising-gradient}
#### The gradient

Raising the index of $df$ gives the **gradient** vector field $(\nabla f)^i = g^{ij}\partial_j f$; on the sphere
$dZ = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$ becomes $-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ (@prp-raise-lower, @exr-raise-index), pointing
towards the north pole with norm $\sin\theta$, the field of @fig-sphere-vector-fields.
:::

Raising the coordinate one-form $d\varphi$ gives a multiple of the coordinate vector $\partial_\varphi$, but not
the vector itself, because $g^{\varphi\varphi} \neq 1$. The second example computes the factor and checks that
lowering again returns $d\varphi$.

::: {#exm-raising-dphi}
#### Raising $d\varphi$

On the sphere $d\varphi$ has components $(0, 1)$ and its raised version is $g^{\varphi\varphi}\partial_\varphi =
\sin^{-2}\theta\,\partial_\varphi$, the rotation field rescaled; lowering it again returns $d\varphi$.
:::

In polar coordinates the inverse metric contributes a factor $1/r^2$ to the $\varphi$ component of a gradient. The
third example computes two gradients there and interprets the norm of $\nabla\varphi$ as a rate of change per unit
length.

::: {#exm-raising-polar-gradient}
#### A gradient in polar coordinates

For $f = r^2$ on the plane, $df = 2r\,dr$ and $\nabla f = 2r\,\partial_r$; for $f = \varphi$, $df = d\varphi$
and $\nabla f = r^{-2}\partial_\varphi$, whose norm $1/r$ is the rate at which the angle changes per unit length
along a circle.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The SageManifolds methods `up` and `down` implement raising and lowering, and the first exercise applies them to
the two sphere computations of the examples. It also verifies that the two operations are mutually inverse on a
concrete vector field.

::: {#exr-raise-index}
#### Raising and lowering with SageManifolds

Raise the index of $dZ = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$ with the round metric using `up`, lower the index of
$\partial_\varphi$ using `down`, and check that lowering then raising returns $\partial_\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\omega^\theta = g^{\theta\theta}\omega_\theta = -\sin\theta$, $\omega^\varphi = 0$: the gradient
$-\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta$ points along meridians towards the north pole, where $Z$ increases, with norm
$\sin\theta$, and vanishes at the poles, the critical points of the height. Lowering $\partial_\varphi$ gives
$\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi$:

{{< sage exr-raise-index >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.raise_dZ >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A gradient computed in polar coordinates must agree with the Cartesian one, and the function $x = r\cos\varphi$ is
the test case: its gradient is the constant unit field $\partial_x$. The second exercise computes three polar
gradients with SageManifolds and checks this on their norms.

::: {#exr-raising-gradient-polar}
#### Gradients in polar coordinates

With SageManifolds and the polar metric, compute the gradients of $f = r^2$, $f = \varphi$ and $f = r\cos\varphi$
and their norms. Why must the last gradient have norm $1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla(r^2) = 2r\,\partial_r$ with norm $2r$; $\nabla\varphi = r^{-2}\partial_\varphi$ with norm $1/r$;
$\nabla(r\cos\varphi) = \cos\varphi\,\partial_r - (\sin\varphi/r)\,\partial_\varphi$ with norm $1$. The last
function is the Cartesian coordinate $x$, whose gradient is $\partial_x$, a unit vector; the polar expression is
$\partial_x$ written in the polar basis, and the norm is a scalar, the same in every chart.

{{< sage exr-raising-gradient-polar >}}
:::

In Minkowski space raising the index of a differential flips the spatial components, and the norm of the gradient
can have either sign or vanish. The third exercise applies this to the phase of a plane wave, where the null case
is the dispersion relation of light, and proves in general that raising inverts lowering.

::: {#exr-raising-minkowski-gradient}
#### Gradients in Minkowski space

For $f = \omega t - k_xx - k_yy - k_zz$, compute $\partial_\mu f$, raise the index with $\eta^{\mu\nu}$ and
compute $\eta(\nabla f, \nabla f)$; when is $\nabla f$ null? Then prove that $(\omega^\sharp)^\flat = \omega$ and
$(X^\flat)^\sharp = X$ for every one-form $\omega$ and vector $X$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_\mu f = (\omega, -k_x, -k_y, -k_z)$ and $(\nabla f)^\mu = \eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu f = (\omega, k_x, k_y,
k_z)$: the wave four-vector. Its norm is $\eta(\nabla f, \nabla f) = \omega^2 - |\vec k|^2$, null exactly when
$\omega = |\vec k|$, the dispersion relation of a massless wave; for a massive field $\omega^2 - |\vec k|^2 = m^2 >
0$ and the gradient is timelike. In general $((\omega^\sharp)^\flat)_i = g_{ij}g^{jk}\omega_k = \delta_i^k\omega_k =
\omega_i$ and $((X^\flat)^\sharp)^i = g^{ij}g_{jk}X^k = X^i$, both from $g^{ik}g_{kj} = \delta^i_j$.
:::
::::

#### Volumes

Integrating a function over a manifold needs a measure, and the metric supplies one through the square root of its
determinant. The definition below gives the formula, warns that the determinant is not a scalar, and explains why
the integral is nevertheless chart independent.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-volume-element}
#### Volume element

The **volume element** of a metric is $dV = \sqrt{|\det g|}\,d^nx$. The determinant is not a tensor (it picks up
the square of the Jacobian determinant under a change of chart, @exm-components-basis-independent), but the
Jacobian of the change of variables in an integral cancels it, so $\int f\,dV$ is chart independent. All the
actions of Part II are integrals against $dV$, written $\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$ in four Lorentzian dimensions, where
$\det g < 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first volume element is the factor $r$ of polar integrals, familiar from calculus as a Jacobian. The example
identifies the two: the metric determinant of a chart of Euclidean space and the Jacobian of the chart carry the
same information.

::: {#exm-volume-polar}
#### Polar coordinates

$\sqrt{\det g} = r$, so $dV = r\,dr\,d\varphi$, the Jacobian of polar coordinates (@prp-polar-metric,
@fig-jacobian-polar): the metric determinant and the Jacobian determinant of @sec-calculus are the same
information.
:::

On a curved surface there is no ambient Jacobian to appeal to, and the volume element from the metric is the
definition of area. The second example computes the area of the sphere and quotes that of the torus, both of which
are checked in the exercises.

::: {#exm-volume-sphere}
#### The sphere

$\sqrt{\det g} = \sin\theta$ and $\int_0^\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\sin\theta\,d\varphi\,d\theta = 4\pi$, the area; for radius
$R$, $4\pi R^2$ (@exr-sphere-area). The torus has area $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} r(R + r\cos a)\,da\,db =
4\pi^2 R r$ (@sec-induced-metrics).
:::

For a product metric the determinant factorises, and integrating over a compact internal space multiplies the
volume element by the internal volume. The third example records this for a circle of radius $R$, keeping track of
the sign conventions in five dimensions, and anticipates how coupling constants are rescaled in higher-dimensional
theories.

::: {#exm-volume-kk}
#### Kaluza-Klein volumes

For a product metric $ds^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - R^2 d\varphi^2$ on $M_4 \times S^1$, $\det g_5 = -R^2\det g_4$
and $\sqrt{|g_5|} = R
\sqrt{-g_4}$, and integrating over the circle multiplies the four-dimensional action by $2\pi R$: this is how the
five-dimensional Newton constant becomes the four-dimensional one in Part III.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The sphere of radius $R$ brings together everything measured so far: its volume element gives the area, its
components give the lengths of parallels and meridians, and its vanishing cross term gives the angle between the
coordinate vectors. The first exercise computes all of these with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-sphere-area}
#### Lengths and areas on the sphere of radius $R$

From the round metric scaled by $R^2$, compute the area of the sphere, the length of the parallel at colatitude
$\theta$, the length of a meridian, and the angle between $\partial_\theta$ and $\partial_\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sqrt{\det g} = R^2\sin\theta$: area $4\pi R^2$; parallel $\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{g_{\varphi\varphi}}\,d\varphi =
2\pi R\sin\theta$; meridian $\int_0^\pi\sqrt{g_{\theta\theta}}\,d\theta = \pi R$; the coordinate fields are
orthogonal. In SageManifolds:

{{< sage exr-sphere-area >}}
:::

The torus area quoted in @exm-volume-sphere is a two-line integral, and its value is the same for the embedded
torus and for the flat torus of the same radii, although the two metrics differ. The second exercise verifies both
with SageManifolds and explains the coincidence.

::: {#exr-volume-torus}
#### The area of the torus

With SageManifolds, compute the volume element and the area of the embedded torus $r^2da^2 + (R + r\cos a)^2db^2$
and of the flat torus $r^2da^2 + R^2db^2$. Why do the areas agree?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sqrt{\det g} = r(R + r\cos a)$ for the embedded torus and $rR$ for the flat one; both integrate to $4\pi^2Rr$
because $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos a\,da = 0$: the outer half of the embedded torus is stretched exactly as much as the
inner half is compressed. The flat torus with these radii is the torus of @exm-flat-torus.

{{< sage exr-volume-torus >}}
:::

The definition asserts that $\int f\,dV$ does not depend on the chart although $\det g$ does, and the third
exercise supplies the proof. Both the determinant and the coordinate volume $d^nx$ change by a Jacobian factor, and
the two factors cancel exactly.

::: {#exr-volume-chart-independence}
#### Chart independence of the volume

Show that under a change of chart with Jacobian $J = \partial x/\partial x'$, $\sqrt{|\det g'|}\,d^nx' =
\sqrt{|\det g|}\,d^nx$, so that $\int f\,dV$ is independent of the chart. Verify on the plane that $dV$ is
$dx\,dy$ in Cartesian and $r\,dr\,d\varphi$ in polar coordinates.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $g' = J^{\mathsf{T}}gJ$ (@exr-metric-chart-independence), $\sqrt{|\det g'|} = |\det J|\sqrt{|\det g|}$. The
change of variables formula of @sec-calculus gives $d^nx = |\det J|\,d^nx'$, so $\sqrt{|\det g|}\,d^nx = |
\det J|\sqrt{|\det g|}\,d^nx' = \sqrt{|\det g'|}\,d^nx'$. On the plane, $\det g = 1$ in Cartesian coordinates and
$r^2$ in polar ones, with $|\det J| = r$: $dx\,dy = r\,dr\,d\varphi$, the familiar substitution.
:::
::::

The proposition that closes this section records the two index manipulations of the examples and the general fact
that raising inverts lowering. The examples that follow read it in matrix form, use it to compute a
norm, and transfer it to the plane, and the exercises extend it to $SU(2)$ and to tensors.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-raise-lower}
#### Lowering and raising on the sphere

Lowering $\partial_\varphi = (0, 1)$ gives $(0, \sin^2\theta)$; raising $dZ = (-\sin\theta, 0)$ gives $(-\sin\theta,
0)$; and raising after lowering returns any vector, $g^{-1}(g v) = v$, where $\sin\theta \neq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.lower_dphi`, `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.raise_dZ` and `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.raise_lower`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.raise_lower >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In components, lowering an index is the product of the metric matrix with a column vector and raising it is the
product with the inverse matrix. The first example spells out the three statements in this language and explains
the role of the hypothesis on $\sin\theta$.

::: {#exm-raise-lower-matrix}
#### The statements in matrix form

With $G = \operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$, lowering is $v \mapsto Gv$ and raising is $\omega \mapsto G^{-1}
\omega$: the first statement says $G(0, 1) = (0, \sin^2\theta)$, the second $G^{-1}(-\sin\theta, 0) =
(-\sin\theta, 0)$, and the third $G^{-1}(Gv) = v$. The last two need $\sin\theta \neq 0$, because $G^{-1}$ exists
only where $\det G = \sin^2\theta \neq 0$ (@prp-sphere-metric); the first needs no hypothesis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Lowering is the matrix-vector product `mulVec` with the metric matrix and raising the same product with the
inverse matrix; `raise_dZ` and `raise_lower` carry the hypothesis `Real.sin (x 0) ≠ 0`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The norm of a one-form can be computed with the inverse metric or by raising its index and using the metric, and
