the two agree. The second example checks this on $dZ$, whose norm $\sin\theta$ is the rate at which the height
changes per unit length along a meridian.

::: {#exm-raise-lower-gradient-norm}
#### The norm of $dZ$

$g^{ij}\partial_iZ\,\partial_jZ = g^{\theta\theta}\sin^2\theta = \sin^2\theta$, and $g(\nabla Z, \nabla Z) =
g_{\theta\theta}\sin^2\theta = \sin^2\theta$ too: the norm of a one-form, computed with $g^{ij}$, equals the norm
of the vector obtained by raising its index. It is $1$ on the equator, where the height changes fastest, and $0$ at
the poles, the critical points of $Z$.
:::

The same three statements hold on the plane in polar coordinates with $\sin\theta$ replaced by $r$, and the
hypothesis becomes $r \neq 0$. The third example transfers them and notes that the inverse of the polar metric
in @prp-polar-metric is exactly what is needed.

::: {#exm-raise-lower-polar}
#### The same on the plane

With $G = \operatorname{diag}(1, r^2)$, lowering $\partial_\varphi$ gives $r^2\,d\varphi$, raising $dr = (1, 0)$
gives $\partial_r$, and $G^{-1}(Gv) = v$ for $r \neq 0$, where $G^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1/r^2)$ by
@prp-polar-metric. The norm of $d\varphi$ is $\sqrt{g^{\varphi\varphi}} = 1/r$, the norm of the gradient of
@exm-raising-polar-gradient.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
On $SU(2)$ the metric has a cross term, so lowering and raising mix the $\varphi$ and $\psi$ components, and the
inverse metric of @eq-su2-inverse is needed. The first exercise performs both operations with SageManifolds and
constructs the orthogonal complement of the $\psi$-direction met in @exr-angle-su2-orthogonal.

::: {#exr-raise-lower-su2}
#### Raising and lowering on $SU(2)$

With the $SU(2)$ metric @eq-su2-metric in SageManifolds, lower the indices of $\partial_\psi$ and $\partial_\varphi$,
raise the index of the one-form $d\psi$, check that lowering then raising returns $\partial_\psi$, and compute
$|\partial_\psi|$ and $|\partial_\varphi - \cos\theta\,\partial_\psi|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\partial_\psi)^\flat = \tfrac14(\cos\theta\,d\varphi + d\psi)$ and $(\partial_\varphi)^\flat = \tfrac14(d\varphi +
\cos\theta\,d\psi)$: each picks up the other's direction through the cross term. $(d\psi)^\sharp =
\frac{4}{\sin^2\theta}(-\cos\theta\,\partial_\varphi + \partial_\psi)$, and `down` followed by `up` returns
$\partial_\psi$. Finally $|\partial_\psi| = \tfrac12$, $g(\partial_\varphi - \cos\theta\,\partial_\psi,
\partial_\psi) = 0$ and $|\partial_\varphi - \cos\theta\,\partial_\psi| = \tfrac12\sin\theta$.

{{< sage exr-raise-lower-su2 >}}
:::

Lowering and raising preserve all the metric information, not just the components. The second exercise asks for
the two identities that express this, that the norm of a one-form equals that of its raised vector and that the
inner product of two vectors can be computed by lowering either of them.

::: {#exr-raise-lower-norms}
#### Norms and inner products are preserved

Define the norm of a one-form by $|\omega|^2 = g^{ij}\omega_i\omega_j$. Show that $|X^\flat| = |X|$ for every
vector $X$, that $g(X, Y) = X^\flat(Y) = Y^\flat(X)$, and that $X$ and $Y$ are orthogonal exactly when
$X^\flat(Y) = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|X^\flat|^2 = g^{ij}X_iX_j = g^{ij}g_{ik}X^kg_{jl}X^l = \delta^j_kX^kg_{jl}X^l = g_{kl}X^kX^l = |X|^2$.
$X^\flat(Y) = X_iY^i = g_{ij}X^jY^i = g(X, Y)$, and by symmetry this is also $g(Y, X) = Y^\flat(X)$. Orthogonality
$g(X, Y) = 0$ is therefore $X^\flat(Y) = 0$: the one-form $X^\flat$ annihilates exactly the vectors orthogonal to
$X$, which is the geometric meaning of lowering an index.
:::

The index operations apply to tensors of any type, and some of the results have names. The third exercise raises
the indices of the metric itself, lowers one index of the inverse metric, and computes the full contraction of the
two, a number that counts dimensions.

::: {#exr-raise-lower-tensor}
#### Raising indices of the metric

Show that raising both indices of $g_{ij}$ gives $g^{ij}$, that raising one index gives $g^i{}_j = \delta^i_j$,
and that $g^{ij}g_{ij} = n$. For a $(0, 2)$ tensor $T_{ij}$ define $T^i{}_j = g^{ik}T_{kj}$ and show that its trace
$T^i{}_i = g^{ij}T_{ij}$ is chart independent.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g^{ik}g^{jl}g_{kl} = g^{ik}\delta^j_k = g^{ij}$; $g^{ik}g_{kj} = \delta^i_j$ by definition of the inverse; and
$g^{ij}g_{ij} = \delta^i_i = n$, the dimension. $T^i{}_j$ is a $(1, 1)$ tensor, being a contraction of tensors, and
its trace is a full contraction, hence a scalar: in another chart $g'^{ij}T'_{ij} = (J^{-1}g^{-1}J^{-\mathsf{T}})^{ij}
(J^{\mathsf{T}}TJ)_{ij} = \operatorname{tr}(J^{-1}g^{-1}J^{-\mathsf{T}}J^{\mathsf{T}}TJ) = \operatorname{tr}(g^{-1}T)$
by cyclicity. For $T = g$ this is the dimension count again; for the Ricci tensor of @sec-riemann it is the scalar
curvature.
:::
::::

### Induced metrics and the running examples {#sec-induced-metrics}

Every surface sitting inside Euclidean space inherits a metric from it, and this is where the metrics of the
circle, the sphere, the torus and $SU(2)$ come from. This section defines induced, flat and product metrics and
isometries, and records the four running metrics with their determinants and inverses, the raw material of every
curvature computation to come.

#### Induced metrics

A curve drawn on an embedded surface is also a curve in the ambient space, and its Euclidean speed can be computed
from the surface coordinates alone. The definition below packages the result as a metric on the surface, which is
the Gram matrix of the chart seen in a new light.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-induced-metric}
#### Induced metric

An embedded surface inherits a metric from the ambient Euclidean space: for a curve on it with coordinates
$x^i(t)$ the ambient velocity is $\dot x^i\,\partial_iE$ (@exm-velocity-ambient), whose squared Euclidean length is
$G_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j$ with the Gram matrix of @def-gram. The Gram matrix of a chart of an embedded surface is
therefore a metric, the **induced metric** (or **pullback** of the Euclidean metric), Riemannian wherever the
chart is regular.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest embedded manifold is the circle, whose induced metric has a single constant component. The first
example computes it for the unit circle and for a circle of radius $R$, where the arc length coordinate makes the
component equal to one.

::: {#exm-circle-metric}
#### The circle

By @exm-circle-gram, $g_{\varphi\varphi} = 1$: $ds^2 = d\varphi^2$. A circle of radius $R$, embedded as
$\varphi \mapsto (R\cos\varphi, R\sin\varphi)$, has $ds^2 = R^2d\varphi^2 = dy^2$ with the arc length $y = R\varphi
\in (0, 2\pi R)$. The only component is constant, which will make its Christoffel symbols vanish.
:::

The sphere's Gram matrix was computed in @sec-manifolds, and here it is collected with its determinant and inverse
as the round metric that every later chapter uses. The example also reads off the lengths of the parallels, which
shrink to zero where the chart degenerates.

::: {#exm-sphere-metric}
#### The round sphere

By @prp-sphere-gram,
$$
ds^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2, \qquad
g = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sin^2\theta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
g^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/\sin^2\theta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\det g = \sin^2\theta ,
$$ {#eq-sphere-metric}
the **round metric** (@prp-sphere-metric); the inverse exists exactly on the chart domain. A sphere of radius $R$
has $ds^2 = R^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$. A parallel at colatitude $\theta$ has length
$2\pi\sin\theta$, shrinking to zero at the poles: the metric components degenerate there because the chart does.
:::

The torus is the first running example whose metric is not of the form "constant times a sphere", and its
component $g_{bb}$ depends on the position around the tube. The example records it with its determinant and area;
the figure shows the two families of coordinate circles whose lengths the components measure.

::: {#exm-torus-metric}
#### The torus

By @exr-torus-gram, $ds^2 = r^2da^2 + (R + r\cos a)^2db^2$ with $\det g = r^2(R + r\cos a)^2$
(@fig-torus-embedding). The area is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} r(R + r\cos a)\,da\,db = 4\pi^2Rr$.
:::

![The torus embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with its coordinate circles: the tube circles $b = \text{const}$ (red), all
of length $2\pi r$, and the axis circles $a = \text{const}$ (blue), of length $2\pi(R + r\cos a)$, longest on the
outer equator. Generated by `figures/torus_embedding.sage`, which also computes the induced metric with
SageManifolds.](figures/torus_embedding.png){#fig-torus-embedding width=55%}

{{< interactive torus_embedding 460 >}}

The group $SU(2)$ is a three-sphere, and its matrix entries in Euler angles provide an embedding into
$\mathbb{R}^4$ whose Gram matrix is the metric. The fourth example records this metric, the only running example
with a cross term, together with its determinant and inverse.

::: {#exm-su2-metric}
#### The bi-invariant metric of $SU(2)$

With the Euler angles of @eq-euler-angles the matrix entries of $g(\theta, \varphi, \psi)$ are (computed in
@sec-exponential)
$$
a = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,e^{-i(\varphi+\psi)/2}, \qquad b = -i\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,e^{i(\varphi-\psi)/2},
$$ {#eq-su2-euler-entries}
so the embedding $S^3 \to \mathbb{R}^4$, $(\operatorname{Re}a, \operatorname{Im}a, \operatorname{Re}b,
\operatorname{Im}b)$, is
$$
E = \left( \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\cos\tfrac{\varphi+\psi}{2},\ -\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\sin\tfrac{\varphi+\psi}{2},\
\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\sin\tfrac{\varphi-\psi}{2},\ -\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\cos\tfrac{\varphi-\psi}{2} \right).
$$ {#eq-su2-embedding}
Its Gram matrix is @eq-su2-gram (@prp-su2-gram), hence
$$
ds^2 = \tfrac14\left(d\theta^2 + d\varphi^2 + d\psi^2 + 2\cos\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi\right), \qquad
g = \frac14\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \cos\theta \\ 0 & \cos\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix},
$$ {#eq-su2-metric}
the metric of the unit three-sphere, also written $\tfrac14(\sigma^1\sigma^1 + \sigma^2\sigma^2 + \sigma^3\sigma^3)$
in terms of the left-invariant one-forms $\sigma^a$ of @sec-maurer-cartan. It is **bi-invariant**: unchanged
under left and right multiplication, as its Killing vectors show in @sec-killing. Its determinant is
$\tfrac{1}{64}\sin^2\theta$, vanishing exactly where the Euler chart degenerates, and its inverse is
$$
g^{-1} = \frac{4}{\sin^2\theta}\begin{pmatrix} \sin^2\theta & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\cos\theta \\ 0 & -\cos\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix}
$$ {#eq-su2-inverse}
(@prp-su2-metric).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The cylinder and the cone are the two surfaces of revolution a sheet of paper can be rolled into, and their induced
metrics should betray this. The first exercise computes both as pullbacks with SageManifolds and finds a vanishing
Riemann tensor for each, although the cone's components are not constant.

::: {#exr-induced-metric-cylinder-cone}
#### Cylinder and cone

With SageManifolds, pull back the Euclidean metric of $\mathbb{R}^3$ to the cylinder $(u, \varphi) \mapsto
(R\cos\varphi, R\sin\varphi, u)$ and to the cone $(s, \varphi) \mapsto (s\cos\varphi, s\sin\varphi, s)$; give the
induced metrics and their determinants, check that both Riemann tensors vanish, and compare the length of the
cone's circle $s = 1$ with its radius measured on the cone.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The cylinder has $ds^2 = du^2 + R^2d\varphi^2$, constant components, $\det g = R^2$. The cone has $ds^2 = 2\,ds^2 +
s^2d\varphi^2$, $\det g = 2s^2$, non-constant but with vanishing Riemann tensor (@sec-riemann): it is flat, as
unrolling it shows. The circle $s = 1$ has length $2\pi$ but its radius measured along the cone is $\sqrt2$, so
circumference and radius are in the ratio $\sqrt2\,\pi < 2\pi$: the unrolled cone is a sector of angle
$\sqrt2\,\pi$, and the missing angle is concentrated at the apex, where the chart and the metric degenerate.

{{< sage exr-induced-metric-cylinder-cone >}}
:::

Any surface can be written locally as a graph $z = f(x, y)$, and the induced metric of a graph has a classical
form. The second exercise derives it by hand and recovers the surface-area formula of multivariable calculus from
the volume element.

::: {#exr-induced-metric-graph}
#### The metric of a graph

For the graph $(x, y) \mapsto (x, y, f(x, y))$, compute the induced metric, its determinant and its volume element,
and show that the area of the graph over a region $D$ is $\int_D\sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2}\,dx\,dy$. Apply it to the
paraboloid $f = \tfrac12(x^2 + y^2)$ over the unit disc.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_xE = (1, 0, f_x)$ and $\partial_yE = (0, 1, f_y)$, so $ds^2 = (1 + f_x^2)\,dx^2 + 2f_xf_y\,dx\,dy + (1 +
f_y^2)\,dy^2$ with $\det g = (1 + f_x^2)(1 + f_y^2) - f_x^2f_y^2 = 1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2$ and $dV = \sqrt{1 + |\nabla
f|^2}\,dx\,dy$, the surface-area element of calculus. For the paraboloid $|\nabla f|^2 = x^2 + y^2 = \rho^2$, and
in polar coordinates the area is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\sqrt{1 + \rho^2}\,\rho\,d\rho\,d\varphi = \tfrac{2\pi}{3}
(2\sqrt2 - 1)$. The metric is Riemannian everywhere, since $\det g \geq 1$: a graph chart is always regular.
:::

The definition speaks of Euclidean ambient space, but the same construction works with any ambient metric, and the
induced metric then need not be Riemannian. The third exercise pulls back the three-dimensional Minkowski metric to
a hyperboloid and obtains the hyperbolic plane with the sign of our convention.

::: {#exr-induced-metric-hyperboloid}
#### Induced metric from a Lorentzian ambient space

Pull back $ds^2 = dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2$ to the hyperboloid $t^2 - x^2 - y^2 = 1$ parametrised by $(\psi, \varphi)
\mapsto (\cosh\psi, \sinh\psi\cos\varphi, \sinh\psi\sin\varphi)$. What is the signature of the induced metric, and
what happens for the hyperboloid $t^2 - x^2 - y^2 = -1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dt = \sinh\psi\,d\psi$, $dx = \cosh\psi\cos\varphi\,d\psi - \sinh\psi\sin\varphi\,d\varphi$, $dy =
\cosh\psi\sin\varphi\,d\psi + \sinh\psi\cos\varphi\,d\varphi$, and $dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 = (\sinh^2\psi -
\cosh^2\psi)\,d\psi^2 - \sinh^2\psi\,d\varphi^2 = -(d\psi^2 + \sinh^2\psi\,d\varphi^2)$. The induced metric is
negative definite, signature $(0, 2)$: every tangent vector to the hyperboloid is spacelike, and $-g$ is the
hyperbolic plane, the sphere's counterpart with $\sin$ replaced by $\sinh$. The one-sheeted hyperboloid $t^2 - x^2 -
y^2 = -1$, parametrised by $(\sinh\psi, \cosh\psi\cos\varphi, \cosh\psi\sin\varphi)$, gives $d\psi^2 -
\cosh^2\psi\,d\varphi^2$, Lorentzian of signature $(1, 1)$: two-dimensional de Sitter space (@sec-einstein-equations).
:::
::::

#### Flat and product metrics, isometries

Some metrics have non-constant components only because of the chart, and a better chart would make them constant.
The next definition names this situation and anticipates the curvature criterion that decides it without searching
for the chart.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-flat-metric}
#### Flat metric

A metric is **flat** if around every point there is a chart in which its components are constant; equivalently
(@sec-riemann) its Riemann tensor vanishes. Constant components are the Euclidean $\delta_{ij}$, the Minkowski
$\eta_{\mu\nu}$, or any constant symmetric matrix of the right signature.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The polar metric is the standard example of a flat metric that does not look flat. The first example points to the
Cartesian chart, where the components are constant, and draws the moral that flatness belongs to the metric.

::: {#exm-flat-plane}
#### The plane in polar coordinates

The polar metric $dr^2 + r^2 d\varphi^2$ is flat although its components are not constant: in the Cartesian chart
the same metric is $dx^2 + dy^2$. Flatness is a property of the metric, not of the chart (@exr-polar-flat).
:::

A manifold can carry a flat metric even when no embedding in three-dimensional space is flat, and the torus is the
example. The second example contrasts the flat torus with the embedded torus of @exm-torus-metric and names the
reductions in which the former is the internal space.

::: {#exm-flat-torus}
#### The flat torus

The **flat torus** is the manifold $S^1 \times S^1$ with the constant metric $ds^2 = r_1^2da^2 + r_2^2db^2$, which no
embedding in $\mathbb{R}^3$ induces: the embedded torus of @exm-torus-metric has non-constant $g_{bb}$ and is
curved. A metric is a structure on the manifold, not a property of a particular picture of it; the flat torus is
the internal space of the toroidal reductions of Part VI.
:::

The circle and the cylinder are flat and the sphere is not, and the difference is decided by curvature rather than
by inspection of components. The third example states both facts and points to the chapter where the sphere's
non-flatness is proved.

::: {#exm-flat-circle}
#### Circles and cylinders

The circle with $ds^2 = R^2 d\varphi^2$ and the cylinder with $ds^2 = R^2 d\varphi^2 + dz^2$ are flat; the sphere is
not, as @sec-riemann shows: no chart makes $d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$ constant.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The flatness of the polar metric can be shown in two ways, by exhibiting the Cartesian chart or by computing the
Riemann tensor, and the first exercise does both. The computation uses the curvature methods of SageManifolds that
@sec-riemann will explain.

::: {#exr-polar-flat}
#### The polar metric is flat

Show that the polar metric is the Euclidean metric in another chart, and check with SageManifolds that its
Riemann tensor vanishes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $x = r\cos\varphi$, $y = r\sin\varphi$, $dx^2 + dy^2 = (\cos\varphi\,dr - r\sin\varphi\,d\varphi)^2 +
(\sin\varphi\,dr + r\cos\varphi\,d\varphi)^2 = dr^2 + r^2 d\varphi^2$. The Riemann tensor (@sec-riemann) is a tensor
field; it vanishes in the Cartesian chart, where the components are constant, hence in every chart:

{{< sage exr-polar-flat >}}
:::

The cone of @exr-induced-metric-cylinder-cone was found flat by its Riemann tensor, and the definition then promises
a chart with constant components. The second exercise finds it by rescaling the polar coordinates, and discovers
that the chart covers the unrolled cone, a sector of the plane.

::: {#exr-flat-cone-chart}
#### Unrolling the cone

For the cone metric $ds^2 = 2\,ds^2 + s^2d\varphi^2$, find coordinates $(\rho, \alpha)$ in which it is the polar
metric $d\rho^2 + \rho^2d\alpha^2$, and hence coordinates in which its components are constant. What range does
$\alpha$ cover, and what does this say about the cone?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Set $\rho = \sqrt2\,s$ and $\alpha = \varphi/\sqrt2$: then $d\rho^2 = 2\,ds^2$ and $\rho^2d\alpha^2 = 2s^2
d\varphi^2/2 = s^2d\varphi^2$, so $ds^2 = d\rho^2 + \rho^2d\alpha^2$, and $X = \rho\cos\alpha$, $Y = \rho\sin\alpha$
give $dX^2 + dY^2$. As $\varphi$ runs over $(0, 2\pi)$, $\alpha$ runs over $(0, \sqrt2\,\pi)$: the cone unrolled
is a sector of the plane of angle $\sqrt2\,\pi$ with its two edges identified. The metric is flat everywhere except
at the apex $\rho = 0$, which is not covered by any chart in which the metric is smooth; the missing angle $(2 -
\sqrt2)\pi$ is the cone's angular deficit.
:::

Both tori can be handled by SageManifolds, which computes Christoffel symbols and the Riemann tensor from the
metric. The third exercise verifies that the flat torus deserves its name and that the embedded torus does not,
finding where the latter is curved positively and where negatively.

::: {#exr-flat-torus-vs-embedded}
#### Flat torus against embedded torus

With SageManifolds, check that the flat torus $r_1^2da^2 + r_2^2db^2$ has vanishing Christoffel symbols and Riemann
tensor and area $4\pi^2r_1r_2$, and that the embedded torus with $R = 2$, $r = \tfrac45$ has a non-vanishing Riemann
tensor; compute its scalar curvature and find its sign on the outer and inner equators.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Constant components make every derivative of the metric vanish, so the Christoffel symbols and the Riemann tensor
of the flat torus are zero, and its area is $4\pi^2r_1r_2$. The embedded torus has scalar curvature
$2\cos a/\big(r(R + r\cos a)\big) = \tfrac{25}{4}\cos a/(5 + 2\cos a)$: positive on the outer equator $a = 0$,
where the surface looks like a sphere, negative on the inner equator $a = \pi$, where it is saddle-shaped, and zero
on the top and bottom circles $a = \pm\pi/2$ (@sec-riemann).

{{< sage exr-flat-torus-vs-embedded >}}
:::
::::

When a manifold is a product, metrics on the two factors combine by addition, and the result has a block-diagonal
matrix with no cross terms. The definition below makes this precise and records the one property of the
determinant that makes volumes of products multiply.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-product-metric}
#### Product metric

On a product manifold $M \times N$ (@def-product-manifold) with metrics $g_M$ and $g_N$, the **product metric** is
$g = g_M + g_N$ in product charts: $ds^2 = g_{\mu\nu}(x)\,dx^\mu dx^\nu + h_{mn}(y)\,dy^m dy^n$, block diagonal with
no cross terms and each block depending only on its own coordinates. Its determinant is $\det g_M \cdot \det g_N$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The cylinder and the flat torus are products of one-dimensional metrics, and the embedded torus is not, although
its matrix is diagonal. The first example makes the distinction, which lies in the dependence of a block on the
other factor's coordinate.

::: {#exm-product-cylinder}
#### Cylinder and flat torus

$dz^2 + R^2 d\varphi^2$ on $\mathbb{R} \times S^1$ and $r_1^2 da^2 + r_2^2 db^2$ on $S^1 \times S^1$ are product
metrics of one-dimensional metrics; the embedded torus metric is not a product metric, since $g_{bb}$ depends on
$a$.
:::

The product metrics that matter most in this book are those of Minkowski space with a compact internal space, and
here the sign convention for the internal block is fixed once and for all. The second example writes down the two
ground states and notes that the departure from a product, the cross terms, is where gauge fields will come from.

::: {#exm-metric-product-kk}
#### Kaluza-Klein ground states

The ground state of Part III is the product metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - R^2 d\varphi^2$ on $M_4 \times S^1$,
and that of Parts IV and V is $\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - R^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$ on $M_4 \times
S^2$ (the internal block enters with a minus sign so that the whole metric has one positive direction, the
convention of @sec-conventions-indices); the Kaluza-Klein ansatz adds cross terms $A_\mu\,dx^\mu\,d\varphi$ to the product, and those cross terms are
the gauge fields.
:::

A block-diagonal metric whose blocks depend on the other factor's coordinates is almost a product, and the name for
it is a warped product. The third example gives the form that appears in brane-world models and notes why it falls
outside the definition.

::: {#exm-product-warped}
#### Warped products

$ds^2 = e^{2A(y)}\,\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - dy^2$ is block diagonal but the first block depends on $y$: a
**warped product**, not a product metric; the Randall-Sundrum models of Part VI are of this kind.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The determinant rule of the definition is the whole content of volume computations on product spaces. The first
exercise applies it to the two Kaluza-Klein ground states, keeping track of the signs that the minus in front of the
internal block introduces.

::: {#exr-product-metric-determinant}
#### Determinants of the ground states

Compute $\det g$ and $\sqrt{|\det g|}$ for $\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - R^2d\varphi^2$ on $M_4 \times S^1$ and
for $\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - R^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$ on $M_4 \times S^2$, and the volume of
the internal space in each case.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $M_4 \times S^1$, $\det g = \det\eta \cdot (-R^2) = R^2 > 0$ and $\sqrt{|\det g|} = R$; the internal volume is
$\int_0^{2\pi}R\,d\varphi = 2\pi R$. On $M_4 \times S^2$ the internal block is $-R^2\operatorname{diag}(1,
\sin^2\theta)$ with determinant $(-R^2)^2\sin^2\theta = R^4\sin^2\theta$, so $\det g = -R^4\sin^2\theta < 0$ (six
dimensions, five negative directions, @exr-minkowski-det-sign) and $\sqrt{|\det g|} = R^2\sin\theta$; the internal
volume is $4\pi R^2$. In both cases the sign of the internal block drops out of $\sqrt{|\det g|}$, which is the
product of the four-dimensional and internal volume elements.
:::

SageManifolds handles Lorentzian metrics in any dimension, and the second exercise uses it to invert the
five-dimensional product metric and a warped metric with an arbitrary warp function. The inverses are block
diagonal, as @exr-inverse-metric-tensor predicts, and the determinants are read off at the same time.

::: {#exr-product-metric-inverse}
#### Inverting product and warped metrics

Declare $\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - R^2d\varphi^2$ and the warped metric $e^{2A(w)}\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu -
dw^2$ as Lorentzian metrics in SageManifolds, and compute their determinants and inverses.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The product metric has determinant $R^2$ and inverse $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1, -1/R^2)$. The warped
metric has determinant $e^{8A(w)}$ and inverse $\operatorname{diag}(e^{-2A}, -e^{-2A}, -e^{-2A}, -e^{-2A}, -1)$:
block diagonal with the reciprocal blocks, the warp factor entering the inverse with the opposite power.

{{< sage exr-product-metric-inverse >}}
:::

How do signatures combine under products, and how do volumes? The third exercise asks for both rules in general,
and the sign convention for the internal block appears as the condition for the product of a Lorentzian and a
Riemannian metric to be Lorentzian.

::: {#exr-product-signature}
#### Signatures and volumes of products

Show that the product of two Riemannian metrics is Riemannian, and that $g_M - g_N$ with $g_M$ Lorentzian of
signature $(1, m - 1)$ and $g_N$ Riemannian is Lorentzian of signature $(1, m + n - 1)$, while $g_M + g_N$ would
have signature $(1 + n, m - 1)$. Show that the volume of a product of compact Riemannian manifolds is the product
of the volumes, and compute the volume of $S^2 \times S^1$ with radii $R$ and $\rho$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The eigenvalues of a block-diagonal matrix are those of the blocks together, so the signature of $g_M \pm g_N$ is
the signature of $g_M$ plus that of $\pm g_N$. Two positive definite blocks give a positive definite matrix. For
$g_M - g_N$ the internal block contributes $n$ negative eigenvalues, so the signature is $(1, m - 1 + n)$, with a
single time direction; for $g_M + g_N$ it would be $(1 + n, m - 1)$, with $n + 1$ positive directions, which is not
Lorentzian. This is why the internal block carries a minus sign in our convention. Since $\sqrt{\det g} =
\sqrt{\det g_M}\sqrt{\det g_N}$ and the integral over $M \times N$ factorises, $\operatorname{vol}(M \times N) =
\operatorname{vol}(M)\operatorname{vol}(N)$; for $S^2 \times S^1$ this is $4\pi R^2 \cdot 2\pi\rho = 8\pi^2R^2\rho$.
:::
::::

A map of a manifold to itself that preserves all lengths and angles is a symmetry of the metric, and such maps are
the subject of the last definition. In coordinates the condition compares the components at a point with the
pulled-back components at its image, and infinitesimally it leads to the Killing vector fields of a later chapter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-isometry}
#### Isometry

A diffeomorphism $F : M \to M$ is an **isometry** of $g$ if it preserves the metric, $g(dF(X), dF(Y)) = g(X, Y)$
for all tangent vectors; in coordinates, the components of $g$ at $F(p)$, transformed back with the Jacobian of
$F$, equal the components at $p$. Isometries form a group, and their infinitesimal generators are the Killing
vector fields of @sec-killing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Rotations preserve the Euclidean inner product of ambient vectors, and since the round metric is induced by that
inner product, they are its isometries. The first example makes this explicit for rotations about the axis, which
act by shifting the angle $\varphi$.

::: {#exm-isometry-rotations}
#### Rotations of the sphere

Every rotation $R \in SO(3)$ is an isometry of the round metric, since it preserves the Euclidean inner product of
ambient velocities; the rotation about the $Z$-axis by $\alpha$ is $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\theta, \varphi +
\alpha)$ in the chart, under which $d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$ is manifestly unchanged.
:::

The isometries of the Euclidean plane are the rigid motions, and a dilation, which preserves angles but not
lengths, is excluded. The second example records this and names the isometries of Minkowski space, the Lorentz
transformations checked in the exercises.

::: {#exm-isometry-translations}
#### Translations and rotations of the plane

Translations $(x, y) \mapsto (x + a, y + b)$ and rotations are isometries of the Euclidean plane; the dilation
$(x, y) \mapsto (2x, 2y)$ is a diffeomorphism that multiplies the metric by $4$, not an isometry. Lorentz
transformations are the isometries of Minkowski space.
:::

The bi-invariance of the $SU(2)$ metric means that both left and right multiplication by group elements are
isometries, which gives a six-dimensional isometry group for a three-dimensional space. The third example identifies
that group and the quotient that relates it to the group itself.

::: {#exm-isometry-su2}
#### Left and right multiplication on $SU(2)$

For the bi-invariant metric @eq-su2-metric, both $g \mapsto hg$ and $g \mapsto gh$ are isometries for every $h \in
SU(2)$; the isometry group of the round three-sphere is $SO(4) = (SU(2) \times SU(2))/\mathbb{Z}_2$, acting this way
(@sec-branching).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Checking whether a given map is an isometry is a substitution into the line element. The first exercise contrasts
two maps of the sphere, a reflection that is an isometry and a compression of the colatitude that is not, and
identifies the former as the restriction of an ambient reflection.

::: {#exr-isometry-check}
#### Checking an isometry

Show that $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\pi - \theta, \varphi)$ (reflection in the equatorial plane) is an isometry of
the round metric, and that $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\theta/2, \varphi)$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Under $\theta' = \pi - \theta$, $d\theta' = -d\theta$ and $\sin\theta' = \sin\theta$, so $d\theta'^2 +
\sin^2\theta'\,d\varphi^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$: an isometry (it is the restriction of the
reflection $Z \mapsto -Z$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$). Under $\theta' = \theta/2$, $d\theta'^2 = \tfrac14 d\theta^2$ and
$\sin^2(\theta/2) \neq \sin^2\theta$: lengths change, not an isometry.
:::

For a constant metric and a linear map the isometry condition is a matrix identity, $\Lambda^{\mathsf{T}}\eta\Lambda
= \eta$. The second exercise verifies it with Sage for a boost and a rotation, finds how a dilation fails it, and
follows a unit timelike vector through a boost.

::: {#exr-isometry-boost}
#### Lorentz transformations as isometries

With Sage, check that a boost of rapidity $\xi$ along $x$ and a rotation by $\alpha$ about $z$ satisfy
$\Lambda^{\mathsf{T}}\eta\Lambda = \eta$, compute $\Lambda^{\mathsf{T}}\eta\Lambda$ for the dilation $\Lambda =
\lambda\,1$, and find the image of $(1, 0, 0, 0)$ under the boost together with its norm.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For a linear map the pulled-back metric is $\Lambda^{\mathsf{T}}\eta\Lambda$, which equals $\eta$ for the boost
(using $\cosh^2\xi - \sinh^2\xi = 1$) and for the rotation (using $\cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\alpha = 1$), while the
dilation gives $\lambda^2\eta$. The boost sends $(1, 0, 0, 0)$ to $(\cosh\xi, \sinh\xi, 0, 0)$, a unit timelike
vector again: isometries preserve the classification of @exr-lowering-minkowski-components.

{{< sage exr-isometry-boost >}}
:::

The definition asserts that isometries form a group, and the third exercise proves it and finds the group for the
flat torus. The answer depends on whether the two radii are equal, a first instance of extra symmetry appearing at
special values of the parameters.

::: {#exr-isometry-group}
#### The isometry group

Show that the composition of two isometries and the inverse of an isometry are isometries. Find the isometries of
the flat torus $r_1^2da^2 + r_2^2db^2$ among the maps $(a, b) \mapsto (a + \alpha, b + \beta)$, $(a, b) \mapsto
(-a, b)$ and $(a, b) \mapsto (b, a)$, and say when the last one qualifies.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $F$ and $G$ preserve $g$, then $g(d(F \circ G)X, d(F \circ G)Y) = g(dF(dG\,X), dF(dG\,Y)) = g(dG\,X, dG\,Y) =
g(X, Y)$, and applying the isometry condition of $F$ to the vectors $dF^{-1}X$, $dF^{-1}Y$ shows that $F^{-1}$
preserves $g$; the identity is an isometry, so the isometries form a group. Translations $(a + \alpha, b + \beta)$
leave $da$, $db$ unchanged and are isometries for all $\alpha, \beta$, a two-dimensional group whose generators
are the Killing fields $\partial_a$, $\partial_b$ (@sec-killing). The reflection $(-a, b)$ is an isometry since
$da^2$ is unchanged. The swap $(b, a)$ sends the metric to $r_1^2db^2 + r_2^2da^2$, an isometry exactly when
$r_1 = r_2$: the square torus has the extra symmetry.
:::
::::

The $SU(2)$ metric was the only running example whose Gram matrix has a cross term, and its determinant and inverse
needed the $3 \times 3$ formulas. The proposition records all three, and the examples
evaluate the metric on the equator, compute the volume of the three-sphere and isolate the round metric hidden
inside it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-su2-metric}
#### The $SU(2)$ metric in Euler angles

The Gram matrix of @eq-su2-embedding is @eq-su2-metric; on the chart domain $\sin\theta \neq 0$ its determinant is
$\sin^2\theta/64$ and its inverse is @eq-su2-inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2_gram`, `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2_metricAt`, `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2_det` and
`KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2_invMetric`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2_invMetric >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the "equator" $\theta = \pi/2$ the cross term vanishes and the metric is a multiple of the identity, so the
three Euler directions are orthogonal there. The first example evaluates the matrix, its determinant and its
inverse at this value and reads off the lengths of the coordinate vectors.

::: {#exm-su2-metric-equator}
#### The metric on the equator

At $\theta = \pi/2$ the matrix @eq-su2-metric is $\tfrac14\,1_3$: the three coordinate vectors $\partial_\theta$,
$\partial_\varphi$, $\partial_\psi$ are orthogonal and each has length $\tfrac12$, the determinant is
$\tfrac{1}{64}$, as $\sin^2\theta/64$ predicts, and the inverse is $4 \cdot 1_3$. Away from the equator
$\partial_\varphi$ and $\partial_\psi$ keep their lengths but the angle between them closes (@exm-angle-su2).
:::

The volume element $\sqrt{\det g} = \sin\theta/8$ integrated over the Euler ranges gives the volume of $SU(2)$,
and the result is the known volume of the unit three-sphere. The second example performs the integral, in which the
range $4\pi$ of $\psi$ is essential.

::: {#exm-su2-metric-volume}
#### The volume of $SU(2)$

$\sqrt{\det g} = \tfrac18\sin\theta$, and with the Euler ranges $\theta \in (0, \pi)$, $\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)$,
$\psi \in (0, 4\pi)$ of @eq-euler-angles,
$$
\operatorname{vol}(SU(2)) = \int_0^{4\pi}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\pi \tfrac18\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi
= \tfrac18 \cdot 2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 4\pi = 2\pi^2 ,
$$
the volume of the unit three-sphere. With $\psi \in (0, 2\pi)$ the integral would give $\pi^2$, the volume of
$SO(3) = SU(2)/\mathbb{Z}_2$, half as large (@exr-su2-metric-volume).
:::

The metric restricted to the directions orthogonal to the $\psi$-circles is, up to a factor, the round metric of
the sphere. The third example isolates it using the orthogonal complement found in @exr-angle-su2-orthogonal, and
this is the first appearance of the fibration of the three-sphere over the two-sphere.

::: {#exm-su2-metric-hopf}
#### The round metric inside $SU(2)$

The vectors $\partial_\theta$ and $H = \partial_\varphi - \cos\theta\,\partial_\psi$ are orthogonal to
$\partial_\psi$ (@exr-angle-su2-orthogonal, @exr-raise-lower-su2), with $|\partial_\theta| = \tfrac12$, $|H| =
\tfrac12\sin\theta$ and $g(\partial_\theta, H) = 0$. The metric on the span of $\partial_\theta$, $H$, written in
the coordinates $(\theta, \varphi)$ that label the $\psi$-circles, is therefore $\tfrac14(d\theta^2 +
\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$: the round metric of a sphere of radius $\tfrac12$. The $\psi$-circles, each of length
$\int_0^{4\pi}\tfrac12\,d\psi = 2\pi$, are the fibres of the Hopf map $S^3 \to S^2$, and this is the first sign of
the quotient $SU(2)/U(1) = S^2$ (@sec-branching).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The $3 \times 3$ determinant of the metric is a short computation by hand, and the first exercise asks for it and
for the points where it vanishes. The expansion along the first row reduces it to the $2 \times 2$ block of
@exr-cross-term-inverse.

::: {#exr-su2-det}
#### The determinant of the $SU(2)$ metric

Compute the determinant of @eq-su2-metric by hand and find the points of the chart where it vanishes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding along the first row, $\det g = \tfrac14\cdot\det\begin{pmatrix} \tfrac14 & \tfrac14\cos\theta \\
\tfrac14\cos\theta & \tfrac14 \end{pmatrix} = \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac{1}{16}(1 - \cos^2\theta) = \tfrac{1}{64}\sin^2\theta$.
It vanishes exactly at $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \pi$, where $\partial_\varphi$ and $\pm\partial_\psi$ become parallel
and the Euler chart degenerates.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2_det`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2_det >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Gram matrix of the embedding @eq-su2-embedding can also be computed by SageManifolds as a pullback of the
Euclidean metric of $\mathbb{R}^4$. The second exercise does this, which requires the half-angle products to be
reduced to $\cos\theta$, and recovers the determinant and the inverse.

::: {#exr-su2-metric-sage}
#### The $SU(2)$ metric as a pullback

With SageManifolds, pull back the Euclidean metric of $\mathbb{R}^4$ through the embedding @eq-su2-embedding, check
that the image lies on the unit sphere, and compare the result with @eq-su2-metric; then compute the determinant
and the inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The four components of $E$ have squares summing to $\cos^2\tfrac\theta2 + \sin^2\tfrac\theta2 = 1$. The pullback
produces entries such as $\tfrac12\cos^2\tfrac\theta2 - \tfrac14$, which `trig_reduce` turns into
$\tfrac14\cos\theta$; the result is @eq-su2-metric exactly, with determinant $\sin^2\theta/64$ and inverse
@eq-su2-inverse.

{{< sage exr-su2-metric-sage >}}
:::

The volume computed in @exm-su2-metric-volume depends on the range of $\psi$, and the third exercise examines this
dependence together with the lengths of the three coordinate circles. The comparison between $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$
is a volume ratio of two, the order of the kernel of the double cover.

::: {#exr-su2-metric-volume}
#### Volumes and circles in $SU(2)$

From @eq-su2-metric compute the lengths of the coordinate curves $\varphi \mapsto (\theta, \varphi, \psi)$,
$\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)$, and $\psi \mapsto (\theta, \varphi, \psi)$, $\psi \in (0, 4\pi)$, with the other coordinates
fixed, and of the curve $\theta \mapsto (\theta, \varphi, \psi)$ for $\theta \in (0, \pi)$; which of them are closed? Then recompute the volume with $\psi \in (0, 2\pi)$ and interpret the
ratio of the two volumes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\partial_\varphi| = |\partial_\psi| = |\partial_\theta| = \tfrac12$ at every point, so the $\varphi$-curve has
length $\tfrac12 \cdot 2\pi = \pi$, the $\psi$-circle $\tfrac12 \cdot 4\pi = 2\pi$ and the $\theta$-curve
$\tfrac12 \cdot \pi = \pi/2$. The $\psi$-circles are great circles of the unit three-sphere, closed since
$e^{4\pi T_3} = 1$; the $\varphi$-curve is only half of one and does not close, since $e^{2\pi T_3} = -1$ sends $g$
to $-g$, the point $(\theta, 0, \psi + 2\pi)$ of the chart. With $\psi \in
(0, 2\pi)$ the volume is $\tfrac18 \cdot 2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 2\pi = \pi^2$, half of $2\pi^2$: the Euler angles with
$\psi \in (0, 2\pi)$ cover $SO(3)$ once, and $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ is two-to-one (@sec-lie-groups), so the volume of
$SU(2)$ is twice that of $SO(3)$ with the metric induced by the covering.
:::
::::

#### The hyperbolic plane

The plane and the round sphere look the same at every point and in every direction. A third surface with this
property, the hyperbolic plane of Lobachevsky and Bolyai, cannot be embedded as a whole in Euclidean space, but it
has a simple chart: the upper half-plane with a rescaled Euclidean metric. Since everything about it is contained in
its line element, it is introduced here as a metric, following @boskoff2024journey [Secs. 4.13 and 7.1].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-hyp-half-plane}
#### Poincaré half-plane

The **Poincaré half-plane** is the open set $\mathbb{H} = \{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : y > 0\}$ with the metric
$$
ds^2 = \frac{dx^2 + dy^2}{y^2} .
$$ {#eq-hyp-half-plane}
It is conformal to the Euclidean metric, with factor $\Omega^2 = 1/y^2$, so its angles are Euclidean angles
(@exm-angle-conformal); with the complex coordinate $z = x + iy$ it reads $ds^2 = |dz|^2/(\operatorname{Im} z)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The metric was found by Beltrami on a surface of revolution, the pseudosphere, whose profile is the tractrix. The
first example shows that a chart of the pseudosphere is a strip of the half-plane, so the two share their local
geometry [@boskoff2024journey, Ex. 4.13.2].

::: {#exm-hyp-pseudosphere}
#### The pseudosphere

The pseudosphere has the embedding $(\sin\sigma\cos\varphi, \sin\sigma\sin\varphi, \cos\sigma + \ln\tan(\sigma/2))$, $0 <
\sigma < \pi/2$, and the induced metric $\cot^2\sigma\,d\sigma^2 + \sin^2\sigma\,d\varphi^2$ (@exr-hyp-tractrix). The
substitution $x = \varphi$, $y = 1/\sin\sigma$ gives $dy = -\cos\sigma\,d\sigma/\sin^2\sigma$, so $dy^2/y^2 =
\cot^2\sigma\,d\sigma^2$ and $dx^2/y^2 = \sin^2\sigma\,d\varphi^2$: the pseudosphere is the half-strip $0 < x < 2\pi$, $y >
1$ of $\mathbb{H}$, with the edges $x = 0$ and $x = 2\pi$ glued. The rim $\sigma = \pi/2$ is the segment $y = 1$, and the
cusp at infinity is $y \to \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The factor $1/y^2$ makes lengths depend on the height. The second example measures a vertical segment, a
horizontal one and a circular arc between the same two points, and finds that the straight segment is not the
shortest of them.

::: {#exm-hyp-lengths}
#### Lengths in the half-plane

The vertical segment from $(x_0, y_1)$ to $(x_0, y_2)$ has length $\int_{y_1}^{y_2}dy/y = \ln(y_2/y_1)$, which diverges as
$y_1 \to 0$: the boundary line $y = 0$ is infinitely far from every point. The horizontal segment from $(-1, 1)$ to $(1,
1)$ has length $2$. The arc of the circle $x = \sqrt2\cos\vartheta$, $y = \sqrt2\sin\vartheta$, $\pi/4 \leq \vartheta \leq
3\pi/4$, joining the same points has $ds = d\vartheta/\sin\vartheta$ and length $\ln\tan(3\pi/8) - \ln\tan(\pi/8) = 2\ln(1 + \sqrt2)
\approx 1.763$, shorter than the straight segment: the arc bulges upwards, where the metric is smaller.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The isometries of the plane were the rigid motions, and a dilation was excluded (@exm-isometry-translations). The
third example finds that the half-plane has a different set of symmetries, in which dilations appear.

::: {#exm-hyp-isometries}
#### Isometries of the half-plane

The translations $(x, y) \mapsto (x + a, y)$, the reflection $(x, y) \mapsto (-x, y)$ and the dilations $(x, y) \mapsto
(\lambda x, \lambda y)$, $\lambda > 0$, are isometries of @eq-hyp-half-plane: the dilation multiplies $dx^2 + dy^2$ and $y^2$
by the same $\lambda^2$. So is the inversion $z \mapsto -1/z$, that is $(x, y) \mapsto (-x, y)/(x^2 + y^2)$: from
$d(-1/z) = dz/z^2$ and $\operatorname{Im}(-1/z) = y/|z|^2$ the ratio $|dz|/\operatorname{Im} z$ is unchanged. All of these
are real Möbius maps $z \mapsto (az + b)/(cz + d)$ (@exr-hyp-moebius), and their Killing fields are found in
@exr-maximal-hyperbolic.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The boundary is infinitely far away, but a region reaching it need not have infinite area. The first exercise
computes three areas with the volume element of @def-volume-element, among them the triangle bounded by three
geodesics that meet only at the boundary.

::: {#exr-hyp-areas}
#### Areas in the half-plane

Find the volume element of @eq-hyp-half-plane and compute the areas of the half-strip $|x| < 1$, $y > 1$, of the region
$|x| < 1$, $x^2 + y^2 > 1$ (an ideal triangle with vertices $-1$, $1$ and $\infty$, all on the boundary), and of the region
$|x| < 1$, $0 < y < 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sqrt{\det g} = 1/y^2$, so $dA = dx\,dy/y^2$. The half-strip has area $\int_{-1}^1\int_1^\infty dy\,dx/y^2 = 2$, although it is
unbounded. For the ideal triangle the inner integral is $\int_{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}^\infty dy/y^2 = 1/\sqrt{1 - x^2}$, and $\int_{-1}^1
dx/\sqrt{1 - x^2} = \pi$. The region near the boundary has area $\int_{-1}^1\int_\epsilon^1 dy\,dx/y^2 = 2(1 - \epsilon)/\epsilon \to
\infty$. The sides of the triangle are geodesics (@prp-hyp-geodesics) meeting at angle zero, and its area is $\pi - (0 + 0 +
0)$, the hyperbolic counterpart of the spherical excess: a geodesic triangle with angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ on the unit
sphere has area $\alpha + \beta + \gamma - \pi$, and on $\mathbb{H}$ it has area $\pi - \alpha - \beta - \gamma$.

{{< sage exr-hyp-areas >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The isometries of @exm-hyp-isometries generate a three-parameter group. The second exercise shows that it consists
of the real Möbius maps, with a computation that is short in the complex coordinate and checked in real coordinates
with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-hyp-moebius}
#### Möbius maps are isometries

Let $w = (az + b)/(cz + d)$ with real $a, b, c, d$ and $ad - bc = 1$. Show that $dw = dz/(cz + d)^2$ and $\operatorname{Im} w
= \operatorname{Im} z/|cz + d|^2$, conclude that the map sends $\mathbb{H}$ to itself isometrically, and identify the
translations, dilations and the inversion of @exm-hyp-isometries among these maps.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dw/dz = (a(cz + d) - c(az + b))/(cz + d)^2 = 1/(cz + d)^2$. Multiplying numerator and denominator by $c\bar z + d$,
$w = (ac|z|^2 + bd + adz + bc\bar z)/|cz + d|^2$, whose imaginary part is $(ad - bc)y/|cz + d|^2 = y/|cz + d|^2 > 0$. Hence
$|dw|^2/(\operatorname{Im} w)^2 = |dz|^2/y^2$. The translation by $b$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & b \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, the dilation by
$\lambda = a^2$ is $\operatorname{diag}(a, 1/a)$, and the inversion is $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. The matrices
$\pm M$ give the same map, so the group is $SL(2, \mathbb{R})/\{\pm 1\}$, of dimension three; the reflection $x \mapsto -x$
reverses orientation and is not of this form.

{{< sage exr-hyp-moebius >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The tractrix is the curve whose tangent segment, from the point of contact to the axis, has constant length. The
third exercise derives the induced metric of the pseudosphere quoted in @exm-hyp-pseudosphere and checks this
property of its profile [@boskoff2024journey, Ex. 4.3.3].

::: {#exr-hyp-tractrix}
#### The tractrix and the pseudosphere

For the embedding $E(\sigma, \varphi) = (\sin\sigma\cos\varphi, \sin\sigma\sin\varphi, \cos\sigma + \ln\tan(\sigma/2))$, $0 < \sigma <
\pi/2$, compute the coordinate velocities and the induced metric. Show that the tangent line to the profile $\varphi = 0$
at the point with parameter $\sigma$ meets the axis $X = 0$ at distance $1$ from that point.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\frac{d}{d\sigma}\ln\tan(\sigma/2) = 1/\sin\sigma$, $\partial_\sigma E = (\cos\sigma\cos\varphi, \cos\sigma\sin\varphi,
\cos^2\sigma/\sin\sigma)$ and $\partial_\varphi E = (-\sin\sigma\sin\varphi, \sin\sigma\cos\varphi, 0)$. Then $g_{\sigma\sigma} = \cos^2\sigma +
\cos^4\sigma/\sin^2\sigma = \cot^2\sigma$, $g_{\sigma\varphi} = 0$ and $g_{\varphi\varphi} = \sin^2\sigma$. On the profile the
point is $(\sin\sigma, \cos\sigma + \ln\tan(\sigma/2))$ in the $(X, Z)$ plane, with tangent direction $(\cos\sigma,
\cos^2\sigma/\sin\sigma) \propto (\sin\sigma, \cos\sigma)$, a unit vector. Moving along it by $-1$ changes $X$ by $-\sin\sigma$, which
reaches the axis: the tangent segment has length $1$, the defining property of the tractrix.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The half-plane treats the boundary point at infinity differently from the points of the real axis. A Möbius map
that sends the half-plane onto the unit disc removes this asymmetry, and the proposition records the metric it
produces, the disc model in which the rotations about the centre are manifest isometries.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-hyp-disc}
#### The Poincaré disc

The map $w = (z - i)/(z + i)$ is a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{H}$ onto the unit disc $\mathbb{D} = \{|w| < 1\}$, with
inverse $z = i(1 + w)/(1 - w)$, and it carries @eq-hyp-half-plane to
$$
ds^2 = \frac{4\,(du^2 + dv^2)}{(1 - u^2 - v^2)^2} , \qquad w = u + iv .
$$ {#eq-hyp-disc}
The unit disc with this metric, the **Poincaré disc**, is therefore isometric to the Poincaré half-plane.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The proof is two lines in the complex coordinate. From $dw/dz = 2i/(z + i)^2$, $|dw| = 2|dz|/|z + i|^2$, and $1 - |w|^2 = (|z +
i|^2 - |z - i|^2)/|z + i|^2 = 4y/|z + i|^2$, so $4|dw|^2/(1 - |w|^2)^2 = |dz|^2/y^2$; since $|z - i| < |z + i|$ exactly when
$y > 0$, the image is the disc. @boskoff2024journey [Sec. 7.1] reaches the same disc with a geometric inversion
centred on the boundary circle; since both maps are isometries onto the disc, they differ by an isometry of the disc. The first example follows a few points and a
line through the map.

::: {#exm-hyp-disc-diameter}
#### The imaginary axis becomes a diameter

The point $z = i$ goes to the centre $w = 0$, and $z = iy$ goes to $w = (y - 1)/(y + 1)$, real: the imaginary axis is
mapped onto the diameter $(-1, 1)$, with $y \to 0$ and $y \to \infty$ at its two ends, and the boundary line $y = 0$ onto the
unit circle minus $w = 1$, the image of $\infty$. The distance from $0$ to $\rho$ along the diameter is $\int_0^\rho 2\,dr/(1 - r^2)
= \ln\frac{1 + \rho}{1 - \rho}$, and with $\rho = (y - 1)/(y + 1)$ this is $\ln y$, the length of the vertical segment from $i$ to
$iy$ (@exm-hyp-lengths), as an isometry requires.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The disc metric depends only on the distance from the centre, so polar coordinates suit it. The second example
rewrites it with the geodesic distance from the centre as the radial coordinate and compares the result with the
round metric of the sphere.

::: {#exm-hyp-disc-polar}
#### Geodesic polar coordinates

In polar coordinates $u + iv = \rho e^{i\varphi}$, @eq-hyp-disc is $4(d\rho^2 + \rho^2d\varphi^2)/(1 - \rho^2)^2$. With $\rho =
\tanh(\psi/2)$, $d\rho = \tfrac12(1 - \rho^2)\,d\psi$ and $2\rho/(1 - \rho^2) = \sinh\psi$, so
$$
ds^2 = d\psi^2 + \sinh^2\psi\,d\varphi^2 ,
$$
the round metric $d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$ with $\sin$ replaced by $\sinh$. The circle of radius $\psi$ about the
centre has circumference $2\pi\sinh\psi$, which grows exponentially, against $2\pi\psi$ in the plane and $2\pi\sin\psi$ on
the unit sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The metric $d\psi^2 + \sinh^2\psi\,d\varphi^2$ already appeared on a hyperboloid in Minkowski space
(@exr-induced-metric-hyperboloid). The third example connects the two through a stereographic projection, the
counterpart of the projection that produced the sphere's conformal chart [@boskoff2024journey, Sec. 7.2].

::: {#exm-hyp-hyperboloid}
#### The hyperboloid model

On the upper sheet of $t^2 - x^2 - y^2 = 1$, parametrised by $(\cosh\psi, \sinh\psi\cos\varphi, \sinh\psi\sin\varphi)$, minus the
induced Minkowski metric is $d\psi^2 + \sinh^2\psi\,d\varphi^2$ (@exr-induced-metric-hyperboloid). The line from the point
$(-1, 0, 0)$ through a point of the sheet meets the plane $t = 0$ at $(u, v) = (x, y)/(1 + t) = \tanh(\psi/2)(\cos\varphi,
\sin\varphi)$, which is the substitution of @exm-hyp-disc-polar. The projection therefore maps the sheet isometrically
onto the Poincaré disc, just as the stereographic projection maps the unit sphere onto the plane with the metric
$4(du^2 + dv^2)/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$: the hyperbolic plane is the sphere of the Minkowski metric, with the sign in the
conformal factor reversed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The circumference of a small circle measures the curvature: it falls short of $2\pi$ times the radius on the sphere
and exceeds it on the hyperbolic plane. The first exercise makes this quantitative with the polar form of
@exm-hyp-disc-polar.

::: {#exr-hyp-circles}
#### Circles and discs

Compute the circumference $C(\psi)$ and the area $A(\psi)$ of the disc of geodesic radius $\psi$ in the metric $d\psi^2 +
\sinh^2\psi\,d\varphi^2$, and the same quantities for the unit sphere. Expand both circumferences to order $\psi^3$ and
show that $\lim_{\psi \to 0} 3(2\pi\psi - C(\psi))/(\pi\psi^3)$ is $-1$ in the first case and $1$ in the second.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$C = 2\pi\sinh\psi$ and $A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\psi\sinh\psi'\,d\psi'\,d\varphi = 2\pi(\cosh\psi - 1) = 4\pi\sinh^2(\psi/2)$; on the sphere
$C = 2\pi\sin\psi$ and $A = 2\pi(1 - \cos\psi)$, the cap of @exr-sphere-gram-cap. Since $\sinh\psi = \psi + \psi^3/6 + \dots$ and
$\sin\psi = \psi - \psi^3/6 + \dots$, $3(2\pi\psi - C)/(\pi\psi^3) \to 3(\mp 2\pi/6)/\pi = \mp 1$. The limits $-1$ and $1$ are the
Gauss curvatures of the two surfaces, computed from the Riemann tensor in @sec-riemann: the formula of Bertrand,
Diguet and Puiseux reads the curvature off the circumferences of small circles.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A rotation $w \mapsto e^{i\alpha}w$ of the disc is evidently an isometry of @eq-hyp-disc, and through the
proposition it must correspond to an isometry of the half-plane. The second exercise identifies it among the Möbius
maps of @exr-hyp-moebius and finds the inversion among the rotations.

::: {#exr-hyp-disc-rotations}
#### Rotations about $i$

Show that $w \mapsto e^{i\alpha}w$ preserves @eq-hyp-disc. Writing the map $z \mapsto w$ as the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \\ 1
& i\end{pmatrix}$ acting by $z \mapsto (az + b)/(cz + d)$, show that the corresponding map of $\mathbb{H}$ is
$$
z \mapsto \frac{\cos(\alpha/2)\,z + \sin(\alpha/2)}{-\sin(\alpha/2)\,z + \cos(\alpha/2)} ,
$$
that it fixes $i$, and that $\alpha = \pi$ gives the inversion $z \mapsto -1/z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|d(e^{i\alpha}w)| = |dw|$ and $|e^{i\alpha}w| = |w|$, so the metric is unchanged. Composition of Möbius maps is
multiplication of their matrices, and a matrix and its non-zero multiples give the same map. The rotation is
$\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\alpha/2}, e^{-i\alpha/2})$, and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \\ 1 & i\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{2i}\begin{pmatrix} i & i \\ -1 &
1\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplying out, $\frac{1}{2i}\begin{pmatrix} i & i \\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} e^{i\alpha/2} & -ie^{i\alpha/2} \\
e^{-i\alpha/2} & ie^{-i\alpha/2}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(\alpha/2) & \sin(\alpha/2) \\ -\sin(\alpha/2) & \cos(\alpha/2)\end{pmatrix}$,
a real matrix of determinant one, hence an isometry of $\mathbb{H}$ by @exr-hyp-moebius. It fixes $i$ since
$i(-\sin(\alpha/2)\,i + \cos(\alpha/2)) = \sin(\alpha/2) + i\cos(\alpha/2)$. For $\alpha = \pi$ the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 &
0\end{pmatrix}$, the map $z \mapsto -1/z$: the inversion of @exm-hyp-isometries is the half-turn about $i$. The rotations
about $i$ form the subgroup $SO(2)$ of $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$, the isotropy group of the point $i$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The computation behind the proposition can be handed to SageManifolds, which pulls a metric back along a map
between two manifolds. The third exercise does this and evaluates the distance between two points in both models.

::: {#exr-hyp-disc-sage}
#### The disc metric by pullback

With SageManifolds define $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{D}$ as manifolds with their charts, the map $w = (z - i)/(z + i)$
in real coordinates, and pull back @eq-hyp-disc. Compare the result with @eq-hyp-half-plane, and compute the distance from $i$ to $2i$ in $\mathbb{H}$ and between their images in $\mathbb{D}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In real coordinates the map is $u = (x^2 + y^2 - 1)/(x^2 + (y + 1)^2)$, $v = -2x/(x^2 + (y + 1)^2)$, and $1 - u^2 - v^2 = 4y/(x^2 +
(y + 1)^2)$. The pullback is $(dx^2 + dy^2)/y^2$. The points $i$ and $2i$ go to $0$ and
$1/3$, at distance $\int_0^{1/3}2\,dr/(1 - r^2) = \ln 2 = \int_1^2dy/y$.

{{< sage exr-hyp-disc-sage >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

#### Why these examples

The circle is the internal space of the original Kaluza-Klein theory (Part III). The sphere is the simplest
internal space with a non-abelian isometry group, $SO(3)$, and is the internal space of Parts IV and V. The group
$SU(2)$ is the isometry group itself up to a double cover, and the sphere is its quotient $S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2)
\cong SU(2)/U(1)$, the coset space of Part V; the metric @eq-su2-metric restricted to the directions transverse to
$\psi$ is, up to the factor $\tfrac14$, the round metric (@exm-su2-metric-hopf), the first sign of this quotient
structure. The torus is the internal space of the toroidal reductions of Part VI.

### Exercises {#sec-metrics-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the sections of this chapter: the torus taken through every operation defined here, the
five-dimensional product metric with a circle, and the sphere seen entirely through its stereographic chart.

The first integrative exercise starts from the embedding of the torus and ends with its area, passing through the
signature, the inverse metric, lowering and raising, an angle and a gradient. Everything is computed by SageManifolds
from the pullback of the Euclidean metric.

::: {#exr-metrics-torus-full}
#### The torus from embedding to area

For the torus with $R = 2$, $r = \tfrac45$, compute with SageManifolds the induced metric as a pullback, its
signature at the outer equator, its determinant and inverse, the one-form $(\partial_b)^\flat$, the gradient of the
height $z = r\sin a$ and its norm, the angle between $\partial_a + \partial_b$ and $\partial_b$ on the outer and
inner equators, and the area.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The pullback is $r^2da^2 + (R + r\cos a)^2db^2$, which at $a = 0$ is $\operatorname{diag}(\tfrac{16}{25},
\tfrac{196}{25})$ with signature $(2, 0, 0)$; $\det g = r^2(R + r\cos a)^2$ and $g^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(r^{-2},
(R + r\cos a)^{-2})$. Lowering gives $(\partial_b)^\flat = (R + r\cos a)^2\,db$; the gradient of the height is
$\nabla z = (\cos a/r)\,\partial_a$, with norm $|\cos a|$, largest on the equators and zero on the top and bottom
circles. The cosine of the angle is $(R + r\cos a)/\sqrt{r^2 + (R + r\cos a)^2}$: $7/\sqrt{53} \approx 0.962$ on the
outer equator and $3/\sqrt{13}$ on the inner one, where the axis circle is shorter and the diagonal direction turns
further away from it. The area is $4\pi^2Rr = 32\pi^2/5$.

{{< sage exr-metrics-torus-full >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise is the five-dimensional ground state of a circle reduction, worked by hand. Its
signature, determinant, inverse and volume element come from the first and third sections, and the norm and lowered
form of the circle direction from the second.

::: {#exr-metrics-kk-circle}
#### The product metric with a circle

For $ds^2 = \eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - R^2d\varphi^2$ on $M_4 \times S^1$, give the signature, the determinant and
$\sqrt{|\det g|}$, the inverse metric, the norm of $\partial_\varphi$ and its lowered form $(\partial_\varphi)^\flat$,
the length of a circle $x^\mu = \text{const}$, and the raised form of $d\varphi$. Which of $\partial_t$,
$\partial_\varphi$, $\partial_t + R^{-1}\partial_\varphi$ are timelike, null or spacelike?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1, -R^2)$: signature $(1, 4)$, Lorentzian in five dimensions
(@exr-product-signature), with $\det g = R^2 > 0$ and $\sqrt{|\det g|} = R$ (@exr-product-metric-determinant), and
inverse $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1, -R^{-2})$. $g(\partial_\varphi, \partial_\varphi) = -R^2$, so
$\partial_\varphi$ is spacelike with norm $R$, and $(\partial_\varphi)^\flat = -R^2\,d\varphi$; the circle has length
$\int_0^{2\pi}R\,d\varphi = 2\pi R$, and $(d\varphi)^\sharp = -R^{-2}\partial_\varphi$. $\partial_t$ has norm
$+1$, timelike; $\partial_\varphi$ is spacelike; $\partial_t + R^{-1}\partial_\varphi$ has $g(X, X) = 1 - R^2/R^2 =
0$, null: a light ray winding around the circle.
:::

The third integrative exercise redoes the sphere in the stereographic chart, where the metric is conformally flat
and regular at the pole. The conformal factor, an angle, the length of the equator and the area are all computed by
SageManifolds, the last by integrating over the whole chart plane.

::: {#exr-metrics-stereographic}
#### The sphere through the stereographic chart

With the stereographic embedding of @exr-sphere-metric-stereographic, compute with SageManifolds the conformal
factor $\Omega^2$, check that the angle between $X = (1, 2)$ and $Y = (3, -1)$ on the sphere equals the Euclidean
angle in the chart, compute the length of the curve $u^2 + v^2 = 1$, and obtain the area of the sphere by integrating
the volume element over the chart plane.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Omega^2 = 4/(1 + u^2 + v^2)^2$ with $g_{uv} = 0$ and $g_{uu} = g_{vv}$. The cosine of the angle is $\sqrt2/10$
with either metric, as @exr-angle-conformal predicts. On the unit circle $\Omega = 1$, so the curve has unit speed
and length $2\pi$: it is the equator of the sphere. The volume element is $\Omega^2\,du\,dv$, and in polar
coordinates of the chart plane $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty 4\rho/(1 + \rho^2)^2\,d\rho\,dt = 4\pi$: the whole
sphere except the north pole is covered by the chart, and the missing point has no area.

{{< sage exr-metrics-stereographic >}}
:::
::::

## Connections and curvature {#sec-connections-curvature}

A connection differentiates vector fields along vector fields; the Levi-Civita connection is the one determined by
the metric, geodesics are its straightest curves, and the Riemann, Ricci and scalar curvatures measure how parallel
transport around a loop fails to return. This chapter develops these notions in five sections. The covariant
derivative explains why derivatives of vector components are not tensors and repairs them with a connection, then
defines torsion and metric compatibility. The Levi-Civita connection derives the Christoffel symbols from a metric
and verifies them for the circle, the polar plane, the sphere and $SU(2)$. Geodesics and parallel transport turns
the connection into ordinary differential equations along curves, with the great circles of the sphere and the
holonomy of a parallel as the central examples. The Riemann tensor measures the failure of covariant derivatives to
commute and specialises to the sectional and Gauss curvatures. Ricci tensor and scalar curvature contracts it to the
quantities that enter the Einstein equations, and closes with the Gauss-Bonnet theorem for the sphere and the torus.
Every statement is followed by three examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty
with hidden solutions; the propositions are proved from the coordinate formulas and many exercises use
SageManifolds. The running
metrics (circle, plane, sphere, torus, $SU(2)$) are all positive definite, and the conventions for the Christoffel
symbols and the curvature tensors are those of @sec-conventions-curvature.

### The covariant derivative {#sec-covariant-derivative}

The partial derivative of a function is a tensor, the one-form $df$, but the partial derivative of the
components of a vector field is not: a constant arrow field has varying polar components, and the derivative of
the components measures the turning of the coordinate basis, not any change of the field. A connection supplies
the correction, and the covariant derivative it defines is a tensor. This section defines connections and
covariant derivatives in general; the one connection that a metric singles out follows in @sec-levi-civita.

#### Why derivatives of components are not tensors

Differentiating the transformation law @eq-vector-transformation of the components of a vector field gives
$$
\partial'_j X'^k = \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^j} \frac{\partial x'^k}{\partial x^l}\, \partial_i X^l
  + \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^j} \frac{\partial^2 x'^k}{\partial x^i \partial x^l}\, X^l ,
$$ {#eq-noncovariant}
and the second term, with the second derivatives of the transition map, spoils the tensor law
@eq-tensor-transformation. @fig-covariant-polar shows the effect: the constant field $\partial_x$ on the plane has
polar components $(\cos\varphi, -\sin\varphi/r)$ whose partial derivatives are not zero.

![Why partial derivatives of components are not tensors. Left: the constant field $X = \partial_x$ on the plane.
Right: its polar components $X^r = \cos\varphi$, $rX^\varphi = -\sin\varphi$ along the circle $r = 1$ vary from
point to point; the covariant derivative, computed with SageManifolds' connection, vanishes. Generated by
`figures/covariant_polar.sage`.](figures/covariant_polar.svg){#fig-covariant-polar width=90%}

#### Connections

The failure of @eq-noncovariant is a single inhomogeneous term built from second derivatives of the transition
map. A connection is the extra datum that cancels it: a set of coefficients with exactly the opposite inhomogeneous
transformation law, so that the sum of a partial derivative and a connection term is a tensor.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-connection}
#### Connection

A **connection** on a manifold is a rule $\Gamma^k_{ij}(x)$, one set of $n^3$ smooth functions per chart, called
the **connection coefficients**, that transforms under a change of chart with an inhomogeneous term cancelling
the second term of @eq-noncovariant:
$$
\Gamma'^k_{ij} = \frac{\partial x'^k}{\partial x^c}\frac{\partial x^a}{\partial x'^i}\frac{\partial x^b}{\partial x'^j}\,
\Gamma^c_{ab} + \frac{\partial x'^k}{\partial x^c}\frac{\partial^2 x^c}{\partial x'^i \partial x'^j} .
$$ {#eq-connection-transformation}
The connection coefficients are not the components of a tensor field, because of the second term.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest connection is the one that vanishes in Cartesian coordinates. Rewritten in polar coordinates it
acquires two non-zero coefficients, produced entirely by the inhomogeneous term of the transformation law, and
these are exactly the numbers needed to cancel the variation of the polar components in the figure.

::: {#exm-connection-trivial}
#### The trivial connection of $\mathbb{R}^n$

$\Gamma^k_{ij} = 0$ in Cartesian coordinates defines a connection on $\mathbb{R}^n$; in polar coordinates the
same connection has $\Gamma^r_{\varphi\varphi} = -r$ and $\Gamma^\varphi_{r\varphi} = 1/r$ by
@eq-connection-transformation (@prp-polar-christoffel), which is exactly what cancels the variation of the
components in @fig-covariant-polar.
:::

On a curved manifold there is no chart in which a natural connection vanishes, and the coefficients carry genuine
information. The sphere is the first such case; its connection coefficients are derived from the metric in the
next section and quoted here as an example of the definition.

::: {#exm-connection-sphere}
#### The connection of the sphere

The six functions $\Gamma^\theta_{\varphi\varphi} = -\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\Gamma^\varphi_{\theta\varphi} =
\cot\theta$ and four zeros of @sec-levi-civita are a connection on the sphere minus the poles; they are the only
torsion-free connection compatible with the round metric.
:::

The same structure appears in electromagnetism, where the potential plays the role of the connection coefficients.
The third example compares the two transformation laws and shows that both consist of a homogeneous part plus a
derivative term that a covariant derivative must absorb.

::: {#exm-connection-gauge}
#### Gauge connections

The electromagnetic potential $A_\mu$ of @sec-abelian-gauge is a connection of the same kind for a complex
field: it transforms with an inhomogeneous term $\partial_\mu\lambda$ under a gauge transformation, and the
covariant derivative $D_\mu\phi = \partial_\mu\phi - iqA_\mu\phi$ transforms as $\phi$ does. The analogy is
exact in the language of bundles (@sec-connections).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The trivial connection of the plane was converted to polar coordinates in the first example without showing the
computation. The first exercise asks for it, so that the reader sees the inhomogeneous term of
@eq-connection-transformation produce a non-zero coefficient out of nothing.

::: {#exr-connection-transformation}
#### The inhomogeneous term

Derive $\Gamma^r_{\varphi\varphi} = -r$ for the trivial connection of the plane from
@eq-connection-transformation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\Gamma = 0$ in Cartesian coordinates only the second term survives: $\Gamma'^r_{\varphi\varphi} =
\frac{\partial r}{\partial x^c}\frac{\partial^2 x^c}{\partial\varphi^2}$. Since $x = r\cos\varphi$, $y = r\sin\varphi$
give $\partial^2_\varphi(x, y) = -(x, y)$, and $\partial r/\partial(x, y) = (x, y)/r$, the sum is $-(x^2 +
y^2)/r = -r$.
:::

The same conversion can be done by SageManifolds, which stores a connection chart by chart and transforms it
automatically. The second exercise declares the flat connection in the Cartesian chart and reads off all its
coefficients in the polar chart.

::: {#exr-connection-polar-sage}
#### The polar coefficients with SageManifolds

Declare the Euclidean metric of the plane in Cartesian coordinates, take its connection, and display its
coefficients in the polar chart. Which coefficients are non-zero?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the Cartesian chart every coefficient vanishes. In the polar chart the non-zero ones are $\Gamma^r_{\varphi\varphi}
= -r$ and $\Gamma^\varphi_{r\varphi} = \Gamma^\varphi_{\varphi r} = 1/r$, the values of @exm-connection-trivial, all
produced by the inhomogeneous term:

{{< sage exr-connection-polar-sage >}}
:::

Connection coefficients are not tensors, but the difference of two connections is, because the inhomogeneous terms
cancel. The third exercise establishes this and draws the consequence that all connections on a manifold are
obtained from one of them by adding tensor fields.

::: {#exr-connection-difference}
#### The difference of two connections

Show from @eq-connection-transformation that the difference $D^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ij} - \tilde\Gamma^k_{ij}$ of two
connections transforms as a tensor of type $(1, 2)$. Conversely, show that a connection plus a tensor field of type
$(1, 2)$ is a connection. What is the difference between the polar connection of the plane and the connection with
$\Gamma = 0$ in the polar chart?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both connections transform with the same inhomogeneous term $\frac{\partial x'^k}{\partial x^c}\frac{\partial^2
x^c}{\partial x'^i \partial x'^j}$, which depends only on the charts; it cancels in the difference, leaving the
homogeneous law of a $(1, 2)$ tensor. Conversely, adding a tensor $D$ to $\Gamma$ adds a homogeneous term to the law,
so the inhomogeneous term is unchanged and the sum is a connection. The space of connections is therefore an affine
space modelled on the $(1, 2)$ tensor fields. In the polar chart the difference between the Levi-Civita connection
and the zero connection is the tensor with components $D^r_{\varphi\varphi} = -r$, $D^\varphi_{r\varphi} =
D^\varphi_{\varphi r} = 1/r$; in Cartesian components it is not zero either, since the zero connection of the polar
chart is not the zero connection of the Cartesian chart.
:::
::::

#### Covariant derivatives

With a connection in hand, the partial derivative of the components can be corrected. The definition adds one
connection term per index, and the cancellation of the inhomogeneous terms makes the result a tensor; the
directional version, the derivative along a vector, is the form used for curves later on.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-covariant-derivative-vector}
#### Covariant derivative of a vector field

The **covariant derivative** of a vector field $X$ with respect to a connection is
$$
\nabla_i X^k = \partial_i X^k + \Gamma^k_{ij} X^j ,
$$ {#eq-covariant-derivative}
a tensor field of type $(1, 1)$: the inhomogeneous terms of @eq-noncovariant and @eq-connection-transformation
cancel. The **covariant derivative along a vector** $Y$ is $\nabla_Y X = Y^i\nabla_i X$, a vector field.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The covariant derivative is `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.covDeriv`, defined by @eq-covariant-derivative.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example returns to the constant field of @fig-covariant-polar. Its polar components vary, but the
connection terms cancel the variation exactly, so the covariant derivative detects that the field does not change.

::: {#exm-covariant-constant}
#### A constant field in polar coordinates

For $X = \partial_x$ with polar components $(\cos\varphi, -\sin\varphi/r)$ and the polar connection, every component
of $\nabla_i X^k$ vanishes (@prp-dx-parallel): $\partial_\varphi X^r = -\sin\varphi$ is cancelled by
$\Gamma^r_{\varphi\varphi}X^\varphi = (-r)(-\sin\varphi/r)$, and similarly for the other components.
:::

The opposite situation also occurs: a field with constant components can have a non-zero covariant derivative.
On the sphere the rotation field $\partial_\varphi$ has components $(0, 1)$ everywhere, yet the connection terms
alone make its covariant derivative non-zero.

::: {#exm-covariant-rotation}
#### The rotation field on the sphere

For $X = \partial_\varphi$, components $(0, 1)$, @eq-covariant-derivative gives $\nabla_\theta X^\varphi =
\Gamma^\varphi_{\theta\varphi} = \cot\theta$ and $\nabla_\varphi X^\theta = \Gamma^\theta_{\varphi\varphi} =
-\sin\theta\cos\theta$: the rotation field is not covariantly constant, although its components are. The
combination $\nabla_i X_j + \nabla_j X_i$ vanishes, which makes it a Killing field (@sec-killing).
:::

In Cartesian coordinates of flat space all connection coefficients vanish, and the covariant derivative reduces
to the familiar partial derivative. The third example records this, which explains why the correction is never seen
in elementary vector calculus.

::: {#exm-covariant-trivial}
#### Cartesian coordinates

With $\Gamma = 0$ the covariant derivative is the partial derivative, $\nabla_i X^k = \partial_i X^k$; the
connection is invisible in Cartesian coordinates and appears as soon as the chart is curvilinear, as in polar
coordinates.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The radial and rotation fields of the plane are the two simplest fields with varying polar behaviour. The first
